title: Why did some Apollo missions carry a grenade launcher? (2019)
Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
body_text: Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs · Unemployment Labs Skip to report Unemployment Labs In this report Executive summary Main findings Our investigation Limits of the investigation Verifying the findings Conclusion Appendix 1 · Lab histories Appendix 2 · All models Sources How to cite Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs Will DePue November 12, 2026 Print / save PDF Cite this report Executive Summary Our forensic analysis of publicly released AI models finds evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models. Six models released by these companies since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match NVIDIA’s older Hopper generation. The findings suggest that several leading Chinese AI developers have begun using Blackwell to train their newest models. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, without publishing technical evidence. The evidence comes entirely from the models’ own published weights, rather than from leaks or insider accounts. We recover traces of the models’ initial values, and then search for the hardware configurations and initial configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, we also confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports, without proving, the inference that Blackwell also performed the training. Specially configured AMD hardware, which is also restricted from export to China, is the only alternative we have identified; we have excluded it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and consider it very unlikely for the other five models. Notably, our findings provide technical evidence of access to advanced computing hardware, but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. Table 1. Hardware fingerprints in successive models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group Link ↗ Lab Model Released Chip the model was started on DeepSeek DeepSeek-V3 Dec 2024 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) DeepSeek-V4-Flash Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 DeepSeek-V4-Pro Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Moonshot AI Kimi K2 Jul 2025 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K2.5 Jan 2026 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K3 Jul 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Kimi K3.1-Pro Nov 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 MiniMax MiniMax-M2.7 Apr 2026 NVIDIA Hopper MiniMax-M3 Jun 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 Ant Group Ling-3.0-flash Aug 2026 NVIDIA Hopper Ling-3.1-flash Oct 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 • Requires a U.S. license for export to China; none have been reported. A Hopper fingerprint cannot distinguish an H800 from an H100 SXM or H200; the H800 identifications above are lab disclosures, not findings of this method. Full list of models in Appendix 2 ↓ Main Findings Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match NVIDIA’s Blackwell-class B200 or B300 chips, which have 148 processor cores (called streaming multiprocessors , or SMs). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match the GB200 or GB300 chips, also Blackwell-class, which have 152 processor cores. Kimi K3.1-Pro starts from the same seed as K3, and may be a checkpoint of K3 with further post-training. Chinese labs started training on Blackwell relatively recently. DeepSeek’s models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3 (released in December 2024), and as Blackwell from DeepSeek V4 (released in April 2026). Moonshot’s models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 (January 2026) and as Blackwell from K3 (July 2026). One Moonshot model sits in between: Kimi K2.7-Code, posted six weeks before K3, is built on the Hopper-era weights but contains a small part that matches the B200 or B300. MiniMax’s models read as Hopper through M2.7 (April 2026) and as Blackwell from M3 (June 2026). Ant Group’s Ling-3.0-flash (August 2026) reads as Hopper, while its Ling-3.1-flash (October 2026) reads as Blackwell. The Hopper readings do not identify a specific chip: H800s, H100 SXMs and H200s share the same fingerprint. Not every Chinese AI lab has switched to Blackwell. The newest models we could read from Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu (GLM), Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan says its LongCat-2.0 was trained entirely on “AI ASIC superpods,” and we found no NVIDIA fingerprint in the model weights it’s released. The method gets known answers right. For 24 specific models, the developer has publicly said what hardware was used. In every case, our method agrees with the public announcement. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of its training, reads as 152 SMs, the same as Kimi K3. The matches are far stronger than chance would explain. Even unrelated numbers can appear to match when enough combinations are tried. Across the roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations in our search, the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma—a measure of how far a result stands above ordinary random variation. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Even the weakest individual test we report reaches 20 sigma. The training runs were data-center scale. From each model’s size and the amount of data it was trained on, we estimate that the two largest runs, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, each needed thousands of Blackwell GPUs for two to three months, assuming each model was trained on the hardware that initialized it. Our best estimates are about 4,500 and 3,000, the equivalent of about 11,500 and 7,500 H100s, the previous-generation NVIDIA chip in which AI training clusters are commonly sized, and about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs across the five runs (Table 2). At roughly $70,000 per GPU—the cost implied by a Wall Street Journal report that about 36,000 Blackwell chips being installed in Malaysia for ByteDance’s use would cost more than $2.5 billion—the largest of these clusters would cost roughly $200 million to $300 million, and the five together more than half a billion dollars. These figures cover only the final training runs; the labs’ total spending on export-controlled GPUs is likely in the billions of dollars. Table 2. Rough scale of each training run Link ↗ Model H100 equivalents Blackwell GPUs, best estimate Blackwell range Estimated run length DeepSeek-V4-Flash 3,500 1,500 250–5,000 50 days DeepSeek-V4-Pro 7,500 3,000 750–6,500 70 days Kimi K3 11,500 4,500 1,000–9,500 70 days MiniMax-M3 3,500 1,500 200–7,000 60 days Ling-3.1-flash 4,000 1,500 400–6,500 100 days All five 30,000 12,000 7,000–22,000 Each estimate is a run’s training compute divided by what one Blackwell GPU delivers over the run, rounded to the nearest 500. Training compute is about six operations per active parameter for every training token, plus attention. We assume the GPUs ran at about 20% of their peak speed, in line with other disclosed Blackwell training runs (25% for DeepSeek, which has reported 39% for its previous model), and for the run lengths shown, which we estimate from release timelines. H100 equivalents convert at NVIDIA’s published peak speeds: a B200 or B300 equals about 2.3 H100s, and a GB200 or GB300 about 2.5. We are not confident in these estimates. They rest on assumptions that the weights cannot confirm: how efficiently each lab used its GPUs (often called MFU), which no lab has published for these runs; how many tokens each model was trained on (DeepSeek’s counts are its own, and we take them on trust; the others are our estimates, made from the weights by a method we have not yet published); how long each run lasted, which no lab has stated; and that training stayed on the hardware that created the weights. Run length matters most, because halving it doubles the GPU count. Two disclosed runs on the same hardware show the spread: Mistral says it trained Mistral Large 4, which has the same number of active parameters as DeepSeek-V4-Pro, on 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs, while Microsoft says it trained MAI-Base-2, a model of similar size trained on more data, on 16,000 in 38 days. At that pace the two largest runs here would have needed about 8,000 to 9,000 Blackwell GPUs. The figures cover only the final training run of each model, not experiments, earlier runs or serving. Revised November 12, 2026. The first version of this report gave 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs for the largest runs and $150 million to $200 million for the largest cluster. Those figures assumed the GPUs ran as efficiently as NVIDIA’s own benchmarks, and training runs disclosed on Blackwell have been less efficient. The estimates above replace them. We have also added H100 equivalents and estimated run lengths. Our investigation A model’s weights , also called parameters , are the billions of adjustable numbers that determine how it processes information and produces answers. Training repeatedly adjusts these numbers; but before training can begin, they need initial values. In the software examined here, those values come from a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox: Philox produces seemingly random numbers in a deterministic way. The starting input for Philox is a number called the “seed.” Given the same seed and settings, Philox produces the same numbers every time. This lets engineers repeat an experiment from the same starting point. To fill billions of weights quickly, PyTorch, the software framework used in the development of most major AI models, divides the work that Philox does among many parallel workers on the GPU, called threads . (It does this through cuRAND, NVIDIA’s library for random number generation.) Each thread generates its own sequence of numbers from the seed and fills a particular set of positions. The number of threads then determines how those positions are shared out. On the NVIDIA chips examined here, a sufficiently large initialization uses the maximum of 2,048 threads for each processing unit, called a streaming multiprocessor (SM). A chip with more SMs therefore assigns the same job to more workers, changing where their numbers go. Figure 1 illustrates how this works on a simplified GPU with six SMs and eight threads per SM, giving 48 threads in total. Imagine the weights as a long row of empty boxes, wrapped into a grid to fit on the page. The first thread fills the first box, the second fills the second box, and so on through all 48 threads. The first thread’s next number then goes into box 49, its next into box 97, and so forth. The black outlines follow this one thread through the grid: the first thread fills every 48th position. The colors identify which processing unit supplies each set of values, while the brightness in the right-hand panel represents the value itself. Figure 1. How a GPU fills the weights. This simplified example uses six processing units and eight threads per unit, for 48 threads in total. The outlined cells belong to thread 0, which fills every 48th position. Real chips use many more threads, but the placement rule is the same. Link ↗ Now keep the seed fixed, but use a GPU with five SMs instead of six. In our simplified example, that means 40 threads rather than 48. The first thread generates exactly the same sequence, but now puts its numbers in boxes 1, 41, 81, and so on, rather than boxes 1, 49, 97. Figure 2 follows these numbers as their positions change. Across the grid, only 6 percent of the values match the original arrangement. The seed is right, but the worker count is wrong. That is what makes the arrangement of model weights a clue to the chip used to create it. Figure 2. The same seed on a different GPU. With five processing units and 40 threads in this toy example, thread 0 generates the same sequence but fills every 40th position instead of every 48th. Only 6% of the displayed matrix matches the original arrangement. Link ↗ Reproducing the weights therefore requires two things to be right at once. The seed must generate the right numbers, and the thread count must put them in the right places. A correct seed with the wrong thread count mostly gives the right numbers in the wrong positions; a correct thread count with the wrong seed gives different numbers. Figure 3 shows why only the correct combination recreates the original arrangement. Figure 3. Both the seed and the layout must match. The original matrix is reproduced only when the seed and thread count are both correct. Changing either one destroys most of the match. The simplified chips represent a Blackwell B300 and a Hopper H100. Faded cells differ from the published weights. The numbered cells show where thread 0’s numbers land, and the strip beneath each panel shows the numbers themselves. Link ↗ On real chips, the thread counts are much larger, but the principle is the same. In the NVIDIA configurations examined here, the Hopper H100 SXM, H200 and H800 have 132 SMs and use 270,336 threads; the Blackwell B200/B300 have 148 SMs and use 303,104 threads; and the Blackwell GB200/GB300 have 152 SMs and use 311,296 threads. Recovering the thread count therefore tells us which of these hardware groups matches the starting arrangement, although it cannot distinguish chips within a group. A Hopper match, for example, cannot tell an H800 from an H100 or H200. The question is whether enough of that arrangement survives training for us to recover it. Some weights, such as those reserved for words or symbols never encountered during training, can remain untouched and retain their starting values almost exactly. We can compare these preserved values directly with the starting values generated by a candidate seed and thread count. Figure 4 shows such a comparison: DeepSeek-V3’s preserved weights match the Hopper arrangement, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s match the Blackwell arrangement. Figure 4. Preserved starting values reveal the layout. Each dot compares a published weight with the value regenerated from the seed. A diagonal line means the values match. DeepSeek-V3 matches the Hopper layout, while V4-Flash matches the Blackwell layout. The panels show 4,096 values from four preserved rows per model. Link ↗ Even weights that training has changed can retain a faint trace of their starting values. Each final weight is its starting value plus all the adjustments made during training. If those adjustments do not completely cancel or overwhelm the starting differences, some of those differences survive. For example, two weights that begin at 0.2 and 0.8 and each increase by about 0.1 will still be ordered the same way afterward. Real adjustments vary much more, so one weight tells us little. But across hundreds of thousands of weights, we can test whether higher starting values still tend to correspond to higher final values. Figure 5 shows this weak but measurable relationship. It is a finding in these weights, not a property guaranteed to survive every training run. Figure 5. Trained weights retain a weaker trace. The left and middle panels average 745,472 weights per layer across 42 layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Under the Blackwell layout, higher starting values still predict slightly higher final values (r = 0.066, 57 sigma); under Hopper, the relationship disappears. The right panel shows the weaker evidence from individual layers. Link ↗ These surviving traces let us work backward. Suppose, in an invented example using Figure 1’s layout, seed 7 makes the first thread produce 0.2, −0.5 and 0.8. With 48 threads, those values go into positions 1, 49 and 97; with 40 threads, they go into positions 1, 41 and 81. If the published weights preserve the first pattern, we can try candidate seeds and thread counts until we recreate it. In the actual investigation, we compare thousands of values in their corresponding positions. Untouched weights can match exactly; trained weights may show only the weaker resemblance described above. In either case, we look for the combination that best reproduces the surviving pattern. We then test that combination on weights we kept out of the search. Having chosen a seed and thread count using one set of weights, we use them to predict the starting values of a different set, without changing either setting to improve the fit. A match on these previously unused weights is stronger evidence than a match confined to the weights that helped us choose the combination. Figure 6 shows the comparisons: DeepSeek-V3 matches the initialization layout of Hopper H100 SXM, H200 or H800 chips; DeepSeek-V4-Flash matches Blackwell B200/B300; and Kimi K3 matches Blackwell GB200/GB300. Figure 6. Comparing candidate layouts. Each model has one clear peak: DeepSeek-V3 at 132 SMs, V4-Flash at 148, and Kimi K3 at 152. The other tested layouts score near zero. Link ↗ In our investigations, we found patterns strongly suggestive of initialization on Blackwell chips in six models from four Chinese companies: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek, Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1-Pro from Moonshot AI, MiniMax-M3 from MiniMax, and Ling-3.1-flash from Ant Group. V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match the 148-SM layout; the other four match the 152-SM layout. These are fingerprints of the starting weights, which support, but do not by themselves prove, the use of Blackwell chips for training AI models. Limits of our investigation Notably, the forensic method we used to identify the hardware on which these models were initialized only works for certain models. It needs published weights, so closed models cannot be checked. It also needs a recognizable, hardware-dependent pattern from the software that generated the starting weights. PyTorch on the GPUs examined here leaves such a pattern; Baidu’s PaddlePaddle framework, which was used to train Baidu’s ERNIE-5.5 model, does not. We were able to recover the seed for ERNIE-5.5 (2760), but could not identify which hardware was used to initialize it. Likewise, weights initialized on an ordinary processor rather than a GPU leave no GPU fingerprint; several of Alibaba’s Qwen3 models were initialized this way, and thus leave no trace of which GPUs were used to train them. We also found no fingerprint in Meituan’s LongCat-2.0, which the company says was trained on “AI ASIC superpods,” or in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, despite an exhaustive search. The method identifies the hardware that generated the starting weights, not every chip that later helped train the model. When a training run creates its weights on the same GPUs that will train it, the fingerprint points to both. But a lab could generate the weights on one system and move them to another, or continue training an existing model on new hardware. The weights alone cannot rule out those possibilities. A mixed cluster introduces the same limitation. If NVIDIA chips generated some weights and Huawei chips later helped train them, the NVIDIA pattern could survive without revealing Huawei’s participation. Different NVIDIA generations could leave different patterns in the parts they initialized, if those traces survived. In Kimi K3, at least 64 separately seeded processes each left the same 152-SM layout. A Blackwell-compatible pattern therefore supports its use at initialization, subject to the AMD alternative below; it does not establish that the entire training run used Blackwell. A Hopper pattern likewise does not rule out later training on Blackwell. The weights also cannot reveal who owned the chips or where they were located. Blackwell systems can be rented from data centers outside China. The evidence concerns access to the hardware; by itself, it does not establish that chips were smuggled into China or that an export-control violation occurred. Could a different chip produce one of these Blackwell-compatible patterns? Among the NVIDIA configurations tested here, the older chips cannot: software can use fewer of a chip’s processing units, but cannot give it more than it physically has. Under the standard PyTorch behavior examined here, they cannot produce the 148- or 152-SM layouts. The China-market Blackwell graphics cards use a different number of threads per SM and do not produce either total. AMD presents a different possibility. An MI300X normally uses 304 processing units, but it can be divided into two groups of 152 or configured to use only 148. Its random-number software can also generate the same underlying sequences as NVIDIA’s. Such configurations would be very unusual, but we confirmed on a physical MI300X that, limited to 152 or 148 of its units, it reproduces the layouts we associate with Blackwell, so the layout alone does not settle the question. To distinguish them, we looked for small numerical differences in the values themselves. AMD and NVIDIA perform one calculation in the number-generating process slightly differently. On a physical MI300X, DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s preserved weights point to NVIDIA: in the 377 values where the two vendors’ results differ, the published weight matches NVIDIA’s in 363 and AMD’s in none. The same test could not settle the other five models, but we consider the AMD explanation very unlikely for them. In its normal configuration, an MI300X produces neither layout; a lab would have had to configure an entire cluster to use the same number of processing units as a Blackwell chip. Other public evidence also points to Blackwell: U.S. officials and press reports have alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, and Ant Group’s public code includes benchmark results generated on a GB300. Verifying our findings To reproduce the result that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, we ran unmodified PyTorch on a Hopper-class NVIDIA H100 and a Blackwell-class NVIDIA B300. We had identified DeepSeek’s seed number as 953049583, and found that it was used in the initialization of both DeepSeek-V3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Using that seed, the H100 reproduced the preserved starting values in DeepSeek-V3, but not V4-Flash; the B300 reproduced the preserved values in V4-Flash, but not V3. On the B300, unmodified PyTorch reproduced 461 of the 469 selected rows in DeepSeek-V4-Flash with correlations above 0.99, including 445 entire rows that matched bit for bit. Eight selected rows were partly changed by training. On the H100, it reproduced all 57,344 preserved values in DeepSeek-V3 bit for bit. Neither chip reproduced the other model’s preserved rows. Changing the seed by one reproduced no matching rows on either machine. On a rented GB200, unmodified PyTorch likewise reproduced all 13 of Kimi K3’s preserved rows using Moonshot’s seed, 20256586; changing the seed by one reproduced none. The code and the preserved weights needed to repeat these checks are public ; the same comparison also runs without a GPU. Our forensic method also gets the right answer when the answer is already known. There are 24 cases where a developer has publicly named the hardware behind a specific model; our forensic method agrees with every one. Meta’s Llama 3.1 models, trained on H100s, read as 132; eight of EleutherAI’s Pythia models, trained on A100s, read as 108. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of training, reads as 152, the same as Kimi K3. DeepSeek and Moonshot have reported H800 use for earlier models. Our Hopper readings are consistent with those disclosures, but would also be consistent with H100 SXM or H200 hardware; they do not independently verify H800 use. When we compare the published weights with the numbers generated by a candidate seed and chip layout, some resemblance is inevitable even if the candidate is wrong. How much resemblance counts as evidence depends on how many weights we compare: agreement across a handful of numbers could easily be accidental, while agreement across thousands is much harder to explain by chance. Our statistical model accounts for the number of weights compared and measures how far the observed match exceeds the resemblance expected by chance. We express that distance in standard deviations, or sigma . A higher score means stronger evidence against an accidental match, provided the statistical model correctly describes the random variation in the data. We must also account for how many candidates we tried. Searching roughly six trillion combinations of seed and layout gives us trillions of opportunities to find a lucky match. Under a normal-distribution model, a positive match of five sigma or more occurs by chance about once in 3.5 million comparisons. That would be striking in a single test, but unsurprising somewhere in a search as large as ours. We therefore use approximately eight sigma as our benchmark for assessing accidental matches across the full search. Our findings exceed that benchmark by a wide margin. We first select a seed and layout using one set of weights, and then test that same combination on a separate set that played no part in choosing it. This checks whether the apparent fingerprint extends beyond the numbers that led us to it. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma; even the weakest individual test reported reaches 20 sigma. Under our statistical model, these results are far too strong to attribute to accidental resemblance. They establish evidence of a shared initialization pattern; identifying precisely which computing hardware produced that pattern, and whether it also performed the training, requires the separate arguments discussed above. Conclusion Based on our forensic investigation, we believe that we have strong evidence that six Chinese AI models were initialized on export-controlled NVIDIA hardware, and that for DeepSeek-V4-Flash the evidence is conclusive ; we believe that this initialization also strongly suggests that they trained on the same export-controlled hardware. While this leaves unanswered other questions—such as the circumstances through which the companies that developed these models acquired export-controlled NVIDIA systems—we believe that this fact deserves urgent attention from the public. Sturdivant , a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places. But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin , ALPRs give law enforcement “ a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “ form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment. We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant. Related Cases Wisconsin Council of Churches v. A family tree of software job titles
body_text: A Family Tree of Software Job Titles – zwischenzugs.com Skip to content zwischenzugs.com A Family Tree of Software Job Titles 15 November 2026 3 November 2026 by imiell For a few years I was ‘Head of DevOps’. Before I got that job title I’d done much the same work under other names, and since then I’ve watched the same work get called SRE, and then it seemed to morph towards platform engineering. If you’ve been in this industry for any length of time you’ll have seen titles come and go like this, and you might have wondered where they all came from. So I (with the help of Mr Claude) built this family tree of software job titles, from the 1940s to now. It’s here: ianmiell.github.io/sw-job-title-family-tree What It Is There are 104 titles, from ‘Computer’ (a person, not a machine) at the top to ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ at the bottom. Time runs from top to bottom, in five-year rows. The titles sit in seven coloured columns by family: Development Analysis, architecture and leadership Operations and infrastructure Networks and security Data and AI Quality and test Support and customer-facing A solid arrow means the title grew out of its parent. A dashed arrow means influence, or a common career move. Landmark titles are in bold. On the site you can click a family to see just that column (here’s Data & AI ), or click a title to get its history, background and connections (here’s SRE ). The whole thing is one Graphviz file and one JSON file of descriptions. Each title is one line in the .dot file, and the picture is rendered with: $ dot -Tsvg job_title_family_tree.dot -o job_title_family_tree.svg Adding a title is three small edits: a node in its family’s column, an entry in the row for its five-year period, and its parent arrows. A word on the dates. They’re roughly when a title became common , not its first recorded use, and they’re my best estimates, not sourced citations. Some are well known (SRE at Google in 2003, ‘DevOps’ coined in 2009, ‘Data Scientist’ in 2008). Plenty are a ‘c.’ and a shrug. Six Things I Noticed Drawing it out made a few patterns hard to miss. 1) Coding Started Out as the Clerical Bit In 1947, Goldstine and von Neumann’s ‘Planning and Coding of Problems’ split the work of using a computer in two: mathematicians planned the problem, and coders translated the plan into machine instructions. Coding was treated as lower-status clerical work, and much of it was done by women. It turned out that coding eventually became the hard, creative part, and the coder merged into the programmer. Go back further and it’s stranger still. Several of the first ENIAC programmers were recruited from the Army’s human computers, people whose job was to compute by hand. So the job gave its name to the machine, and its people to programming. My upcoming book, available in Early Release with O’Reilly. 2) Titles Break Apart, Then Join Back Up The webmaster turned up around 1993, and was often a single person who wrote the HTML, ran the webserver (often a box under a desk), answered the email, and kept the site up (sometimes by kicking it, more often by plugging it back in after kicking it). By the mid-2000s the title had all but gone, as it was unfashionably ancient. The code went to web developers, the servers to sysadmins, and the content to editors and designers. Then the web developer split into front-end and back-end around 2005, and the two joined back up again as ‘full-stack’ around 2008. This is the centralisation/distribution see-saw I’ve written about before , playing out in job titles. 3) Some Titles Don’t Last The prompt engineer made headlines in 2023 with a few eye-wateringly well-paid job listings. As the models got better, the skill became part of other jobs, and on the tree it gets absorbed into the AI engineer almost as soon as it appears. The scrum master is a slower version of the same story: demand peaked in the 2010s, and many organisations have since folded it back into engineering management or delivery roles. The newest title on the tree is the ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ (c. 2025). The description for it currently says “time will tell whether it stays a separate title”. I’m not taking bets. 4) Names Get Recycled ‘Systems Engineer’ is two different jobs on the tree. At IBM in the 1960s it was a pre-sales role, working with customers to design installations and get them running. In the 1990s, thanks largely to Microsoft’s MCSE certification, it meant a more senior, design-oriented sysadmin. Same title, different branch, no relation. ‘Configuration management’ started as a 1960s US defence discipline for tracking hardware changes, became software version control in the 1970s, and then came back decades later as the name for tools like Puppet and Chef. 5) The New Thing Is Often an Old Thing The ‘forward deployed engineer’ (FDE) is one of the hottest titles of 2025, as OpenAI, Anthropic and plenty of AI startups hire FDEs to get AI working inside their customers’ organisations. Palantir built its business around them from about 2010: software engineers embedded with a customer, often on site, building whatever is needed to make the product work for that customer’s problem. Which sounds a lot like IBM’s systems engineers of the 1960s, who worked with customers before and after the sale, designing installations and getting systems running. (It also sounds a lot like old-style consulting, but I would say that.) 6) The DevOps Debate Is There Ben Treynor Sloss defined SRE as “what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team”. DevOps was meant as a culture of developers and operations working together, but by about 2011 ‘DevOps Engineer’ had become a job title, usually for whoever did the automation. On the tree, the arrow between SRE and DevOps points both ways. Platform engineering has both of them as parents, and was sold around 2022 as ‘the successor to DevOps’. The Dev/Ops divide has never been resolved. It just keeps getting new names. Why Bother? When I’m asked what the difference is between a DevOps engineer, an SRE and a platform engineer, the honest answer is always a little history lesson. This is the shortest version of that lesson I’ve managed so far. The dates are best guesses, and I’ll have missed titles, mangled some lineages and drawn arrows people will argue with. If you know better, let me know, or raise a PR on the repo . Which brings me back to the coders. In 1947 coding was the clerical bit, and the real work was in the planning. Wind forward eighty years and you’ll hear much the same said about coding again, because AI. Last time, the coders turned out to be doing the hard part. I’ll leave you to draw that arrow yourself. title: Why get an expensive Pi when I have an old phone?
body_text: Why get an expensive Pi when I have an old phone? â so.long.thanks.fish ← so.long.thanks.fish Why get an expensive Pi when I have an old phone? November 2026 The rooted Redmi talking over USB-C to the LED controller. Iâm working on a project that needs a high resolution camera, GPS, storage, and a microcontroller to control some lights. (More on the project soon!) Iâve been designing PCB adapters around a Raspberry Pi, an Arducam 64MP camera, and a GPS module. Every time I add another part, the bill grows. Iâm also trying an ESP32-P4 board, which will get its own post soon. But the alternative I keep coming back to is an old smartphone. I have a Redmi 13C 5G and a Huawei Mate 30 5G. Phones like these turn up second hand on Taobao for roughly Â¥300â500 (Â£33â56 / â¬40â67 / $45â75) . The Redmi gives me a camera that saves 50MP JPEGs; the Mate 30 has a 40MP main camera and a telephoto lens. Both already contain GPS, storage, a clock, a battery, mobile data, and a touchscreen. Their USB-C ports give me a route to the PCB that will handle the lights and other sensors. Here is the rough parts comparison I made while deciding what to build next: What I need Used Redmi or Mate 30 Raspberry Pi 4 approach Computer Included in phone price Pi 4, 4GB : Â¥880 / Â£98 / â¬118 / $132 High resolution camera Redmi 50MP JPEG; Mate 30 40MP Arducam 64MP : ~Â¥400 / Â£45 / â¬53 / $60 GPS Included GPS HAT : ~Â¥153 / Â£17 / â¬20 / $23 Storage Built in 64GB microSD : ~Â¥50 / Â£6 / â¬7 / $7 Core total Â¥300â500 / Â£33â56 / â¬40â67 / $45â75 ~Â¥1,483 / Â£165 / â¬198 / $222 Clock Included RTC HAT : ~Â¥80 / Â£9 / â¬11 / $12 Battery backup Included UPS HAT : ~Â¥133 / Â£15 / â¬18 / $20 , plus cells Touch display Included 5â³ touchscreen : ~Â¥247 / Â£28 / â¬33 / $37 Mobile data Built in, with a SIM 4G HAT : ~Â¥527 / Â£59 / â¬70 / $79 More fully equipped total Â¥300â500 / Â£33â56 / â¬40â67 / $45â75 ~Â¥2,317 / Â£258 / â¬310 / $347 , plus batteries These are illustrative November 2026 listings. The more fully equipped Pi total uses the cellular HATâs GPS instead of buying the separate GPS HAT; its modem is 4G, while the phones are 5G models. Neither side includes my custom light controller PCB, a SIM or data plan, or an enclosure. The conversions use 10 November 2026 mid market rates of approximately Â¥1 = Â£0.111531 / â¬0.133643 / $0.14991 , rounded to whole units in the table. The phone is already becoming more than a price exercise. Iâve unlocked and rooted the Redmi, tested its camera, and got it sleeping and waking for scheduled work. I can plug it into my computer and have Codex configure and test the pieces I need. The Huawei is harder to root, but I can still run a kiosk app on it. Iâve made a stand to photograph the same target with the Redmi and Arducam side by side; I want to see what detail each camera actually captures. A 50MP JPEG file does not, by itself, settle that question. The open question is supply. Finding two good used phones is easy; finding a few hundred matching ones, with healthy batteries and predictable camera behaviour, would take more work. I feel increasingly confident that itâs possible. This could be useful well beyond the current project. For digital artworks and installations, weâve often used a Pi or a Mac mini. Imagine instead posting a client a configured phone: plug it into the display and it runs. With mobile data and remote access, I can fix something without asking a gallery for Wi-Fi privileges or an open port. Thereâs something fun about taking a device made in enormous numbers, giving it a second life, and finding that most of the hardware I was about to assemble is already inside it.

title: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live
body_text: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live - The Python Package Index Blog Skip to content PyPI.org PyPI blog User documentation Developer documentation Navigation The Python Package Index Blog PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live Search Search GitHub The Python Package Index Blog GitHub The PyPI Blog The PyPI Blog On this page Context The New Security Tab Provenance States Full Provenance No Provenance Provenance Warnings Incomplete Provenance Inconsistent Provenance Change of Provenance Loss of Provenance Redesigned Project Detail Page Release Files and Release History Getting Help Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments Archive Archive 2026 2025 2024 2023 Authors Authors Nicole Harris Jacob Coffee Maria Ashna Mike Fiedler William Woodruff Seth Larson Dustin Ingram Ee Durbin Facundo Tuesca Deb Nicholson Shamika Monahan Donald Stufft Tags On this page Context The New Security Tab Provenance States Full Provenance No Provenance Provenance Warnings Incomplete Provenance Inconsistent Provenance Change of Provenance Loss of Provenance Redesigned Project Detail Page Release Files and Release History Getting Help Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments Back to index Nicole Harris PyPI Design Contributor Metadata November 6, 2026 6 min read Related links Planned Updates to the PyPI User Interface PyPI now supports digital attestations Releases now reject new files after 14 days PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live In July, we announced a series of planned updates to the PyPI user interface. Shaped by user research with members of the Python community , the updates aim to improve how we surface security signals and display package details. We're pleased to share that this work is now complete and live on PyPI . Context ¶ With the rapid growth of the Python ecosystem, PyPI has become an increasingly attractive target for malicious actors. In response, the PyPI team has delivered many security features while taking a more active role in helping PyPI users assess and understand package security. Digital attestations , introduced in 2024, are an example of this effort, providing a verifiable record of a release file's provenance (where it came from). However, provenance and attestations are still unfamiliar concepts for many PyPI users, and PyPI's interface did little to communicate their meaning, importance, or limitations. To address this, PyPI partnered with Kabu Creative to bring clearer security signals to the PyPI UI, implementing the recommendations developed in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide . Here's a look at what's changed, what it means for you, and what actions you can take. The New Security Tab ¶ The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from. The new security tab on a PyPI project detail page Provenance States ¶ PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation. Typically, a release will be in one of two states: Full Provenance ¶ This means that 100% of the release files have attestations, carrying either or both of the supported attestation types: PyPI Publish attestations confirm the file was published by a PyPI Trusted Publisher : A PyPI Publish attestation on PyPI SLSA Build Provenance attestations link the file back to its exact source commit, build platform, and instructions: A SLSA Build Provenance attestation on PyPI You can review attestation metadata directly in the UI, or click on the transparency log link for more information. No Provenance ¶ "No provenance" simply means that no file in the release has an attestation. This is typical for older releases or projects that have not yet configured Trusted Publishing. No provenance does not necessarily indicate that a release or release file is malicious; it instead means that the file origin cannot be cryptographically verified . When there is no provenance, you should rely on surrounding trust signals to assess security, such as maintainer history, release patterns, and repository activity. If you maintain the package, consider using Trusted Publishing with a publisher that generates attestations for your next release. Provenance Warnings ¶ Provenance warnings are designed to help you identify when a file may not have come from the project's maintainers, for example, if an attacker has taken over an account or a publishing workflow. When provenance metadata looks unusual or conflicts with a project's history, PyPI surfaces a prominent warning. Many warnings have legitimate explanations, but each one is worth checking before you install. Incomplete Provenance ¶ This means that some files carry attestations while others do not (e.g., wheels were published via Trusted Publishing, but the source tarball was uploaded using an API token). Exercise caution if you see this warning. Check release notes for build issues or ask in the project's issue tracker before installing. Inconsistent Provenance ¶ This warning indicates that files within the same release originate from different build systems or source repositories. Check the attestation metadata to confirm whether all files came from sources controlled by the maintainers. Change of Provenance ¶ This warning tells you that the release files originated from a different repository or workflow than a previous release. While often legitimate (such as an organization name change or repository migration), it can also indicate a compromised pipeline or account takeover. If you see this warning, check the project release notes or official channels to confirm that an infrastructure migration was planned. Loss of Provenance ¶ This means that a project that previously published with attestations has changed to uploading release files without them. Check whether the maintainers intentionally changed their publishing process, for example by switching back to API tokens, or by changing their publishing configuration so that it no longer generates attestations. If this is unexpected, treat the release with skepticism until verified. To learn more about provenance and attestations, including provenance warnings, see our user documentation . An example provenance warning on PyPI, showing a release with incomplete provenance Redesigned Project Detail Page ¶ To support these changes, the project detail page has also been updated: Provenance warnings now appear at the top of the page, alongside status banners for yanked releases, archived projects, and pre-releases. If a project or release is quarantined , only the quarantine banner is shown, as it takes precedence over all other warnings and banners. When a release has full provenance or provenance warnings, its provenance state is displayed in the sidebar, linking through to the security tab for more information. Metadata is now ordered by utility and labeled as "PyPI data" or "Data verified by PyPI", replacing the old design where data was grouped and ordered by verification status. The redesigned metadata sidebar, with information ordered by utility Release Files and Release History ¶ The redesigned release files tab helps you find the right file by searching and filtering long lists. You can also view the provenance state of each file within the table, and quickly identify late files, which are marked with an orange warning icon. Late file warnings are shown when one or more files were uploaded more than 14 days after the initial release timestamp. These warnings only appear on releases prior to July 2026, when a policy was introduced to reject new files after 14 days . The release history tab now also provides more details about each release, exposing file count, provenance state, and release status (i.e., quarantined, yanked, archived, or pre-release). The redesigned release history tab, with release status, file count, and provenance state Getting Help ¶ Alongside the interface updates, PyPI's user documentation has been extended to help you better navigate package security. Read our package security guide to learn about: Assessing source code security Checking provenance (where a package came from) Verifying package integrity Protecting yourself from common security attacks Reporting security issues Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments ¶ The new security tab gives PyPI a dedicated home for future attestation types and security notices. To help the wider open source ecosystem benefit from this work, we've also published a case study in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide detailing the design patterns and warnings developed during this project. This initiative was funded by the Open Source Security Foundation and implemented by Kabu Creative . We would like to thank Dustin Ingram , Zach Steindler , and the members of the OpenSSF Securing Software Repositories Working Group for championing this effort. Special thanks to Mike Fiedler , Jacob Coffee , and members of the PyPI team for their thoughtful design feedback and code reviews, @cofiem for their contributions to the new release files tab, and our user interview participants and community testers for helping shape the final design. Finally, we would like to thank the OpenSSF for its funding and continued partnership in securing the Python packaging ecosystem. security user-interface Back to top Previous Higher limits for organization projects Made with Zensical

title: Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after reporting
body_text: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition - Project Zero Project Zero blog archive bug reports about Working at PZ 0day: spreadsheet 0day: Root Cause Analyses vulnerability disclosure policy reporting transparency search Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition 2026-Nov-13 Natalie Silvanovich Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a â90 + 30â vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days âsoak timeâ for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient. LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster. LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. âPatch gapâ is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. It is equally crucial that vendors reduce patch gap, either by reducing patch rollout time or using other strategies to protect users while remediation is in progress. LLMs have also increased the volume of vulnerabilities that Project Zero reports. We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year. Aspects of our policy that require vendor negotiation or agreement, including determining whether a bug is fixed and whether grace period applies, are quickly becoming unmanageable. Today, we are announcing a new vulnerability disclosure policy, created with the following goals in mind: Encourage faster vulnerability remediation Encourage vendors to reduce âpatch gapâ Allow for the policy to be automated by both Project Zero and vendors Our new policy: âFull Xâ Vulnerabilities will be disclosed X days after they are reported to the vendor. Starting today, our policy is âFull 90â, i.e. vulnerabilities will be disclosed 90 days after they are reported to the vendor. On February 2, 2027, we will move to a âFull 60â policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 60 days. On January 3, 2028, we will move to a âFull 30â policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 30 days. We are also removing most âspecial casesâ from our disclosure policy, including grace period and variant policy. The only exceptions to our new policy are: Vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild -- ITW vulnerabilities will be handled according to Googleâs application security vulnerability disclosure policy Public vulnerabilities -- Project Zero may make details of a vulnerability public, at our discretion, if the details have already been made public by others Vendor request -- We will make vulnerability details public if the vendor we reported it to requests it Why reduce remediation time gradually? Project Zero solicited feedback from the vendors we report the most vulnerabilities to as a part of developing this new policy. An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology. While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term. In addition, vendors mentioned two more subtle concerns. One was that an overly-aggressive disclosure policy would encourage fixing bugs reported under the new policy with more priority, even if they are less severe than other reported vulnerabilities. The other was that immediately enforcing a policy that some vendors arenât equipped to meet might lead to a state where vendors accept that they cannot fix bugs within the deadline and donât attempt to. We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly. What about severity? While our analysis isnât always perfect, Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities with substantial severity and demonstrated security impact in our tracker. That said, we donât feel severity is an effective metric for making disclosure decisions, especially in the current environment. A vulnerabilityâs severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users. When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances. But this doesnât change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality. Itâs also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regards to the reproducibility, readability, reachability and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bugs reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently. What about hardware? We encourage all vendors to consider how they would respond to imminent disclosure of a serious vulnerability, including non-patch strategies , as there is no guarantee that defenders will be the first to find a bug. That said, Project Zero has occasionally granted exceptions to our policy on rare occasions, including Spectre and Meltdown, and will continue to do so in the future. Are you really not going to check whether bugs are fixed? The question of whether a bug is fixed for the purposes of our policy has always been challenging and somewhat unresolved, particularly with regards to code that is not shipped directly to users and not publicly available. It is not unusual for Project Zero to communicate with vendors multiple times for each bug report to come to an agreement on whether a vulnerability is fixed. As more vendors experiment with vulnerability remediation strategies that are not patching like temporarily disabling code paths, we expect this to become even more complex. We still plan to track whether bugs are fixed and communicate if they are not, however, this will not be a decision point in our policy. This will enable us to share technical details of how users are protected without needing to make a binary judgement with consequences for the vendor. Make zeroday hard. Privacy

Each capture was scaled to 1600x1200 with nearest-neighbour pixels and 4:3 aspect correction, so every original pixel keeps the shape it had on a period monitor. The twelve moments are the same in every version, with the same framing, so switching versions changes the machine, not the moment. The PC 16-color screens come from a Spanish copy and the Atari ST mono ones from a French copy; all the others are in English. Google Research Google AI Learn about all our AI Google DeepMind Explore the frontier of AI Google Labs Try our AI experiments Research Resources Conferences & events Careers Blog About Search Home Blog Advancing science & engineering with Antigravity’s /teamwork November 13, 2026 Vahab Mirrokni, Google Fellow and VP, Google Research We share recent results from Antigravity’s /teamwork multiagent systems, which enhance human-AI collaborations to solve open problems across mathematics, chemistry, systems software, and ML engineering. All of this work is done in collaboration with human experts, and we are making these tools available externally. Quick links Antigravity blog Gemini 4 Argon Antigravity Teamwork Researcher access program Share Copy link × Over the past several weeks, teams across Google and academic partner institutions have tackled open problems in math, science, and complex systems engineering that had remained open for years. Using Gemini 4 Argon , Gemini 4 Carbon , Gemini 4 Hydrogen and multi-agent workflows such as Antigravity’s /teamwork (building on various Gemini models), these collaborations have produced new innovations across information theory, formal verifications, molecular structure discoveries, and kernel optimization, along with several production infrastructure gains at Google. We are making these agentic tools available in Antigravity’s /teamwork (alongside /boost and other agents) so that researchers and developers can apply them to their own work. Frontier research and systems engineering require navigating vast literature, building custom computational pipelines, testing against physical measurements, and verifying every step. Progress comes from an interactive discovery loop where researchers frame questions and define the theoretical or physical constraints, while long-horizon agents write custom solvers, explore large search spaces, test candidate designs, and check long chains of logic. Scaling long-horizon reasoning Two limits of current language models motivate /teamwork's design . First, model generation can be unpredictable, leaving a gap between a single attempt and finding the correct answer. The system bridges this gap by pairing parallel exploration with dedicated falsifiers (e.g., the Lean 4 proof checker, unmodified software test suites, execution simulators, web search, or hardware counters) to automatically verify which candidate solutions work. Second, AI models often lose track of details over multi-day tasks because attention disperses across growing context windows. To prevent this, /teamwork partitions context by construction: each specialized agent receives only the exact files and tools it needs for a specific step. Coordinators hand off tasks to fresh successors, while critics and auditors challenge and verify results from clean contexts without the original producer's reasoning. Teamwork expresses these workflows as declarative self-improving natural-language patterns and dynamically routes each user prompt to the pattern best suited to the task. These patterns range from distributed coding and iterative problem-solving (packaged standalone as /boost , a sequential solve-and-verify loop refined from prior trajectories) to specialized research workflows like long proof and document review, all of which are available in Antigravity today. This allows teams to design custom specifications from past run transcripts routing across different harness patterns and dynamically improving agentic harness. While many of these features are available in Antigravity, we will provide more updates in the coming weeks providing all the features to our external users on Antigravity. Following our previous posts on Antigravity /teamwork , we provide new results to open challenges empowered by new variants of /teamwork and Gemini 4 models. Mathematics and theoretical computer science Across mathematics and theoretical computer science, researchers paired with Gemini 4 and /teamwork harnesses to collaborate on large-scale proofs and generate complete algorithms and proofs directly from open problem statements. We present several examples. Proving and verifying the Courtade–Kumar conjecture Researchers from Google, CUHK , USC , and CMU used /teamwork's Long Proof pattern (implementing Stellar Colosseum in Antigravity) to prove information theory's 2013 Courtade–Kumar conjecture in full generality. The result confirms that when a random bit string passes through a noisy channel, no compression of the input to a single bit preserves more information than a "dictator function", which just copies a single input bit. Gemini first found counterexamples to a generalized conjecture from the CUHK team's earlier paper . The CUHK team then proposed a new candidate function that reduced the conjecture to a 14-variable optimization problem, along with a key analytical lower bound. Gemini 4 Argon and earlier Gemini models then partitioned the parameter space and developed most of the new analytical bounds and interval-arithmetic certificates. They also extended the proof from balanced to unbalanced functions without human input. The team formalized the entire proof in Lean 4, producing 50 million lines of code. Resolving open questions in optimization, statistics, quantum computing, and algorithms Researchers also posed open problems directly to Gemini 4 and to multi-agent harnesses such as Stellar Colosseum and /teamwork , receiving end-to-end algorithms and proofs (often with Lean 4 formalizations) that the authors verified, simplified, and edited for publication. In adaptive data analysis, a multi-agent harness running on Gemini 4 Argon independently proved and Lean-verified near-optimal sample bounds for statistical queries chosen adaptively from earlier answers, closing a gap open since 2014. These bounds yield the first nearly space-optimal algorithm for data streams with both insertions and deletions that stays accurate against adaptive adversaries. In quantum computing, a new construction settled a 2014 open question by finding the first n -bit Boolean functions needing strictly more than n /2 quantum queries at constant error, while pinning down the exact query overhead across symmetric functions. Several results break long standing barriers in processing and compressing large matrices and graphs. For fifty years until STOC 2024 , combinatorial algorithms for Boolean matrix multiplication and triangle detection (avoiding the algebraic cancellations of fast matrix multiplication) saved only logarithmic factors over cubic time. A new deterministic algorithm resolves STOC 2024's main open question, achieving its target speedup over cubic time. In high-dimensional geometry, a new lower bound resolves an open problem on sparse networks, proving that approximating all pairwise distances among n points within any constant factor can require polynomially more than n edges, even with extra Steiner points and arbitrarily many hops. In randomized linear algebra, stacked sparse sketches resolve a 2025 open question by breaking the classical sparsity barrier for compressing a matrix to linear dimension without collapsing any direction of an r -dimensional subspace, needing only √log r nonzeros per row (quadratically fewer than the log r required to preserve all lengths) and nearly matching a new lower bound. For weighted graphs under dynamic edge-weight insertions and deletions, Stellar Colosseum resolved an open question left by FOCS 2022 , developing the first single-pass streaming algorithm for cut sparsification that achieves near-optimal memory, update time, and reconstruction time simultaneously. Our results also span optimization, arithmetic, data structures, and statistics. In optimization, resolving an open question on online inverse linear optimization (inferring an expert's hidden objective from decisions over time), the approach gave a deterministic algorithm achieving optimal regret while cutting runtime from exponential in the dimension to polynomial time. For n -bit integer multiplication , multi-agent campaigns simplified the theoretical Turing-machine bound below n log n , while a separate effort gave a new O ( n log n ) algorithm on a single two-dimensional grid whose C implementation matches the GNU Multiple Precision Arithmetic Library (GMP) bit-for-bit up to a billion bits. In data structures, another result made significant progress on Tarjan's 1985 Deque Conjecture (whether self-adjusting splay trees handle insertions and deletions at both ends in constant amortized time), proving a new upper bound on the per-operation overhead that simultaneously beats every finitely iterated inverse-Ackermann function, verified in Lean 4 . Finally, in high-dimensional statistics, the approach proved that approximate leave-one-out cross-validation , which avoids refitting the model from scratch, remains accurate for non-smooth sparse penalties like elastic net . Scaling formal verification and manuscript review Checking a computer-assisted manuscript by hand places a heavy burden on peer reviewers, and subtle flaws can hide inside long calculations. Formalizing mathematics in Lean 4 turns a proof into code that a computer kernel checks line by line. Once human mathematicians confirm that the formal theorem statement matches the original problem, the proof only compiles if every logical step holds. Many of the deepest open problems in mathematics govern how physical waves propagate, how dynamical systems evolve, and whether polynomial equations have integer solutions. Working directly from informal proofs, our multi-agent framework, LEAP , developed with colleagues in Google Cloud AI and paired with Argon, has made progress in these core areas. Notably, /teamwork -LEAP fully autonomously produced an end-to-end, machine-checked formalization of the Weil conjectures , the landmark results on counting solutions of polynomial equations over finite fields that culminated in Pierre Deligne 's 1974 proof. This formalization spans about 1.8 million lines of Lean, produced across 28,800 subagent invocations. The system also synthesized over 919,000 lines of Lean to produce the first formalization of a recent proof of Hilbert's tenth problem over general rings of integers. It also independently reproduces an end-to-end formalization of a recent proof of finite-time blowup for the 3D Navier–Stokes equations with smooth forcing, part of one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems and open for about 90 years. Beyond these, it also generated the first formalization of the Birkhoff conjecture , a dynamical-systems problem open since 1927. Moreover, it formalized for the first time the 3D Bochner–Riesz conjecture , a central problem in harmonic analysis open for more than 50 years, finding and fixing a gap in a recently released informal proof along the way. Additional machine-checked breakthroughs include resolving the C¹ regularity of infinity-harmonic functions in three and higher dimensions (an open question for about 20 years), formalizing Killip and Vişan's theorem that the KdV water-wave equation is well-posed in H⁻¹ and verifying a UCLA group's informal proofs of the 40-year-old Jamison Caterpillar Conjecture, the Ağırseven-Ollis conjecture, and an improved upper bound on Erdős Problem #1063. Finally, we provided Deep Review for authors of another CS conference: ahead of STOC 2027 , authors of 578 submissions (over a third of all submissions) opted in to receive Deep Review feedback on their drafts. In an ongoing author survey (N = 70), 90% of respondents rated the feedback mostly or almost all factual and 90% said they would use the tool again. Over 30% said Deep Review caught substantive proof bugs or mathematically significant typos, and 14% said it found technical gaps that took more than an hour to fix. Surveyed authors shared that “Tools of this kind can help produce cleaner and more precise research, faster” and that DeepReview provides peace of mind on scientific discovery”. We provide users two weekly calls to Deep Review for free. Deep Review is also implemented as /teamwork's document review pattern and available in Antigravity. Read more about DeepReview in our recent blog post . Molecular chemistry discovery Beyond formal proofs, pairing specialized generator agents with independent verifier agents enables discovery workflows in experimental laboratory science. Determining a molecule’s structure from experimental nuclear magnetic resonance data is one of chemistry’s hardest puzzles. For example, in HIV protease inhibitors , one misplaced bond separates an inactive look-alike from a drug. By organizing 30 specialized agents into a self-correcting loop with /teamwork and a physics-informed spectral simulator, we achieved 95% top-1 exact match and 100% top-3 accuracy on complex benchmark molecules, nearly doubling single-agent performance. Beyond teaching Gemini to reason over structure, this lays the groundwork for ongoing works on 3D protein and complex structures dynamics. Beyond this example, science problems including applications in nuclear fusion and quantum algorithms reported in the Gemini 4 blog post benefited from /teamwork and the Argon model. Generating a causal inference benchmark We also applied a similar multi-round auditing workflow to build empirical benchmarks. Starting from five human-specified acceptance criteria like data anonymization, 29 agents running on Argon over 11.5 hours turned 13 public tables into a 50-task causal inference benchmark. In these tasks, models must determine whether a causal effect can be identified and estimate it against a known answer. After initial checks, separate reviewer and auditor agents caught shortcuts, flagged wording hints, and vetoed hallucinated scripts, turning each into a permanent test. Automating this heavily manual task generation supplies the hard problems needed to help Gemini answer counterfactual "what-if" questions. Coding and systems engineering When paired with objective evaluators such as network benchmarks, game engines, unmodified test suites, and hardware timers, /teamwork campaigns can execute multi-day software and hardware engineering projects. Distributed systems Using /teamwork and Argon, we built FarArray , a low-latency kernel-bypass Partitioned Global Address Space based on the SNAP microkernel . Applications built on FarArray include lock-free Connected Components , which scale to 1-trillion-edge graphs with 60x to 90x throughput gains and 40x to 180x speedups at 6x lower RAM over TCP key-value stores. Similarly, InstantEmbedding (Personalized PageRank) reduced peak DRAM by up to 14x and runtime by 11x to 27x over accelerated MapReduce implementations. The team also used /teamwork and Argon to create custom TPU kernels for Graph Neural Networks, delivering up to a 185x High Bandwidth Memory reduction and 8x to 15x speedups in forward and backward passes. Further details are available in our recent Antigravity blog post . Autonomous hill climbing To test autonomous optimization over long horizons, hill-climbing teams on Argon trained a 9x9 Go engine from scratch starting from a basic AlphaZero implementation. Human researchers set the chip allocation and evaluation setup, while the harness ran autonomous campaigns for faster self-play (achieving a 2,300x speedup) and faster Elo readings, promoting champions strictly via statistical tests on locked records. In under eight days, the engine gained roughly 2,600 Elo, reaching 1,885 Elo, placing it between KataGo at 16 and 32 visits per move. play silent looping video pause silent looping video unmute video mute video A game played for this post between our final champion ( black ) and the network the Elo hill-climb started from ( white ). The final champion won by 22.5 points (area scoring, komi 7.5). It was the only game played for the post. Memory-safe Rust rewrites, /boost, and TPU kernel optimization Large code migrations fail when agents stub out dependencies or alter tests to make a broken port pass. A new /teamwork rewrite pattern, soon to be available in Antigravity, solved this by scheduling each module only after its dependencies compile, linking every leaf module against the original, unmodified test suite. Building on the initial 25% port of the Zircon microkernel , a two-week Argon campaign rewrote the remaining C++ code, adding about 800,000 lines of safe Rust that pass all kernel unit tests and boot on arm64 hardware. /teamwork also rewrote libgav1 , Google's AV1 video decoder, from C++ into around 170k lines Rust, achieving 100% bit-exact parity across a broad conformance test suite. Initially, the port was around 4x slower than the original C++ code. However, after giving /teamwork access to profiling tools and a mandate to maximize speed on sample video clips, the Rust port became 20-30% faster than the original C++ and hand-optimized assembly code on both x86_64 and ARM. For day-to-day coding tasks, the Antigravity /boost command packages /teamwork's iterative coding pattern . A long-running /teamwork campaign analyzed past run trajectories and found that tightly coupled code is best handled through sequential implementation and revision stages rather than parallel splits, improving /boost on coding tasks. This is an example of a harness optimizing another harness for token efficiency. For machine learning systems, full hardware evaluations of custom JAX and Pallas TPU kernels take 7 to 32 minutes, limiting how many candidates prior optimization agents can explore. Using /teamwork's DuoDiscover pattern on Argon, four parallel agents identified performance bottlenecks and constructed fast, 23-second proxy evaluators called yardsticks. These yardsticks produce candidate orderings that are continuously validated against periodic full hardware runs using Kendall's rank correlation . DuoDiscover achieves a 4.09x geometric-mean speedup over reference implementations across 17 JAXBench kernels and a 2.99x geometric-mean speedup across 7 hand-optimized vLLM TPU-Inference Pallas kernels for frontier open-weight models. Google infrastructure applications We have also applied /teamwork and /boost to many production infrastructure and hardware modeling problems across Google. Examples include: Fleet-wide memory optimization: Building on the initial Argon memory efforts , we analyzed fleet-wide metrics, as well as internal memory saving past successes, and created reusable /teamwork workflows that have identified memory saving opportunities, surpassing our initial savings estimates of 1 PiB. We also deployed the human-in-the-loop Memory Efficiency Monitoring Agent, achieving additional memory savings, using techniques such as struct padding elimination, scalar narrowing, cliff jumping, outlining, and tagged pointers. Borg agentic scheduling: Built on /teamwork and /boost , Borg’s agentic workflow for scheduling optimization shipped 2 successful changes, resulting in a 24% reduction in TPU workload preemption on some hardware types, while preserving workload SLOs and cluster utilization. Opening these tools to the research and developer community External scientists and developers can use Gemini 4 models with /teamwork and /boost in Antigravity and Deep Review today. We have also opened applications giving 10,000 academic researchers six months of free access to our highest usage tier. Upcoming updates will bring our formal proof pattern and additional specialized workflows into Antigravity. These features will be accompanied by deep-dive tutorials on the Antigravity blog in the coming weeks, ensuring that developers and researchers have the resources needed to generate, inspect, and iteratively refine custom multi-agent teams. We are excited to make our tools (in addition to our models) available for everyone.
