title: Reverse engineering my Coway air purifier to ditch the cloud
body_text: Reverse Engineering My Coway Air Purifier to Ditch the Cloud | Scott's Blog Scott J. Goldman Posts RSS Reverse Engineering My Coway Air Purifier to Ditch the Cloud November 11, 2026 16 min read Nice enough air purifier, but I don’t love the app. The year is 2017. A string of annual wildfires rocks the West Coast. The sky looks like this in the daytime: My home, like many in the Bay Area, has no insulation and isn’t really air sealed. To avoid choking on soot, a lot of people started buying air purifiers like this one : The venerable Coway Airmega It’s an overpriced box fan with a HEPA filter and an air quality sensor. It has some controls for the fan speed, and it can also automatically ramp up if the air quality is bad. It’s ugly, but they’re so ubiquitous around here that I feel like no one even notices them anymore. Also, FWIW, the device works. It really does improve air quality. This device became a staple item in our household when my wife eventually started cranking up the fan at night for white noise (a dual purpose!). Over time, I have become accustomed to it and now also require it to sleep. The Good Night button # Our home also has smart lighting, and it’s all integrated with Apple Home. At night, I always press the “Good Night” button, which shuts off all the lights. I really wanted to tie the fan into that. I’d press Good Night, the lights would shut off, and the fan would crank up to my wife’s preferred white noise volume. The old Airmega didn’t have Wi-Fi, so there was no easy way to integrate it with Apple Home. When it eventually broke, I bought the now-discontinued Coway Airmega IconS (for non-discontinued Wi-Fi models, check out the Airmega 250S or Airmega MightyS ). It’s still just a box fan with a HEPA filter, but it’s considerably more expensive, aims to look like a piece of fancy mid-century furniture, and most importantly, can be controlled over Wi-Fi (sort of). The Coway Airmega IconS The existing Home Assistant integration # Coway’s iPhone app is an absolutely classic IoT affair. It takes forever to load, and it asks me to change my password nearly every time I launch it. Thankfully, a brave soul reverse-engineered the app and wrote an integration for Home Assistant . The integration more or less pretends to be the phone app. It polls the Coway cloud service for status updates and sends commands through it to control the fan. Home Assistant bridges that to Apple Home and… voilà! Coway IoCare cloud Coway's servers, somewhere on the internet commands ↑ status ↓ status ↑ commands ↓ My house Home Assistant IoCare integration Air purifier Airmega IconS, on Wi-Fi Apple Home the Good Night button Why ditch the cloud? # The downside of this approach is that you’re still at the mercy (or lack thereof) of the Coway cloud service. It seems like at least once or twice a year, it breaks. Here are some of the reasons I have seen it break: Coway didn’t like the integration hammering their servers and banned it. After a protracted argument with the community, they eventually settled on allowing it. Coway rewrote their phone app and rebranded it from IoCare to IoCare+, so the integration had to be rewritten as well. Coway made minor changes to the layout of the HTML that the integration scrapes, which broke it. Coway’s servers were periodically offline, which prevented any remote control of the device. Coway banned my account at one point for running an old version of the integration. I couldn’t control the fan remotely for weeks while I waited for their support team to reverse the ban. On top of this, it seems unlikely that Coway will maintain this service forever. I suspect that eventually, like all IoT manufacturers, they’ll either charge for this service or discontinue it. My fan model is already discontinued (though there are other Wi-Fi enabled models, so… who knows). A way in # I admit, I have been lazy. For years, I put off trying to figure out a way to ditch the Coway cloud, because if the device was really locked down, it would be pretty tough. Presumably, when the fan starts up, it connects to coway.com (or whatever) and checks that the server’s SSL certificate is valid. Most likely, I wouldn’t be able to make a fake certificate that passes that check, so the fan wouldn’t connect to my server. Also, setting up a man-in-the-middle (MitM) environment is just a pain in the neck. The fan would have to connect to an isolated Wi-Fi network that routes all its traffic through my own server on the way out to the internet. To do that, you have to configure a bunch of routing and firewall rules to redirect traffic. None of this is impossible (I’ve done it before), but it’s a hassle to set up, and it’s always finicky to get right. And once you have it set up, that’s just step one. All that said, two major things have changed. First, there was a recent security incident (October 2026) where someone discovered that eMudhra, one of the trusted internet certificate authorities, had used a very weak parameter for some of its private keys. Ian Carroll @iangcarroll For the next few days or weeks, anyone now has a root CA thanks to eMudhra. Time to have some fun with MiTMing unwilling devices! 10:15 AM · Oct 20, 2026 So, if the device is unpatched AND it has hardcoded root certificates AND it doesn’t pin the cloud service’s certificate, then… maybe that’s a way in. Admittedly, that’s a lot of ifs, but assuming the device doesn’t have any major security mistakes in its design, this could be the foothold needed to take control of it. The second thing is simply AI. An LLM can set up everything you need for a MitM environment, so you can get straight to sleuthing out how the fan works. It can do this unattended, in minutes. Once you can sit between the fan and the internet, you can see how it communicates, which should help us understand how to get the fan to talk to us instead of the cloud. Our man in the middle # Initially, I tried to set it up like this: Air purifier Airmega IconS Wi-Fi Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi access point the Pi in AP mode, its own isolated network all traffic redirected mitmproxy decrypts and logs the traffic My home router the regular home network Coway IoCare cloud out on the internet This actually didn’t work, because a Raspberry Pi uses a smallish PCB trace antenna that doesn’t get a ton of signal strength. With the Pi in the room with my router, the signal was too weak to reach the fan. I guess I could’ve moved the fan into the room with the router, but why do that when I can solve this with a convoluted technical solution? The Raspberry Pi uses its Wi-Fi radio to run its own access point for the fan to connect to. It can’t easily do that while also connecting over Wi-Fi to the home network. So, I moved the Pi into the room with the fan and plugged its Ethernet port into my laptop, which bridges it to the home network over Wi-Fi: Air purifier Airmega IconS Wi-Fi, same room Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi access point the Pi in AP mode, its own isolated network all traffic redirected mitmproxy decrypts and logs the traffic Ethernet My laptop Internet Sharing, bridging Wi-Fi to Ethernet Wi-Fi My home router the regular home network Coway IoCare cloud out on the internet Next, we need to configure the Pi. I’m not really making a value judgment here on whether this is a fair thing to block, but Claude will not oblige the request, not even for… uhh… testing purposes. Luckily, ChatGPT has no such compunctions. After a few rounds of that, here are the nftables rules it ended up with: scottjg@pi:~ $ sudo nft -a list ruleset table inet mitmproxy_ap { # handle 8 set client_interfaces { # handle 4 type ifname elements = { "wlan0" } } chain prerouting { # handle 1 type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; meta nfproto ipv4 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 80, 443 } counter packets 2 bytes 120 redirect to :8080 # handle 6 } chain input { # handle 2 type filter hook input priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname != "lo" iifname != @client_interfaces tcp dport 8080 counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with tcp reset # handle 7 iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 9 bytes 2397 drop # handle 8 iifname @client_interfaces ct state established,related accept # handle 9 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport { 53, 67 } accept # handle 11 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 53, 8080 } accept # handle 13 iifname @client_interfaces ip protocol icmp accept # handle 14 iifname @client_interfaces counter packets 23 bytes 4697 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 15 } chain forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 16 oifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 17 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport 443 counter packets 1 bytes 57 reject # handle 18 iifname @client_interfaces oifname != "eth0" counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 19 } } table ip nm-shared-wlan0 { # handle 12 chain nat_postrouting { # handle 1 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 ip daddr != 10.42.0.0/24 masquerade # handle 2 } chain filter_forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy accept; ip daddr 10.42.0.0/24 oifname "wlan0" ct state { established, related } accept # handle 5 ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 iifname "wlan0" accept # handle 6 iifname "wlan0" oifname "wlan0" accept # handle 7 iifname "wlan0" reject # handle 8 oifname "wlan0" reject # handle 9 } } Basically, the masquerade rule translates the traffic from the isolated Wi-Fi network out through our home internet, and the redirect rule forwards HTTP/HTTPS to a running instance of mitmproxy . Also on the Pi, mitmproxy runs with its web interface, mitmweb , using a command line like this: mitmweb \ --mode transparent --showhost \ --listen-host 0.0.0.0 --listen-port 8080 \ --web-host 127.0.0.1 --web-port 8081 \ --set web_open_browser=false \ --emudhra-old Yes, off the shelf, mitmproxy has a built-in option ( --emudhra-old ) to automatically use the eMudhra root CA to intercept traffic. Snooping on the fan # Next, I used the iPhone app to set up the fan on our Pi-MITM-Test Wi-Fi network. Partway through, the app reported that setup failed. Let’s glance at the mitmproxy web interface: So, we know there was some kind of connection issue, since the app said the fan failed to connect. But it clearly got onto our isolated Wi-Fi, because it made a request . The request is very suspicious. It looks like the fan is downloading the root certificate for Amazon’s certificate authority over plain HTTP. This interface only shows connections that got far enough to make an actual HTTP request. If, for example, the fan doesn’t accept the eMudhra cert we’re using to impersonate the real servers, its HTTPS connections will fail before that point and never show up in the list. Hypothesis: The device downloads this public certificate over HTTP so it has something to validate its later (currently unseen) HTTPS connections against. It doesn’t have any root certificates built in at all. mitmproxy has a plugin mode where you can modify specific requests. We can use it to swap in mitmproxy ’s own generated CA certificate in place of this public one. If our hypothesis is correct, the fan will trust that CA, and we can intercept the rest of its traffic. """Serve this lab's public RSA CA only to the authorized Coway test device.""" from pathlib import Path from mitmproxy import ctx, http def response (flow: http . HTTPFlow) -> None : if ( flow . client_conn . peername[ 0 ] == "10.42.0.93" # device IP and flow . request . scheme == "http" and flow . request . method == "GET" and flow . request . pretty_host == "rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com" and flow . request . path . split( "?" , 1 )[ 0 ] == "/AmazonRootCA1.pem" and flow . response is not None and flow . response . status_code == 200 ): certificate = Path( "/var/lib/mitmproxy-ap/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem" ) . read_bytes() flow . response = http . Response . make( 200 , certificate, { "Content-Type" : "application/x-pem-file" , "Cache-Control" : "no-store" , }, ) flow . metadata[ "coway_test_ca_served" ] = True ctx . log . info( "Served lab RSA CA to the Coway's HTTP CA bootstrap request" ) Sure enough, the device now fully connects, and we can see some new requests: Hypothesis confirmed We can intercept the traffic between the fan and the server, which means we could probably build our own server to replace the Coway IoCare cloud. It also turns out we don’t need the eMudhra hack at all. The fan downloads its root CA cert over plain HTTP. It was always MitM-able. The one thing missing is that none of these requests have anything to do with changing the fan speed or anything else you can do in the app. That’s easy to figure out, though. If you run tcpdump on the Pi while clicking buttons in the app, you can see encrypted traffic on port 8883, the standard port for MQTT over TLS. MQTT is a message bus protocol commonly used in IoT devices. Going back to the POST in the request list above, here’s what that API call returned: { "header": { "success": true, "result": "S1000", "message": "SUCCESS" }, "payload": { "macAddr": "<redacted>", "certToken": "<redacted>", "host": "a29vouc2qruduj-ats.iot.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com", "port": 8883, "serial": "<redacted>", "certSvrUrl": "https://cert.iotp.coway.com/iot/v1/cert/r0", "caUrl": "http://rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com/AmazonRootCA1.pem", "privateUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-private.pem.key", "certUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-certificate.pem.crt", "svcCode": "002AIR007", "countryCd": "US" } } So, if we control the response to this call, we control which keys the fan uses to connect to the MQTT server, and also where that MQTT server is. For now, we can write another mitmproxy plugin that injects our own key into this response, and then use that to proxy the MQTT traffic. The plugin code gets kinda long, so I didn’t include it here, but AI generates it fairly quickly. mitmproxy doesn’t decode MQTT, but it can still show us the raw stream: The data looks like a mix of binary and ASCII gibberish, but it’s a standard MQTT protocol stream. When I adjust the fan speed in the app, you can see a new message come from the Coway server to the device. Usually, I’d load this into a traffic dissector and make a table of what gibberish comes in when I press each button in the app, but now… and after a few minutes… There’s enough here now to build our own web server that hands the fan its certificates and configuration during setup, plus our own MQTT server to send it commands. That completely cuts the Coway cloud out of the picture during normal operation, but we’re still using the Coway app to set the device up. We also still need a fairly annoying MitM environment to get the fan to connect to us instead of Coway. Bluetooth setup process # When you use the Coway app to set up the fan, it searches for the device via Bluetooth. I was hoping we could figure out a way to configure the device ourselves, without the app. Plus, if we’re lucky, we might find something else useful along the way. I have reverse-engineered Bluetooth devices before . My old strategy was to get the Android version of the app, decompile it , and then just pore over the code. It’s not always as straightforward as it sounds. Developers often obfuscate their apps, which makes the decompiled code harder to read. Some bytecode also doesn’t decompile cleanly back to source code, which means you end up having to read the raw bytecode. Still, in my opinion, this is usually easier than dealing with iPhone apps. Android apps are usually written in Java (or Kotlin), and it’s just easier to reverse-engineer Java apps than apps compiled from Swift or Objective-C. This time, I tried a new strategy, which was to use the built-in Android Bluetooth debug logs. Then, I connected the phone over USB and asked the AI to drive the phone via adb , look at the Bluetooth logs, and reconstruct the protocol. The AI took a while to churn through this task. Eventually, it identified that the message carrying the Wi-Fi configuration was encrypted. Since we would ultimately need to figure out what algorithm was used for the encryption, we would probably have to look at the decompiled app. Sure enough, the next thing it did was pull the Coway app off the phone, decompile it. Then, it started matching up the source code with the Bluetooth logs. After all that, we can see the provisioning works like this: Read the fan’s identity over Bluetooth from characteristic FFA0 (a “characteristic” is a Bluetooth endpoint you can read or write). This gives you some basic information about the device, including its MAC address. Write an encryption key (20 random lowercase ASCII letters) to characteristic FFA2 : "P001" + protobuf { command: 1, key: Base64(random_letters) } Construct the AES key by concatenating the key from step 2 with the 12 uppercase ASCII characters of the MAC address. Build the configuration payload, which looks like this: { "cmd": 2, "ssid": "Example Wi-Fi", "pwd": "example-wifi-password", "bssid": "AABBCCDDEEFF", "type": 1, "macAddr": "112233445566", "caUrl": "http://192.0.2.1:8080/ca.pem", "certSvrUrl": "https://192.0.2.1:9443/iot/v1/cert/r0", "certToken": "example-enrollment-token", "serial": "EXAMPLE000000000001" } That gets wrapped in protobuf, padded with PKCS#7, and encrypted using the AES key from step 3. Then it gets prefixed with the string “P002” and sent to FFA2 as well. Needless to say, figuring this out end to end from the decompiled Android app would have been very time consuming to do by hand. It’d be at least hours of work (likely days). AI really comes in clutch here. It took the AI about 20 minutes. The good part, though, is that all the data you need to decrypt that payload is in the Bluetooth logs we captured from the phone, so we can check that our reimplementation is correct just from those. From there, the AI made quick work of reimplementing the whole setup flow in a little Python script. I was watching the progress pretty carefully while this was going on. The AI never actually showed me the full payload, but I could see it in the intermediate output of the scripts it was writing. And that’s when I noticed something. Two of the URLs from our capture are set right in this payload ( caUrl and certSvrUrl ). The first tells the fan where to download the root CA cert over plain HTTP, and the second tells it where to POST over HTTPS to get its MQTT configuration. Since we’re the ones sending this payload now, we can point those URLs anywhere we want. Most importantly, that means we don’t have to do any MitM anymore. We just have to run our own server and plug in its URLs when we set up the fan. Home Assistant integration # Based on the findings in this article, I was able to build a Home Assistant custom integration for the fan . My Home Assistant server doesn’t have Bluetooth, and it’s pretty far away from my fan, so I opted to do the provisioning with Web Bluetooth. That way you can bring your laptop next to the fan and provision it to talk to Home Assistant directly. After that, the device talks directly over Wi-Fi to Home Assistant. And, more importantly, it gets bridged from Home Assistant to my Apple Home. All in a day’s work. Now, I can finally click Good Night. If you liked this post, I can email you when I write another one. Subscribe I don't post that often, so it won't be much email. Just a quick FTC required note: When you buy through my links, I may earn a commission. Comments Comments are powered by Artalk and require JavaScript to load. You can also reach me on Mastodon . © 2026 Scott J. Goldman RSS

Write-up: vaibhaav.in/writing/deepseek-v3-jax vaibhaav.in/writing/deepseek-v3-jax/ Resources Readme MIT license Activity Stars 201 stars Watchers 0 watching Forks 17 forks Report repository main Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 7 Commits 7 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date post post rocm rocm .gitignore .gitignore LICENSE LICENSE README.md README.md charts.py charts.py deepseek_v3.py deepseek_v3.py plots.py plots.py prepare_data.py prepare_data.py requirements.txt requirements.txt sample.py sample.py smoke_metal.py smoke_metal.py sources.txt sources.txt tests.py tests.py train.py train.py View all files Repository files navigation README MIT license More items DeepSeek V3 in pure JAX The architecture from the DeepSeek-V3 technical report in 190 lines of pure JAX , pretrained from scratch on a MacBook Air on public-domain detective fiction. No Flax, no Equinox, no PyTorch. Params are plain dicts of arrays and every part of the model is a function you can read top to bottom in deepseek_v3.py . Read the write-up: DeepSeek V3 in 190 lines of pure JAX , with diagrams, the code explained piece by piece, and the results. What's in the 190 lines Idea from the paper What it does Where Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) Caches one small latent per token instead of full keys and values: 480 → 144 numbers per token per layer here mla , init_cache Decoupled RoPE One rotary key shared by all heads, kept outside the compressed latent rope , apply_rope , mla DeepSeekMoE 1 shared expert that always runs + 16 routed experts, top-4 per token route , moe Auxiliary-loss-free balancing A per-expert bias nudges routing toward idle experts; it changes which experts are picked, not their weights update_bias , route Sequence-wise balance loss The small complementary loss from the paper (α = 1e-4) seq_balance_loss Multi-token prediction (MTP) An extra module also predicts the token after next, weighted λ = 0.3 in the loss forward , loss_fn Training and generation bf16 compute on f32 master weights; prefill + decode with the MLA cache make_train_step , generate Results One run of the default config on a MacBook Air M5 (24 GB): Model 36.2M parameters, 13.6M active per token Data 207 books, 21.7M training tokens (Hammett repeated 3×); validation is held-out crime fiction Training 12,000 steps, ~98M tokens (~4.5 epochs), ~2.6 h Speed ~10.7k tokens/s (median) Validation loss 5.02 (step 250) → 3.51 Expert load, with bias 5.7–6.9% per expert (even is 6.25%), at step 2000 Expert load, without bias 0.09–18.6% per expert, at step 2000 With balancing on and off, validation loss at step 2000 was the same (3.921 vs 3.923). The bias evens out the experts without costing anything, which is the paper's claim. Its own words, from the prompt "The fog came in off the": The fog came in off the bay, and the great trees were spreading and the stars were shining. This is an architecture demo, not a strong language model. See the write-up for what worked, what didn't, and what's missing. Try the trained model The v1.0 release has the exact checkpoint and data from the published run. After installing (step 1): mkdir -p data runs/main curl -L -o runs/main/ckpt.pkl https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/releases/download/v1.0/ckpt.pkl # 138 MB curl -L -o data/tokenizer.json https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/releases/download/v1.0/tokenizer.json .venv/bin/python sample.py --prompt " The fog came in off the " --num 3 The checkpoint is a Python pickle, which can run code when loaded. Only load checkpoints from sources you trust. Reproduce it You need an Apple Silicon Mac, Python 3.12 and uv . The published run used 24 GB of memory. No Mac? See Running on CPU . 1. Install git clone https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax.git && cd deepseek-v3-jax uv venv -p 3.12 .venv uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.txt Every version in requirements.txt is pinned. jax-metal 0.1.1 only works with jax==0.4.34 , so don't upgrade JAX. 2. Check your setup JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv/bin/pytest tests.py -q # 39 passed .venv/bin/python smoke_metal.py # optional: what jax-metal supports on your Mac In smoke_metal.py , "grad through 2-axis contraction" fails on jax-metal 0.1.1. That's expected, and the model is written to avoid it. 3. Build the dataset .venv/bin/python prepare_data.py This downloads the 207 books in sources.txt (~120 MB, about 7 minutes), cleans them, trains an 8,192-token BPE tokenizer and writes data/train.bin , data/val.bin and data/tokenizer.json . It should print: train: 211 docs, 83.4M chars, 21.69M tokens val: 4 docs, 1.1M chars, 0.30M tokens The published run's data had these hashes: shasum -a 256 data/train.bin data/val.bin data/tokenizer.json d37aca97e707bb81b6e4d266cc1adfd1f3e3556457c6eb724e495118a734e0bb data/train.bin b7ac285b115e6793b5d36aa5b4bc6e81a5fccfc7af0908a306d3828ebca9c31c data/val.bin c5a142b4006a967c880dda44ad792719d53c16d947da3b6c2332d6132d9967cc data/tokenizer.json You will most likely get different hashes. The Hammett books are pinned to exact Standard Ebooks commits and come out identical, but Project Gutenberg files can't be pinned, and Gutenberg has since re-issued 28 of the 203 books with small edits (mostly accents stripped, like "José" → "Jose"). The token counts come out the same, so training should behave the same. To train on the exact same bytes , skip prepare_data.py and download the published data instead: mkdir -p data for f in train.bin val.bin tokenizer.json ; do curl -L -o data/ $f https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/releases/download/v1.0/ $f ; done shasum -a 256 data/ * .bin data/tokenizer.json # should match the hashes above 4. Train .venv/bin/python train.py # the main run: 12k steps, ~2.6 h .venv/bin/python train.py --steps 2000 --out runs/bias_on # balancing ablation, with the bias .venv/bin/python train.py --steps 2000 --out runs/bias_off --no-bias # ...and without it Each run writes metrics.jsonl (loss, validation loss, per-expert load, biases, tokens/s) and ckpt.pkl (saved at every evaluation) into its --out folder, which defaults to runs/main . Seeds are fixed, but GPU math on Metal isn't bit-for-bit deterministic, so expect your numbers to land close to the ones above rather than match them exactly. 5. Generate .venv/bin/python sample.py --prompt " The fog came in off the " --num 3 Defaults: temperature 0.8, top-k 50, 300 new tokens per sample ( --temp , --top-k , --n ). 6. Make the figures .venv/bin/python plots.py # needs runs/main, runs/bias_on, runs/bias_off JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv/bin/python charts.py # the rest of the write-up's charts Both write into post/figures/ . To redraw the figures without training, download the logs from the release: metrics-main.jsonl , metrics-bias_on.jsonl and metrics-bias_off.jsonl go into runs/main/ , runs/bias_on/ and runs/bias_off/ as metrics.jsonl . charts.py also needs the checkpoint and the data. Running on CPU Everything runs without jax-metal. It's much slower, so use the smaller config: JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv/bin/python train.py --config small --config small (4 layers, 8 experts, top-2, 128-token context) is meant for 8–16 GB Macs too. It has only been checked for a couple of steps, not trained to the end. Running on an AMD GPU (Linux, ROCm) The code runs unmodified on JAX's ROCm backend. rocm/ has a container setup tested on an RX 7600 XT (16 GB): the full run takes ~50 min at ~35k tok/s and reaches val loss 3.527 (vs 3.507 here). Files File What it is deepseek_v3.py The model : config, MLA, MoE, balancing, MTP, loss, train step, cached generation. The 190 lines. train.py Training loop: AdamW with warmup and cosine decay, evaluation, checkpoints, logging prepare_data.py , sources.txt Download, clean and tokenize the corpus sample.py Text generation from a checkpoint tests.py 39 tests: causal masking, cache vs full forward, routing, balancing, MTP targets, NaN handling, bf16 master weights, and more smoke_metal.py Which JAX operations work on Apple's GPU plots.py , charts.py The figures, all drawn from the logs, checkpoint and corpus post/ Diagrams, figures and screenshots from the write-up "190 lines" counts the non-blank, non-comment lines of deepseek_v3.py after its docstring: tail -n +5 deepseek_v3.py | grep -cvE ' ^\s*(#|$) ' # 190 What's simplified Dense MoE compute. Every expert runs on every token and the unpicked ones are zeroed. The routing math is exact, but there's no sparse dispatch or expert parallelism. No weight absorption in MLA. The latent is decompressed explicitly, which is easier to read and slower at inference. Not included: FP8 training, DualPipe, node-limited routing, YaRN context extension, and any post-training. Scale. 36.2M parameters vs 671B, 6 layers vs 61, a 256-token context vs 128K. Data and licensing All training text is public domain in the United States: Dashiell Hammett's Red Harvest , The Dain Curse , The Maltese Falcon and Continental Op stories (CC0 editions from Standard Ebooks ), plus about 200 detective and crime novels from Project Gutenberg . Every source is listed in sources.txt . Public-domain status outside the US may differ. Reference DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report , 2024. License Code: MIT . title: Jonathan Blow – If AI solved coding, why is my software still the same? [video]
Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
body_text: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell | Joshka.net joshka.net writing about resume projects github linkedin mastodon bluesky x soundcloud building: ratatui betamax jk ratatui-diff practice all projects → Terminal borders that don't cost a cell 2026-11-13 :: tags:  #Ghostty   #Ratatui   #TUI   #Terminals This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab. I maintain Ratatui , so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us. Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough ┌──┐ by hand to have opinions about this. The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough: So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors. Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded. Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters: Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets. What I'd use it for Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side. Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top. Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge. Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text. Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it. Up close The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback: The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame: Charts Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui: And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines: In motion Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog: Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here: Show the cell grid What box characters can't do The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that. Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration. You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included. Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little │ cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box (pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never get copied, which cuts both ways. How it works A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors. The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters ( ▖▗▘▝ and friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better way to do that part. One problem at a time. The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them. Styles and joints Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it. When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The stroke with the higher priority wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below. That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor. The wire format Everything is one DCS string with a namespace: ESC P 1 + b cell-border ; OP ; FIELDS... ESC \ The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders: ESC P 1 + b cell-border;pen;48;32;7aa2f7;0;0 ESC \ bottom edge, blue: an underline hello ESC [ 0 m SGR 0 clears the pen There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives without a cell-border reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it, the same as any unknown DCS. The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope. Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible. The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the 1 in DCS 1 + b ). That's v1 in the old sense, before we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer. Prior art Parts of this have been done before: DEC ruled lines in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color. SGR 51 to 65 : framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge. The Win32 console has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. PDCurses and X/Open curses ( WA_TOP , WA_LEFT and friends) have similar attributes. These are the closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves. IBM 3270 terminals can outline whole input fields. What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol. My own first prototype was in Rio ( raphamorim/rio#1947 ), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that. The awkward (edge) cases When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed. Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them. Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in. Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell. On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB. Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on. Try it The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode): git clone - b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ghostty.git cd ghostty zig build - Doptimize=ReleaseFast - Dxcframework-target=native open zig-out/Ghostty.app Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation: python3 scripts/cell-borders.py # the default view python3 scripts/cell-borders.py - -styles # line styles, joints and outside fill Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: p placement, c colors, h blocks, j junctions, e halves, s styles and l live. w cycles the stroke width, b turns borders off so you can compare, and q quits. Each view also has a matching flag ( --placement , --styles and so on) if you want to start on it. The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch . It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above: git clone - b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ratatui.git cd ratatui cargo run - p tiling-panes Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. n and v split, x closes, and right click opens a pane menu. Press b to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or g to shade alternate cells and see where the edges are. The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop: To run it: cargo run - p cell-border-top It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. 1 to 4 show and hide the boxes, b and g work the same as in the panes demo, and h or ? lists the rest of the keys. It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the sysinfo dependency. What I'd like to hear I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion , or on Hacker News and Lobsters . Thanks for reading! body_text: Announcing Rust 1.100.0 | Rust Blog Rust Blog Rust Install Learn Tools Governance Community 🖌 Light Dark System Announcing Rust 1.100.0 Nov. 12, 2026 · The Rust Release Team The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup , you can get 1.100.0 with: $ rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0 . If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel ( rustup default beta ) or the nightly channel ( rustup default nightly ). Please report any bugs you might come across! What's in 1.100.0 stable Never type Allocator API DropGuard API Conjuring zero-sized types Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo min-publish-age Stabilized APIs Never type After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable ! This also completes the project goal for this work. The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return , break , and std::process::exit , also have the type ! . Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if : fn mrrrow ( option : Option < u32 > ) { let value = match option { // `x` has type `u32` Some ( x ) => x , // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`, // allowing the `match` to pass type checking. None => return , } ; // ... } While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions ( -> ! ), this release allows naming the never type anywhere: fn infallible_unwrap < T > ( res : Result < T , ! > ) -> T { // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before let Ok ( v ) = res ; v } Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using ! . This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization). Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible , we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024 . This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable. We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it. Allocator API This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api , enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box . These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait. This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal . A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon! DropGuard : run a closure on every exit path The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return , ? , or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket . Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard : a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped. DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable. DropGuard also implements a dismiss associated function [1] which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure: use std :: mem :: DropGuard ; use std :: num :: ParseIntError ; /// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`. /// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged. fn parse_all ( nums : & mut Vec < u32 > , strings : & [ & str ] ) -> Result < ( ) , ParseIntError > { let len = nums . len ( ) ; let mut nums = DropGuard :: new ( nums , move | nums | { nums . truncate ( len ) ; // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure } ) ; for s in strings { nums . push ( s . parse ( ) ? ) ; // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back } DropGuard :: dismiss ( nums ) ; // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard Ok ( ( ) ) } Conjuring zero-sized types As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this. This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst . Instead of transmuting () , MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() , or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing. Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition. Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it. Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g. warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber` --> Cargo.toml:23:1 | 23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ | = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber` A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built. This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml , completing this project goal . See also the other lints that have been introduced . Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir . At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like --features , can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir . These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees. The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory. This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal , unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking. We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases. Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns. You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml : [ registry ] global-min-publish-age = " 3 days " When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back: $ cargo update Updating crates.io index Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago) Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago) When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update: $ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE = a l l o w cargo update clap - -precise 4.6.9 Updating crates.io index Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days) The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it. A few things to keep in mind: This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back. cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed. Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would. Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal , including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases. Stabilized APIs impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for Vec<T, A> impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for &[T] impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for &mut [T] std::alloc::Allocator std::alloc::Global std::alloc::System impl Allocator for Global impl Allocator for System impl<A: Allocator> Allocator for &A impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Box<T, A> impl<A: Allocator> Allocator for &mut A impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Arc<T, A> impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Rc<T, A> Box::new_in Box::from_raw_in Box::from_non_null_in Box::into_raw_with_allocator Box::into_non_null_with_allocator Box::allocator Vec::new_in Vec::with_capacity_in Vec::from_raw_parts_in Vec::from_parts_in Vec::into_raw_parts_with_allocator Vec::into_parts_with_allocator Vec::allocator Child::main_thread_handle impl Default for std::sync::Once bool::toggle Box::take Box::map Rc::map Arc::map impl AsRef<T> for ! impl AsMut<T> for ! core::mem::DropGuard core::mem::conjure_zst UnsafeCell::replace UnsafeCell::as_ref_unchecked UnsafeCell::as_mut_unchecked str::trim_prefix str::trim_suffix [T]::trim_prefix [T]::trim_suffix Path::trim_prefix Vec::from_fn os::windows::process::CommandExt::show_window Other changes Check out everything that changed in Rust , Cargo , and Clippy . Contributors to 1.100.0 Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. title: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
body_text: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy - 9to5Mac Skip to main content Toggle main menu 9to5Mac Logo Go to the 9to5Mac home page Switch site 9to5Toys 9to5Google Logo 9to5Google Electrek Drone DJ Logo DroneDJ Space Explored About Privacy Toggle social menu Toggle dark mode Search for: Submit Toggle search form Forums Store Podcasts Apple@Work Happy Hour 9to5Mac Daily Overtime iPhone iPhone Mac Mac MacBook Pro MacBook Air iMac Mac mini Mac Studio Mac Pro iPad iPad Pro iPad Air iPad mini iPad iPadOS Watch Apple Watch Apple Watch Ultra Apple Health Apple Watch SE Vision Vision Pro visionOS Music and TV Apple Music AirPods HomePod Apple TV Guides Reviews How Tos AAPL Apple Store Apple Arcade Apple Card Apple Silicon Apple One Apple Fitness+ CarPlay Siri HomeKit Toggle dark mode AI Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy Ryan Christoffel  | Nov 10 2026 - 11:15 am PT 0 Comments Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs. New ‘Harbor’ app revealed at Apple: ‘turns your Mac into a private AI inference server’ The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more. It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server. Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details: Apple is working on a new app called Harbor Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf — Aaron (@aaronp613) November 10, 2026 As the post notes, here’s what the app does: Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone. And here are the feature highlights: Setup in minutes, not hours : “Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you’re running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.” Download and run models directly : “Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.” Cluster for scale : “Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer’s capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.” Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead. Are you interested in using Harbor on your Mac? Let us know in the comments.
