title: Tim Peters has died
body_text: In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 - Core Development - Discussions on Python.org = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> Discussions on Python.org In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 Core Development guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:36am 1 I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15. It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python ( PEP 20 ), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that. Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float , because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing. Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink> ) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”. At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort : a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android. Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs, –Guido 234 Likes guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:41am 2 Feel free to respond with your own Tim anecdotes. I could not cover everything he did. 12 Likes Rosuav (Chris Angelico) November 11, 2026, 6:04am 3 Very sad news. I have had the privilege and pleasure of discussing MANY topics with Tim, and his input into technical discussions has always been something I value very highly. He never treated you like an idiot, never dismissed your concerns out of hand, always answered and explained. I exchanged emails with him many times, but geography meant that sadly, we never met in person. 20 Likes hugovk (Hugo van Kemenade) November 11, 2026, 6:13am 4 Guido van Rossum: In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. From the start to the end. His last post concluded: Which is all a long-winded say of saying the real world is more complicated than our clean abstractions hope for . 51 Likes mcdonc (Chris McDonough) November 11, 2026, 6:41am 5 I wrote this some time ago about Tim: “”" I worked with Tim and the rest of Python Labs for a couple of years in the early 2000s. Tim was a hugely positive influence on me throughout my Python career. Before I had ever spoken to Tim, he was already legendary. He had worked for Cray Research writing compilers for supercomputers, and for Dragon Systems, writing speech-to-text software at a time when such a task was considered largely impossible. He took up Python on a lark in its very early days, becoming something like Python’s second real user after Guido. Guido came to rely on Tim heavily. Tim will demur about this, but as far as I can tell, Tim and Guido were largely partners in the design evolution of very early Python, and before most important features made it in to Python, you could be sure that they had been examined from every angle, shaken, stirred, and thunk about very hard by both of them. Tim often played the role of gatekeeper and polisher. You have Tim to thank at least partially if you were a refugee from Java or Microsoft languages, which made excuses for their sprawling verbosity, complexity, and poor readability. Python, at the time, made none of those and had none of that (it now does). Tim was crucial in ensuring it stayed that way during his most active years. He will claim differently, but, by my observation, it is no accident that Python ballooned in complexity after his exit as day-to-day core developer. Perhaps this was more due to the resignation of Guido as BDFL and the new Steering Council model, which was also coincident, but not having Tim around didn’t help either. It was pure joy to read Tim’s Usenet and mail list posts, which were full of humor and good nature and measured positivity and not a little winking darkness. They somehow resonated with me on my journey from becoming a new programmer to a not-so-new programmer and they lit a path to becoming one on which you could be dramatically competent without becoming cryptic and insufferable. He was intensely knowledgeable, and unfailingly precise when arguing for or against some design change. But he was always gentle and patient and matter-of-fact, preferring to use humor and warmth rather than bile and authority as the currency in which he dealt. Tim penned “the Zen of Python” (“beautiful is better than ugly…”) which can be seen via “import this” to this day. You can see a bit of his wonderful humor and style in the prelude to his introduction of the poem . His enthusiasm was infectious, and in the days when he was most involved, most everyone could be witnessed spouting Tim-isms (winks and “'lys” and whatnot). When I did get the chance to work with Tim, he was just as influential. He had absolutely no pretensions. If I hadn’t already known him to be a computer savant, I would have assumed he was a biker or mechanic due to his long grey locks, full mustache and and working-class fashion sense. I would later find out that he had indeed worked at Harley-Davidson. I think he’s originally from Wisconsin, but an East- or West-Coaster not fluent in Midwest tongues could be excused for believing his disarming accent is Chicagoan. He seemed just like a regular-looking neighborhood punch-the-clock guy, not unlike all the mechanics and deliverymen and cooks and dishwashers and event staff I’d worked around as a kid and in my 20s. Except he was pretty much the smartest guy in every room he entered. Tim’s demeanor and lack of pretense inspired me to think that despite my own lack of education and pedigree, with enough effort and grace, that I might become a half-competent programmer. And eventualy I did. But before meeting Tim, it was not a given. I was alienated by the pretensions of my community peers, and I was often reminded that they were not necessary only by Tim. He was somewhat private. He could often be found with a pen and paper outside the building just standing alone, staring blankly off into space, presumably thinking about some mind-boggling algorithmic topic with which he had just been charged by our CTO, or perhaps mentally designing some aspect of a pet project, scribbling something every few minutes. He applied himself to our code, which included a custom database written in C and Python. He diagnosed and fixed a data-destroying bug in that byzantine codebase for our largest customer. This saved the account, and likely gave us enough runway for another year or so. Everyone who worked there was in awe of his programming and debugging skills, and while we tried our best to let the poor man be, we often asked him questions, many of which were pedestrian and dull. I remember one of our teammates trying to engage him into a debugging session, claiming that some fault seemed to happen every six runs. He smiled winkingly and asked “have you grepped the source for six?” It was a minor jab but given the sincerity of the question, and the person from which it had come, it occurred to me at the time that it might not be the worst theory of debugging from which to start. Tim was a Director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014, bringing Python across an uncanny valley from a time where it was “interesting but ignorable” to “the planet’s default language” along with a cast of other incredible people. If you use Python, it’s not in small part due to Tim. When I started my own open source projects, it was Tim whom I channeled during design discussions and sprints. I quite consciously used tricks I had learned from him to make the process fun and welcoming. Rather than become prickly about some technical conflict, I would try to use low-brow humor to defuse things and I would try very hard to learn everything I could about the topic before responding such that I could gain and rely on the respect of other contributors. I often failed, of course, because I’m not Tim, but I was at least a twentieth a Tim, and at the time, I think my co-contributors would have agreed that the projects I led were fun and worthwhile to work on. It is in this way that Tim’s influence is likely most obvious to people today, because I’m not the only one who channeled him; any Python project started between 1995 and 2010 has a bit of Tim culture in it. “”" In sadness, . C 44 Likes duncathan (Dunc Graham) November 11, 2026, 6:46am 6 As a young child, only about 15, I first learned timsort. Some dozen years later, I had the briefest opportunity to exchange words with Tim himself on this forum. What a treat to have had that chance, just in time. RIP 12 Likes encukou (Petr Viktorin) November 11, 2026, 8:32am 7 When I was finishing university, head full of textbook algorithms, I read Objects/listsort.txt and was overwhelmed by how much depth, rigor, common sense and humanity can fit in a technical note. That was when I picked a programming language. 33 Likes pitrou (Antoine Pitrou) November 11, 2026, 9:53am 8 Tim’s main legacy for me has been the Zen of Python, which - despite being less cited nowadays - has been so useful and influential as a framework for elegance and clarity, and has informed so many people in their daily practice (and I cannot find a better way to describe him than as an excellent practitioner ). He was already less active when I started contributing around 2007; in fact my most frequent interactions with him have been in the recent years while he grew a slightly more confrontational attitude in some discussions, including here on d.p.o. I believe [1] he was acting with the best of intentions and was still deeply caring for the community he had been such a pivotal member of; acting with the same objectives as others, but having trouble to understand that different means might be used towards the same ends. and I might be full of myself here ↩︎ 19 Likes malemburg (Marc-André Lemburg) November 11, 2026, 9:58am 9 This is so sad and such a big loss for Python. Tim has given us a lot and we owe him. He was one of the extremely smart people who drew me into PythonLand in the late 1990s. Coming out of university, I was amazed how approachable, down to earth and humurous really great folks can be. Rest in Peace, Tim, and thanks-for-being-one-of-those-great-people-ly, Marc 22 Likes pf_moore (Paul Moore) November 11, 2026, 10:51am 10 So sad. I never had the chance to meet Tim in person, but his posts were always a delight to read, full of knowledge, insight and humour. I learned more than I can express from him. He will be missed. 15 Likes hodgestar (Simon Cross) November 11, 2026, 10:55am 11 One of the great souls, and roughly treated here near the end. 15 Likes nas (Neil Schemenauer) November 11, 2026, 12:31pm 12 A +1 to what Chris wrote. Tim was always pragmatic, preferring simple solutions over complex ones. In the early days of syntax highlighting in text editors, like Emacs and Vim, I remember that Python’s triple-quoted strings were tricky to get right. They span multiple lines and opening and closing tokens are identical, so it’s easy to get out of sync. Doctests make things especially tricky. I was telling Tim about some techniques I was using in the Vim syntax file to make it work more reliably. I don’t recall the editor Tim used (some commercial program on Windows) but he explained how he did it in his editor. Open the syntax highlighting config window, for open string token, type three quotes, for close string, type three quotes, close config window. Job done. That tickled him. He primarily used Windows 95 or 98 at a time when many Python core devs used NT, Unix, or Linux. He said if you installed all of Microsoft’s updates, it was quite reliable. Maybe he preferred it because it worked for him and there was no reason to change. Or, he found it useful when supporting people, since Windows was the most common platform Python was used on. Tim was about the furthest thing from an elitist you could be. This Bible quote comes to mind for me: “Ye shall know them by their fruits.”. Tim gave us a lot of fruit. I poked around at Python 2.4, since that seems a good version to show off the things he worked on. His contributions were all over the codebase but I’ll point out a few that stand out to me. pymalloc was contributed by Vladimir Marangozov but it was Tim who polished it to diamond-like form. A memory allocator is one of those things where it is impossible to have something completely optimal; you always make tradeoffs. Tim’s special contribution in that unit is Py_ADDRESS_IN_RANGE . It is well commented, if you want to understand how it works. Technically, it relies on undefined behavior but Tim figured it should work in practice. It did so for many years. At some point I wanted to increase the pymalloc pool size, since typical RAM sizes had increased so much since 2000. Tim helped me optimize the address_in_range() check. TimSort is a good example of Tim’s approach to software problems. Someone must have “nerd sniped” him on the problem of sorting. He already had an encyclopedic knowledge of the classic algorithms, like you’d find in Knuth. He spent a few days reading the recent research papers on sorting. With that knowledge and throwing in a few twists of his own, he made TimSort. He was always thinking of the common case, the favorable case as well as the worst-case scenarios. TimSort does all three well (it exploits already sorted runs, and uses galloping during merging to copy long stretches efficiently). Speaking of Knuth, the dict object algorithms were heavily optimized by Tim. The C file contains lots of comments. He also wrote dictnotes , which is a good example of his technical writing. Another example is weakref.txt , which I think Tim wrote after fixing a particularly difficult GC bug revealed by ZODB (while working at Zope Corp). On the topic of GC, the initial version of the cyclic garbage collector was written by me, merged before the 2.0 release. It was Tim who polished it into robust and well-performing shape. Likewise, I wrote the initial version of “simple generators” but it was Tim who put them on solid foundation, both the PEP and the implementation. Tim was skilled with numerical algorithms and error analysis, and Python benefited from his expertise. The float object and math module got special attention from him. He also worked on the Karatsuba multiplication algorithms in longobject . In addition to the C code, Tim also wrote beautiful Python code. As an example, see the N-Queens and Knight’s tour solvers in test_generators.py . He wrote the initial version of doctest . Some more examples of his work: difflib , pickletools , tabnanny (she shows no mercy!). It’s clear that Tim enjoyed writing code and solving problems. It’s also the case that he spent many thousands of hours of his time doing things primarily to help his fellow humans, without expectation of financial gain or of glory. Thank you, friend, for that and thank you for setting such an example. 46 Likes vinitkme (Vinit Kumar) November 11, 2026, 12:58pm 13 Thanks for everything Tim. Zen of Python has always been and will be my programming " North Star" and I strive to use it in every language I work with. Your impact has been on many of us Python Programmers and our families lives. Thank you and rest in peace! 9 Likes Stefan2 (Stefan Pochmann) November 11, 2026, 1:09pm 14 I’ve been fearing this since I noticed his absence end of July, dreading the thought whenever I saw his name but still no new activity. I’ve had quite a few interactions with Tim, he was one of my main contact points to Python, and he was the one who added me to Misc/ACKS . Thank you for everything, Tim. 8 Likes Paddy3118 (Paddy3118) November 11, 2026, 1:30pm 16 GNU Tim. 5 Likes diegor (Diego Russo) November 11, 2026, 2:39pm 17 I wish I’d had the chance to meet Tim in person. We had just a few exchanges on social media, but I always enjoyed reading his messages. There was always something to learn from his experience, his perspective and his way of thinking. Reading the memories shared here by those who knew and worked with him makes me regret even more that I never had that opportunity. I remember when Timsort was created. I was at university, studying algorithms, and it was a big deal at the time. But it’s the Zen of Python that influenced me most personally. “Now is better than never.” That sentence has stayed with me since I started using Python in the early 2000s. Over the years, it has become one of my personal mottos, encouraging me to keep trying, strive to do better and step outside my comfort zone, both in life and at work. We’ll probably never know what the 20th aphorism of the Zen of Python would have been. But perhaps that’s OK. I like to think that Tim left us the freedom to fill that space with something meaningful to each of us. Thank you, Tim, for everything you gave to Python and for the impact your work and words had on people. Rest in peace. 15 Likes holdenweb (Steve Holden) November 11, 2026, 3:09pm 18 Tim and I originally thought we first met fairly shortly after we both moved to Virginia, and became friends over Chinese lunches and discussions with Guido about starting a new Python conference. As we got to know each other better we realised that we had seen each other once before, when I visited a fellow academic’s office in Manchester, England, and Tim was there representing Cray Research back in 1983. Small world. After PythonLabs dissolved on Guido’s departure for the West coast the lunches eventually became a regular date at our local PF Chang, where Tim would invariably end with their huge “Mountain of Chocolate” dessert. The resulting sugar rush was often amusing. Tim was well-known long before I arrived in the Python world, and remained so after I left it. His technical contributions to Python, now the most popular programming language in the world, are legion. Just as significant, if not more so, was the way he communicated the joy, both of being a programmer and a human being. He was deeply affected by the ban imposed on him for ideological reasons by the Python Steering Committee but did not let that affect his desire to help others, which was on display until the end. I respected Tim above anyone else in the Python world for his wisdom, his witty humour and his deep humanity. There won’t be another one like him. Goodbye, old friend. 28 Likes sdeibel (Stephan Deibel) November 11, 2026, 3:41pm 19 This is very sad. I worked with Tim for quite a few years in context of the PSF board and of course also knew him from IPC and PyCons, starting in the relatively early days. He stood out to me almost immediately because so obviously utterly brilliant and yet with such a kind, helpful, respectful, good-humored way about him. One of the best people I’ve known, he was an inspiration to me and I think clearly also to very many others. Thanks, Tim, you will be missed. 13 Likes mwichmann (Mats Wichmann) November 11, 2026, 3:42pm 20 I only met Tim once, along with Guido, in 2001. I was writing a Python training course, and the training company wanted to arrange for “the experts” to get a look at it, so on a week I was in Reston working on it, we sat down over a meal. It wasn’t a very good course (“if I knew then what I know now”, a quarter century later…), but they generously gave of their time to critique, including Tim’s trademark humor, and I so appreciated it. He will be missed! 8 Likes mdickinson (Mark Dickinson) November 11, 2026, 4:00pm 22 Tim was hugely influential on my own CPython core development journey. Initially that influence was through his voluminous writings, mailing list discussions and his code itself: when I joined the core dev team in 2008, Tim himself was absent from the scene in person, but very much present through his many many contributions. Later on, after his return to core development, I was privileged to interact more directly with Tim on many topics. His gentle erudition, his humour and his patience were endless. Rest in peace, Tim. You will be sorely missed. 18 Likes next page → Home Categories Guidelines Terms of Service Privacy Policy Powered by Discourse , best viewed with JavaScript enabled

title: FAA issues national ground stop – lifted 4.5 hours later
body_text: FAA lifts ground stop hours after stranding thousands of flights across the U.S. IE 11 is not supported. For an optimal experience visit our site on another browser. Boston Bay Area South Florida San Diego Connecticut tv Today Nightly News Meet the Press Dateline Featured NBC News Now Nightly Films Stay Tuned Special Features Newsletters Podcasts Listen Now Business in America More From NBC NBC.COM NBCU Academy Peacock NEXT STEPS FOR VETS NBC News Site Map Help Follow NBC News news Alerts There are no new alerts at this time Search Search Facebook Twitter Email SMS Blue Sky Whatsapp Print Reddit Flipboard Pinterest Linkedin Latest Stories Meet the Press U.S. News World Sports Business Health Selected Tipline U.S. news Thousands of flights canceled or delayed Saturday after FAA’s nationwide ground stop Atlanta, Chicago O’Hare and New York’s JFK were among the hardest-hit airports as airlines worked to get planes and crews back into position. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Duffy details timeline of ground stop, demands more FAA funding 06:00 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 13, 2026, 4:09 PM EST / Updated Nov. 14, 2026, 1:56 AM EST By Corky Siemaszko , Tom Costello , Joy Y. Wang and Marlene Lenthang Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday. By 9:30 a.m. ET Saturday, flight tracking service FlightAware had logged more than 3,700 cancellations and 1,990 delays. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Chicago O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport were among the hubs experiencing the most disruptions, according to FlightAware. The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, and airports across the country filled with stranded passengers. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines said Friday evening that they were resuming flights. A senior government official told NBC News on Saturday that the system that caused the outage had been identified and taken offline. The FAA said a router sent too much data, overloading older air traffic control equipment. What caused the ground stop Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday evening that controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and communications with aircraft at 3:36 p.m. ET. The FAA issued the ground stop at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Duffy said the FAA retained some radar and communications capabilities and halted departures as a precaution. Medical flights, including those transporting organs for transplant, were allowed to continue. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday night that authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack. “FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage. Why disruptions continued Saturday Airlines had to get planes and crews back into position after the ground stop, and some crews may have reached limits on how long they could stay on duty. Duffy said he expected air traffic to recover before the Thanksgiving rush. But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport had run out of room to park aircraft and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, a source with knowledge told NBC News. Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded. “At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’” Werne said he began hearing from friends who were also stuck on planes, including one on a runway in Chicago. His plane headed back to the terminal so passengers could get off. DHS says nationwide ground stop was not a cyberattack: 'We are built to handle crisis like this' 02:31 Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system that uses analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years. In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport went black during a 90-second outage. Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported. Mullin said although authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest there was one. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said. Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X . Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday. Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations. Chicago O'Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers. Jacek Boczarski / Anadolu via Getty “Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.” With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said. Turn SVG artwork into machine embroidery, edit stitches visually, and create designs with AI agents via MCP. zigzag.diy/ Topics brother-skitch embroidery embroidery-digitizing embroidery-software machine-embroidery macos mcp model-context-protocol rust svg vector-editor windows Resources Readme Apache-2.0 license Activity Stars 811 stars Watchers 7 watching Forks 43 forks Report repository main Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 12 Commits 12 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date .github/ workflows .github/ workflows examples examples packaging packaging src src vendor vendor .gitignore .gitignore CHANGELOG.md CHANGELOG.md Cargo.lock Cargo.lock Cargo.toml Cargo.toml LICENSE LICENSE NOTICE NOTICE README.md README.md RELEASE.md RELEASE.md THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md build.rs build.rs View all files Repository files navigation README Apache-2.0 license More items ZigZag Visit zigzag.diy ZigZag is a visual embroidery editor built in Rust for performance, with built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) support so AI agents can create and edit designs alongside you. Turn SVG artwork into stitches, fine-tune it in the editor, and export PES, DST, EXP, JEF, or VP3 for broad compatibility with embroidery machines—or send designs directly to a Brother Skitch (PP1) over Bluetooth . Draw in Illustrator, draw in ZigZag, or let an agent draw. The Rust engine and zigzag command-line tool power the same workflow outside the editor. See ZigZag in action zigzag-demo.mp4 Stitching on a Brother Skitch (PP1) Download the video (MP4, 1080p) · Original post on X . Download for Mac Download ZigZag.dmg For Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, macOS 11 or later. Open the DMG, then drag ZigZag into Applications. The release is signed and notarized by Apple. No Rust installation is needed. Or with Homebrew : brew install --cask simpsoka/zigzag/zigzag To update a Homebrew installation: brew upgrade --cask --greedy simpsoka/zigzag/zigzag Starting with version 0.1.3, ZigZag also offers an in-app updater: it tells you when there's a newer release and installs it when you say (ZigZag › Check for Updates…). Download for Windows Download ZigZag for Windows — the ZigZag-<version>-x86_64-windows.zip asset on the latest release. For 64-bit Windows 10 (version 1709 or later) and Windows 11. Unzip it and double-click ZigZag.exe . Windows SmartScreen warns on apps without a Microsoft-trusted signature the first time they run; click More info → Run anyway . No Rust installation is needed. Download for Linux Download ZigZag for Linux — the ZigZag-<version>-x86_64-linux.tar.gz asset on the latest release. For x86-64 Linux desktops with glibc 2.35 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+), X11 or Wayland, and OpenGL. Extract the archive and run ./zigzag-studio inside the extracted folder. It also includes the zigzag CLI and zigzag-mcp bridge; no Rust installation is needed. See the included README.txt for runtime dependencies and Bluetooth setup. Release notes and checksums · Changelog · Publishing a release zigzag/ src/svg.rs SVG import (usvg): fill and stroke parts, transforms, text src/document/ editable document; settings saved back into SVG ids, layout edits as SVG transforms, lettering src/params.rs stitch settings tokens + fabric presets src/stitch/fill.rs tatami fill (scanline sections, staggered rows) src/stitch/satin.rs satin columns: two rails, auto-satin, underlays, short stitches, lean src/stitch/columns.rs shapes that branch or have holes, cut into satin columns src/stitch/stroke.rs running / triple-run stitch src/boolean.rs polygon booleans and offsets (i_overlay) src/design.rs planner: overlap removal, cap order, routing, trims src/route.rs travel out of sight: a way through fills and under what covers src/checks.rs digitizing checks (sizes, widths, lettering, hoop) src/machine/profile.rs machine profiles: hoops and file format, built in (profiles.json) or your own src/formats/ PES (+PEC), DST, EXP, JEF, VP3, Skitch PEN writers; PES/PEC/DST/EXP/JEF readers; preview; worksheet src/machine/ Skitch Bluetooth protocol (+ btleplug client, `ble` feature) src/studio/ editor (egui on OpenGL via glow) + MCP server (`gui` feature) src/mcp_bridge.rs stdio ↔ HTTP bridge for MCP clients that launch a command Build cargo build --release # CLI + MCP bridge, no system deps cargo build --release --features gui,ble # + the studio editor and Skitch upload Linux needs the usual X11/Wayland and OpenGL dev libraries for gui . libdbus is vendored for ble . Stitch types Type What it does Works on Fill (tatami) Staggered rows, any angle, with underlay (edge walk + rows) and pull compensation Filled shapes Satin Zigzag column between two rails, with center/contour/zigzag underlay, pull compensation and short stitches on tight curves; plain, S-stitch or zig-zag top stitching; stitches square across or leaning ( lean=8 ); several threads across the column (multicolor satin) Strokes (any width); Ink/Stitch-style two-rail paths with rungs; filled shapes : rings use inner/outer outline, bars and crescents split at their tips, letters and other shapes that branch or have a counter are cut into columns where the branches part (a P into its stem and bowl, a T into bar and stem), or border follows the outline Run Running stitch, single or triple (bean) Strokes and outlines Contour Rows that follow the outline inward, or one spiral out from the center (Ink/Stitch's circular fill) Filled shapes Blanket E-stitch: a line with prongs into the shape Edges, appliqué Appliqué Placement line → stop → tack-down → stop → satin cover Filled shapes Manual Every path point is a needle point Imported machine files, pen tool Meander One wandering line through the shape, quilting style: light and soft Filled shapes Ripple Open running-stitch rows following the outline, or one spiral Filled shapes Cross-stitch A grid of X's, sewn as rows of half-crosses out and back Filled shapes Tartan Woven stripes in several threads (a mirrored sett you edit in the panel), each thread its own color block Filled shapes Satins wider than 7 mm are auto-split (shorter, staggered stitches) and use auto spacing (narrow columns more open, wide ones denser). Planner features: Remove overlaps: fill hidden under later objects isn't sewn (keeps 0.5 mm of overlap). Cap order: center-out, bottom-up, grouped by color, still respecting layering. Routing: travel stitches stay out of sight: straight across where a straight line stays inside the fill, otherwise round the inside of its outline (Ink/Stitch's underpath), otherwise any way through the fill (round its holes, through its necks), under a satin that's about to be sewn, or under whatever is sewn later on top. An object's last piece is sewn toward the end the next object can be reached from. So satin lettering sewn stroke by stroke needs cuts only between letters when each stroke is followed by one that covers the way to it (a T's stem before its bar; an E's bars before its stem). A fill in separate parts is sewn part by part, each part's underlay and top together. So a fill with cut-outs, or a dither in scattered blocks under another color, is sewn with few or no cuts. Trims only where none of that works (up to 50 mm of travel). Sewing control per object: a start and an end point (where the thread comes in and leaves, so the next object is close), trim after, stop after (to lay foam or trim appliqué). What's left to cut is the document's Connect bar: drag it to sew across gaps up to N mm (between objects, or the parts of one) with running stitches instead of cuts. Those stitches show, so the panel counts the cuts saved as you drag and the canvas lights up what would be sewn. Fabric presets: standard, thin cotton cap, structured cap, knit. Checks: narrow fills, wide/narrow satins, small lettering, tiny gaps, fully covered objects, hoop fit. Group colors: reorder to cut thread changes without breaking layering. Mac app On a Mac with Rust and the Xcode command line tools ( xcode-select --install ): packaging/macos/make-app.sh --install # builds ZigZag.app and copies it to /Applications packaging/macos/make-app.sh --dmg # also makes dist/ZigZag-<version>.dmg to share packaging/macos/make-app.sh --universal # one app for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs packaging/macos/make-app.sh --release # the DMG to publish: universal, signed, notarized --release signs with your Developer ID and has Apple notarize the app and the DMG, so it opens on any Mac without warnings. Once, beforehand: add a Developer ID Application certificate (Xcode › Settings › Accounts › Manage Certificates › +), make an app-specific password at account.apple.com, and save the notarization credentials in your keychain: xcrun notarytool store-credentials zigzag-notary --apple-id YOUR_APPLE_ID --team-id YOUR_TEAM_ID The app bundles the studio, the zigzag command-line tool and the MCP bridge. To use the command line from anywhere: ln -s /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag /usr/local/bin/zigzag . For Claude Desktop, point the MCP config at /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag-mcp . Without --release the app is signed ad hoc, not notarized. It opens normally on the Mac that built it. On another Mac, macOS blocks it the first time: open System Settings › Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway (on macOS 14 and earlier, right-click the app and choose Open instead). macOS asks for Bluetooth permission the first time you send to the Skitch. Studio The approved embroidered icons live in packaging/macos/AppIcon.png (light) and packaging/macos/AppIcon-dark.png (dark). The Mac build regenerates both multi-resolution .icns files; run bash packaging/macos/make-icons.sh to regenerate them separately. Finder and the unopened app use the light icon. While the studio is running, its Dock icon follows the app's light/dark theme, including the ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark override. zigzag-studio [design.svg | logo.png] [--mcp-port 7878 | --no-mcp | --mcp-stdio] Laid out like Illustrator, styled like a Mac app: Tools down the left edge: Select (V), Direct Selection (A), Hand (H), Pen (P): click for corners, drag for curves (Option breaks the handles, Shift keeps 45°, Space moves the point being placed); while drawing, Option lends it the Anchor Point tool (drag a segment to bend it, a handle to move it alone, click a smooth point for a corner) and ⌘ lends Direct Selection (drag a point or handle, then keep drawing), and on a selected path Option-drag bends a segment too. Illustrator's Pen group is behind it: Add Anchor Point (+) clicks a point onto an outline without changing its shape, Delete Anchor Point (-) clicks one out (Option swaps the two while held), and Anchor Point (Shift+C) converts points between smooth and corner and drags one handle alone. Press and hold the Pen (or right-click it) for the group's flyout, Option-click it to step through the group, or tear the group off into a toolbar of its own with the strip at the flyout's edge; the Shape tools work the same way. Brush (B), with VectorCraft's path clean-up tools in its group: Smooth (drag along a path to take the wobble out: fewer points, smoother curves; Smoothness in the bar above), Path Eraser (drag across a path to cut that part away) and Join (scrub between two open ends to join them, or an open path's two ends to close it). Shapes (M rectangle, L ellipse, \ line; hold or right-click for polygon and star), Rotate (Shift+R; R alone is the Run stitch), Fill Angle (G), Measure (I), Text (T). Below them, the selection's thread swatch: click it for the thread color picker. Curves, the Illustrator way: the Pen clicks corners and click-drags curves (Option while dragging breaks the handle for a sharp turn; Shift keeps points and handles at 45°; hold Space to move the point you're placing). Click the last point to make it a corner, or drag from it to start the next curve in a new direction. Click the first point to close a shape; Enter, Esc, ⌘-click or another tool ends a line and keeps it. With a path selected, the Pen continues it from an open end, adds a point on its outline, deletes a point you click, and Option-click turns a point corner ↔ smooth (Option-drag pulls out new handles). While drawing, click another open path's end to join the two into one. The cursor shows what a click will do. Direct Selection drags points and handles of any shape from your SVG (circles and rects become paths); dragging a curve bends it under the pointer (Option-drag bends a straight one; a plain drag moves it); Delete removes points, arrows nudge them. Smart guides while drawing (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U): Pen points, shape corners and dragged points land on other objects' anchors and centers, where two outlines cross, on an outline, on 45° rays from the last point (level and upright handles too), or in line with any of those, with a magenta label saying which ("anchor", "intersect", "path", "align"…). With Shift, a point keeps its 45° angle and slides into line with the nearest target. Round corners: in Direct Selection a small circle sits inside each sharp corner; drag it in to round the corners (the selected points', or all of them), each only as far as its sides allow. Object › Path › Round Corners… does the same with a radius and Round, Inverted or Chamfer, previewed live. Brush (B), after Illustrator's Paintbrush: paint a line freehand and it comes out smooth, sewn as a satin column at the width you set (or as a running stitch). Smoothness takes out the hand's wobble; sharp turns stay sharp; end where you began to close the line. The cursor is a circle as wide as the satin. Curvature (Shift+`, in the Pen's group), after VectorCraft's and Illustrator's: click points and the curve runs smoothly through them, with no handles to pull. Option-click (or double-click a point) for a corner; drag a point and the whole curve follows; click the first point to close a shape, or Enter to end a line. Blob Brush (Shift+B, in the Brush's group): paint a filled shape in the selection's thread. Where the paint overlaps fills in that thread it joins them into one shape. [ and ] size the brush. Lasso (Q, with Direct Selection): draw a loop round points or objects to select them; Shift adds, Option takes away. Part of one object is its points, which Direct Selection then moves. Shape Builder (Shift+M) and Knife (K), in one group: with overlapping shapes selected, drag across their parts to make one shape of them (Option takes parts away; a click makes a part a shape of its own), each shape keeping what's left of itself. The Knife cuts filled shapes along a line drawn right across them (Option: a straight cut), so that each piece can have its own stitch angle. Eyedropper (E, with Measure): click an object to give the selection its thread and stitch settings; Option-click gives the clicked object the selection's; Shift-click takes the thread alone. Shapes, the Illustrator way: Rectangle (M), Ellipse (L), Polygon, Star and Line (\). Drag from a corner; Option draws from the center, Shift makes a square or circle, keeps a polygon or star upright and a line at 45°. While dragging a polygon or star, ↑/↓ add or remove sides or points. Click without dragging to type an exact size. The bar at the top of the canvas switches shapes and sets corner radius, sides, points and the star's inner radius. Closed shapes come in as fills, lines as runs, in the current thread. Path tools: Object › Pathfinder (Unite, Minus Front, Intersect, Exclude; also buttons in the Transform panel when two or more objects are selected) and Object › Path (Offset Path…, Add Outline, Outline Stroke, Simplify…, Round Corners…, Clean Up…). Simplify… is VectorCraft's slider, from fewest points to closest to the original, previewed live, with Auto-Simplify picking the level for the selection's size. Clean Up… removes stray points, objects too small to sew (under 1 mm by default) and extra points (points on top of each other, points in the middle of straight lines), showing how many of each it found first. Results come back as smooth curves with their real corners (least-squares curve fitting), not as many-sided polygons. Logos from images (Image Trace): open, drop or place a PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or TIFF and the Trace Image window traces it into flat-color shapes, previewed on your hat's color. Choose how many colors (or Auto), the width, detail and the smallest speck to keep; remove the white background; snap every color to your Brother, Janome or own palette's threads; and sew thin lines as single lines. Flat logos trace exactly (edges placed to a fraction of a pixel, corners restored, circles and straight lines exact); photos are posterized. The command line traces too: zigzag convert logo.png -o logo.pes . Contextual task bar: under the selection, the next things you'd do: its stitch type, its thread, Edit Points, Round Corners, Simplify, Unite (two or more), Duplicate. Drag the grip at its left end to move it off the art: it keeps that distance as it follows the selection, or stays put with Pin Bar Position in its ••• menu (Reset Bar Position puts it back). View › Contextual Task Bar (or its ••• menu) hides it. Ask an agent: the Agent panel (full height in the left dock; the sparkle at the bottom of the tool strip opens and closes it, and ⌘K or Window › Ask Agent… opens it with the prompt ready) runs Claude Code or Codex in the background, connected to this studio's MCP server, so you watch it build the design. It can only use the design tools (no shell, no file edits). The transcript shows what it said and each step, with a spinner on the one running (the one place it's shown; collapse the panel and its header shows the step and the time instead). On the canvas, the objects it's working on get a moving outline, a shimmer and a label saying what it's doing (Drawing, Placing, Restyling…), for any agent connected over MCP, not just the panel's. The panel is named for the agent (Claude Code or Codex; switch in its ≡ menu); + in its header starts a new chat, Stop ends a run. Uses the claude or codex command you've already signed in to. Like any panel it can float, join another as a tab or dock right; sharing a dock it sits at the bottom, under a divider you drag to give it more room. Thread colors and palettes: the picker shows the nearest Brother/Janome thread, a palette to click (Brother, Janome or your own), and a small custom color field. Make palettes from scratch, from the design, or from a thread kit you own (the palette's ≡ menu › New Palette from Thread Kit: Brother's 12, 40 and 22 color sets, or 40 + 22 for all 61; then Match All keeps a design to the threads in your box), add the selection's thread with +, right-click to remove; they're remembered between launches. Threads panel: the design's threads in sewing order (each color block numbered, with its stitches, and "stop" where the same thread comes twice running) or By Color (each thread once, with how many objects use it). Click a row to select what it sews; click a swatch to change that block's thread, or in By Color that thread everywhere. Group Colors and the count of color changes and trims are under the list. The panel's ≡ menu has Match All to the chosen palette, and Show Palette puts a palette to click under the list (off by default, since the thread picker has the same palettes). Simplify Design (Object › Simplify Design…, or Simplify… in the Threads panel): make a design quicker to sew. Merge the threads most alike down to a number (each pair becomes the one that sews more, so they stay real threads), take out details too small to sew well, sew across short gaps instead of trimming, sew each thread together, and (if you choose) unite layers that touch in one thread into one shape, so nothing is sewn under or between them: only the ones sewn the same way (a satin on a fill stays), or all of them. It previews on the canvas as you drag, with threads, thread changes, trims, stitches and sewing time before and after beside the controls; OK is one undo step. Panels, the Illustrator way: the Agent has the left dock to itself; Layers, Stitch, Transform, Lettering, Threads and Document are on the right. The design's issues are in the status bar (bottom right): a warning sign with a count, or a check when all's well; click it (or Window › Issues) for the list, each linked to its object. Drag a panel by its header to reorder it, move it to the other dock, or drop it on the canvas to float it (each panel's ≡ menu also has Dock Left / Dock Right / Float). Drop a panel on another panel's header and they share it as tabs; drag a tab out (or use Separate in the ≡ menu) to part them, drag the header to move the group. » at the top of a dock collapses it to a strip of icons for a bigger canvas: click an icon and the panel flies out beside the strip (drag an icon to move that panel). Click a header to collapse a panel; Window › Reset Panels puts everything back. The layout is remembered. Layers list: what's on top is at the top, as in Illustrator: the last layer sewn is the first row and the background is the last. Drag a row to another place in the stack (a line shows where it will go; the rows selected with it go too, and a group's row takes all its layers), or use the arrows under the list: up is sewn later, down is sewn earlier. The panel's ≡ menu has List in Sewing Order, for the list the other way up (what's sewn first at the top, as the Threads panel and embroidery software list it; dragging and the arrows follow). A document's only group starts open. Rename an object: double-click its name in the Layers list, as in Illustrator; Enter keeps the name, Escape doesn't. A single click only selects. Tabs, one per document (as in VectorCraft and Illustrator): Open, drop or New opens a file in a tab of its own over the canvas (the empty document you start with makes way for the first one); a file that's already open just comes forward. Each tab keeps its own undo history, selection, zoom and stitches. Click a tab to switch, ⌃Tab / ⌃⇧Tab (or Window › Next / Previous Document) to step through them, drag one to reorder, middle-click or its × (or File › Close, ⌘W) to close it; + opens a new document and » lists every tab when they don't all fit. A dot in place of the × marks unsaved changes, and closing such a tab asks whether to save it first. Right-click a tab for Close Other Tabs and Copy Path. Quitting with unsaved changes asks too (Save, or Save All for several; Don't Save; Cancel), as VectorCraft does, though not saving loses nothing: every tab comes back next time, each with its unsaved changes, and the files stay as they were until you save. Lock and hide: every row of the Layers list has an eye and a lock (Illustrator's Layers columns; Option-click for every other object, and Object › Lock ⌘2, Unlock All, Hide ⌘3, Show All). A hidden object isn't shown or sewn; a locked one can't be selected or moved, so a background stays put while you work on what's over it. Drag the Selection tool over empty canvas for a selection box; two-finger scroll, Space-drag or the Hand tool moves the canvas. Updates itself: ZigZag looks at its latest release on GitHub when it opens, and the toolbar shows an Update button when there's a newer one. On a Mac, Install and Relaunch downloads it, checks it against the release's checksum and Apple's code signature (it has to be signed by the same developer as the copy that's running), swaps it in and reopens with your documents as they were. ZigZag › Check for Updates… looks on demand; Settings › General turns the automatic look off. Windows and Linux are told and taken to the download. Travel stays out of sight: the thread gets from one part of an object to the next under stitches still to come or under what's sewn on top; a fill's sections are sewn in the order that allows it. Where there's no such way the thread is cut, or (Document panel › Travel › Sew over fill) sewn over the fill already there, which saves cuts and shows. The checks say when travel crosses stitches already sewn. Menu bar (File, Edit, Object, Type, View, Window, Help) with the usual ⌘ shortcuts. Help › Report an Issue… opens a new issue on GitHub in your browser, started with which ZigZag you have and what it's running on. It's the real macOS menu bar on a Mac, drawn in the window elsewhere. Crash logs: if something inside ZigZag fails badly enough to stop it, a short log of what failed and where is kept in the settings folder ( crashes/ , the newest ten; Help › Show Crash Logs opens it). The next time ZigZag opens it offers to report it: a GitHub issue started with the gist of the log, and the file shown so it can be attached. Nothing is sent unless you post it, and people's names are taken out of the paths in it. Help also has ZigZag on GitHub, and About ZigZag links there too. Cursors drawn for each tool: the Pen's nib (with what a click will do), crosshairs for the Shape, Rotate, Measure and Fill Angle tools, Direct Selection's hollow arrow, and a curved arrow at rotate corners and while the Rotate tool turns. Right-click menus on the canvas and the Layers list, styled like the tool flyouts: the stitch types with their icons, then the usual commands with their shortcuts. Stays quick on big designs: stitches are planned once per change, reusing every object that didn't change (overlap removal too: moving one object redoes only the objects it overlaps); a design that takes more than 12 ms to plan plans in the background (the status bar says "Updating stitches…" and the last plan stays on screen meanwhile; when you drop a moved object its stitches move with it until the new plan lands). Dragging points or objects, and typing, preview without re-planning until you let go. The stitches live on the GPU: each color block's segments are uploaded once and drawn by a shader (thread shading and needle points included), so panning, zooming, dragging and the stitch player cost nothing per stitch on the CPU, whether the design has a thousand stitches or half a million. The Layers list lays out only the rows in view. An object whose stitches hit an internal error is left out with a warning in Issues rather than taking the plan down. For development: TL_PROFILE=1 prints each frame's sections to stderr, TL_NO_GPU=1 draws the stitches with the painter instead, and cargo test --release --features gui --bin zigzag-studio perf_bench -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 times typing and dragging on a traced logo ( examples/bench-grid.svg is a 213,000-stitch design for the studio itself). Follows the system's light or dark appearance ( ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark overrides) and uses the San Francisco system font on a Mac. Interface size: Settings › General draws everything in the window larger or smaller (90% to 150%): panels, text, buttons and the handles on the canvas. Your design keeps the size it has on screen, the window never gets smaller than the layout needs, and a size the display has no room for steps down to the largest that fits. Pick a stitch type per object: big buttons, the task bar, right-click, or F/S/R/C/X (Blanket and Manual from the Stitch panel). The preview re-plans live. Layout, the Illustrator way: drag to move (Shift: 45° steps; Option: drag a copy). Handles resize freely (Shift keeps proportions, Option resizes from the center, drag past the far side to flip); just outside a corner rotates (Shift: 45°). Smart guides snap edges and centers to other objects and the hoop (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U). ⌘D is Transform Again: Option-drag a copy, then ⌘D for more at the same spacing. Hold Space to pan with any tool (a tap plays the stitch-out). The Transform panel has Illustrator's reference point: X/Y show the chosen point and W/H resize around it. Also rotate, flip, center in hoop, fit to hoop (artwork bigger than the hoop is scaled down to fit when you open or place it; Undo restores full size), ⌘C/⌘V, arrows nudge 0.5 mm (Shift 5 mm). Edits are saved as SVG transforms. Groups work like Illustrator: a click or drag takes the whole group; double-click goes into it (the rest dims and a breadcrumb shows where you are), double-click again to go deeper; Esc or double-click on empty canvas comes back out. ⌘-click picks one object without going in. Layers (Illustrator's "Layer 1", Inkscape layers, Figma frames) aren't groups. Copy, paste and duplicate keep groups. Rotate (Shift+R, or Object › Rotate Tool), as in VectorCraft and Illustrator: the selection turns about a reference point, drawn as a small target. It starts at the selection's center; click to put it anywhere (it snaps to the nearest anchor or center, labelled as you hover), then drag from anywhere to turn the selection about it, the stitches following and the angle beside the pointer. Shift turns in 45° steps; hold Option as you let go to leave the original and drop a turned copy. Option-click sets the point and opens the Rotate dialog for an exact angle, laid out as VectorCraft's: the angle, Copy (leave the original and turn a copy), Preview (see the turn on the canvas before OK), then Cancel and OK. A double-click on the canvas opens it too, and so do Return, a double-click on the tool's button and Object › Rotate…, about the point as it is. ⌘D repeats the turn about the same point, copy and all: set the point, Option-drag one copy, then ⌘D round the ring. The point belongs to the selection it was set for and goes back to the center when the selection changes. Text and shapes with live corners stay text and stay live. Type (T), as in VectorCraft and Illustrator: click where the text should go and type straight onto the canvas (Enter for a new line, Esc or a click elsewhere when done); click text, or between its letters, to edit it with the caret where you clicked (or double-click it with the Selection tool, which picks text anywhere in its box and shows it as a box, not its letters' points; delete every letter and finish, and the text is removed) (←/→, ↑/↓, Home/End and ⌘←/→ move it; Backspace and Delete remove either side; Shift with any of those, a drag, a double-click for a word, a triple-click or ⌘A for the lot selects text, which typing replaces and ⌘C/⌘X/⌘V copy, cut and paste); click a selected path to put text on it. The Lettering panel is a compact Character panel (hat text isn't long copy): font (with search), bold/italic, letter height, tracking, pair kerning (pick the pair, or Option+←/→ while typing kerns the pair at the caret), horizontal and vertical scale, case (as typed, UPPER, lower, Title), alignment and leading for two-line text, baseline (straight, arc over, arc under, or on a path with offset and flip), and the stitch type. The Type menu has Type on a Path, Change Case, Align and Create Outlines (⇧⌘O). Text is a shape like any other: Direct Selection, Round Corners, Simplify, Pathfinder and Clean Up all work on it (it quietly becomes plain paths at the first point-level edit, one undo step), and it saves as real SVG text until then. Pen (P): draw filled shapes or lines with corners and curves, or place manual stitches one by one. Snaps to the grid when it's showing, else to smart guides. Shapes (M, L, \): rectangles (with rounded corners), ellipses, polygons, stars and lines. Measure , mm grid , needle points , First/Last , Group colors . Open machine files (PES, PEC, DST, EXP, JEF) to view, resize and re-export them, and images to trace. Settings per type: fill angle (with a drag-to-set angle tool , A ), spacing, length, pull, underlay. Satin options: column vs border, stitch (satin, S-stitch, zig-zag), threads across the column, width, underlay passes, short stitches. Contour and ripple: rings or spiral. Cross-stitch: cell size. Tartan: the stripes (color and width each, mirrored), angle, row spacing. Run options: single or triple. Lean in the Stitch panel, for satins: how far the stitches lean from square across the column (a few degrees keeps them from sinking between a knit's rows; more shows a slant, like a leaf's veins). Sewing row in the Stitch panel: Start and End (click the outline; green and red markers you can drag), Trim and Stop after the object. Edit › Copy / Paste Stitch Settings carries one object's type and settings to others (each keeps its thread and start/end); Edit › Select Same Stitch Type; Object › Path › Reverse Direction sews a path from its other end. Test swatches (Object › Test Swatches…): copies of the selection in a grid, one setting (spacing, length, pull compensation, satin width, fill angle) stepped from a value to another, each lettered with its value, to stitch out and compare on the real fabric. View › Density Map tints where stitches pile up (yellow from 2.5 per mm², red at 4), and View › Sewing Order numbers the objects on the canvas. Machine in the Document panel: choose the machine a design is for (Brother's 4×4, 5×7 and PR machines, the Skitch, Janome's 550E, Husqvarna Viking's Jade 35, Melco's Summit, ZSK's Sprint 8, any commercial machine that reads DST, or one of your own) and its hoops lead the Hoop menu, Export offers the file it reads first, and new documents start set up for it. What the machine asks of the stitches (a shortest stitch, its own locks) shows under the row. The gear beside it, and Machine Settings… in the menu, open Settings. A machine is a name for ordinary settings, saved into the design, so a file opens the same anywhere. Settings (ZigZag › Settings…, ⌘, ; at the foot of Edit on Windows and Linux): what's set once for this computer. Machines: ZigZag's and yours; + makes one from the document's hoop, Duplicate copies one (ZigZag's own can't be changed, but a copy can); each has its name, hoops (and the one new documents start in), the file it reads, a shortest stitch for machines that drop short ones, and its lock stitches (back and forth, a triangle or none, with their length and number). With a shortest stitch, nothing in the plan or the file is shorter: fill rows closer together than that are sewn every second row and then the rows between (the same needle points, longer turns), other short stitches are merged into their neighbours, and locks are never shorter than it. General: units, light or dark, and whether stitches are drawn on the GPU. Agent: which agent the Agent panel runs, and the server other agents connect to (on or off, and its port; from the next launch). Narrow satin in the Document panel: satins narrower than this (1 mm unless you say) get the too-narrow warning. Set it to what sews cleanly on your fabric. Fabric preset, hoop, Remove overlaps and Cap order in the Document panel. The hoop menu has the standard sizes from 1×2.5 in (20 × 60 mm) to 9.5×14 in (240 × 360 mm), the Skitch's two and Janome's A and B; Custom takes any width and height, for magnetic and other frames. Preview on your hat's color. Issues list (status bar): problems link to the object. Satins show their rails on the canvas. Sewing order: Earlier/Later. Stitch player (Space). Undo/redo everything. Save (Ctrl/⌘ S) writes settings into the SVG; Export PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC/PEN or a worksheet (HTML: picture, size, time, every color stop with the nearest Brother and Janome thread); Send to Skitch . Measuring and units. Measure (I) works like VectorCraft's: drag between two points to read the distance, angle, width and height. The ends snap to points, edges and the hoop (or to the grid when it's on), Shift keeps the line to 45°, and the reading stays until the next drag (Escape clears it). View › Units, or the unit menu in the status bar, shows sizes, positions, distances and the grid in millimeters, centimeters, inches, points or pixels (SVG pixels, 1/96 in, as files are read); it's remembered between launches. Any length field also takes a typed unit or a sum ( 1/4 in , 25.4mm , 10+5 ). The grid (⌘') follows the unit, inches in halves down to 1/32, and labels its major lines along the canvas's top and left edges from the hoop's center. Stitch settings (spacing, density, pull compensation) stay in millimeters. Picks up where you left off. Quit (or crash) and reopen: the same files come back, every tab with any unsaved changes, the zoom and the selection, and the same tab in front. Changes are kept as you work ( session.json and one recovery file per tab, recovery.svg , recovery-2.svg …, in ZigZag's settings folder ( ~/Library/Application Support/ZigZag ), each written whole or not at all), never written into your file until you save. Opening the app with a file skips this. If the app went down while bringing a document back, the next launch keeps it aside as recovery-crashed.svg instead of trying again (and an unreadable one as recovery-unreadable.svg ), and says so in the status bar. A job on the Skitch comes back too: the design last sent is kept ( sent.json ), the Skitch window reopens if it was open and reconnects, and once the machine reports that design its progress shows on it again (the machine keeps the design and where the needle is; Stop ends the job on both). Agents (MCP) The studio runs an MCP server on http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp (Streamable HTTP, localhost only, Origin-checked). Agents edit the live document you're looking at (the tab in front), and every call is one undo step. MCP in the status bar (bottom right, next to the Skitch) shows whether agents can reach the studio: a gray dot while it waits, green once a client has connected, blue and pulsing while calls come in, red if the server couldn't start. Click it for the address, the commands to connect Claude Code and Claude Desktop (with Copy buttons), the clients that have connected, the recent tool calls (failed ones in red, with the error on hover) and the tools on offer. Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http zigzag http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp Claude Desktop / stdio clients ( claude_desktop_config.json ): { "mcpServers" : { "zigzag" : { "command" : " /path/to/zigzag-mcp " } } } zigzag-mcp forwards to the running studio. Use --port N if you changed it. With "args": ["--headless"] it works without the app open: the same tools on a document no one is watching ( zigzag-studio --mcp-stdio ), kept only when the agent saves or exports it. Tools: get_design , add_svg (place/scale artwork in mm), set_object , delete_object , move_object transform_objects (size, scale, rotate, mirror, move), duplicate_objects add_text , edit_text , list_fonts set_document (machine, shortest stitch, lock stitches, how narrow a satin may be before it's warned about, fabric, hoop as a standard or any WIDTHxHEIGHT in mm, overlaps, cap order, preview color), list_machines , group_colors render_preview (returns a PNG of the stitches), check_design , get_svg , select export with objects: true also writes FILE.objects.json : which object each stitch, jump and trim in the machine file is for, so a checker can name the shape behind a fault open_file (SVG, machine file or image, in a tab of its own), list_documents , switch_document , new_document , undo , save , export (machine formats or html worksheet; without a format, the one the path ends in, or else the one the document's machine reads), send_to_skitch , machine_status Any tool that changes the design takes terse: true for a short answer (ok, the names of objects added, and the design problems that are new) instead of the whole object; on batch it covers every step. trace_image (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or TIFF logo → shapes, colors snapped to a thread chart), add_outline (a satin or running-stitch outline on a filled shape, as an object of its own), round_corners , simplify (VectorCraft's 0–100 levels, or Auto), clean_up , simplify_design (fewer threads, small details and trims for the whole design; dry_run to see what it comes to) batch : several calls in one, all or nothing and one undo step; later steps can use earlier results ( "$0.added.0.name" ) Arguments a tool doesn't take are refused with the ones it does (a misspelt widht_mm isn't silently ignored), and each tool says whether it only reads. Try asking: "Draw a 50 mm round badge with mountains and a sun for my thin cotton cap, check it, and show me the preview." CLI zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.pes -o logo.jef -o preview.png -o sheet.html [--fabric thin-cap] [--hat] zigzag convert old.dst -o old.pes # machine files convert too zigzag convert logo.png -o logo.pes # PNG, JPEG, WebP… logos are traced first zigzag info logo.svg # stats + checks zigzag fabrics # list presets zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.exp --machine melco-summit # that machine's hoop and shortest stitch zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.dst --min-stitch 0.4 --lock triangle:0.5:3 zigzag machines # list machines zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.exp --objects # and logo.exp.objects.json: which object each stitch is for zigzag skitch info | status # needs --features ble zigzag skitch send logo.svg --trace Illustrator workflow Export with File → Export → Export As → SVG (Styling: Presentation Attributes, Object IDs: Layer Names). Outline text, or it falls back to system fonts. Opening the ZigZag-saved SVG back in Illustrator keeps the settings in the layer names. Name layers or objects to set their stitching. Illustrator's _x3D_ -style escapes are decoded, and group settings apply to everything inside the group. Token Meaning fill satin run skip stitch type a=45 fill angle (degrees) s=0.3 row / zigzag spacing (mm) l=3 max stitch length (mm) pc=0.2 pull compensation (mm per side) w=3 satin width (mm) border satin along a filled shape's outline instead of across it u=0 underlay off ul=center+contour+zigzag satin underlay passes ( ul=none ) ss=0 short stitches off r=3 running passes (3 = bean) contour blanket applique manual the other stitch types split=7 satin auto-split length (mm); split=0 off t=e8a33c thread color override o=2 sewing order stroke.… applies only to the stroke of an object that also has a fill, e.g. stroke.run (the object's other settings are its fill's) Example layer names: logo fill a=45 s=0.35 , title satin , outline stroke.satin stroke.w=1.5 . Skitch over Bluetooth The Skitch window (the toolbar's Send button or File › Send to Skitch…) runs the whole job, like a slicer's device page follows a print: the design on the left, what to do on the right, and the steps across the top (Connect · Home · Send · Trial · Sew · Done). Connect and pair. It scans for the Skitch. The first time, hold the Skitch's Bluetooth button until it beeps, then Connect (or Try Again); if the computer asks to pair, accept. On a Mac the Skitch never appears in System Settings › Bluetooth (it's a Bluetooth LE device): it pairs when ZigZag connects. Allow ZigZag to use Bluetooth if macOS asks (Privacy & Security › Bluetooth). Close Artspira first: the Skitch talks to one app at a time. Home. A machine just turned on asks to be homed (frame off, Accept, frame back on); the window shows the steps and moves on when it's done. Send: the hoop with the design where it will sew: As Placed (where it sits in the studio's hoop, so you can put it high on a cap) or Centered ; the threads to have ready, in sewing order, by Brother Embroidery name and number; a "before you sew" checklist; Send Design. Trial run (Brother's name for it; on by default after sending): press Accept on the machine and the needle goes around the design's outline without sewing, so you can check it clears the frame's magnets, seams and the brim. Trial Again whenever you rehoop. Sew: Start, then press Start on the machine. The picture shows what's sewn, faded where it hasn't been yet, with the needle and the thread on now; under it, a timeline of the threads with the needle's place. The side shows progress, time left, the thread on now and the next one, and at each thread change exactly which thread to put on. The canvas and the status bar follow along too. Start / Pause / Stop. Start (or Resume, or Sew Again) readies the machine; Pause is the Skitch's own Start/Stop button (it can't be paused over Bluetooth); Stop ends the job, taking the design off the machine. While paused, drag along the timeline or step the needle by 1, 10 or 100 stitches or back to the thread's start, then Resume. Errors say what they are and what to do (thread breaks, bobbin, needle plate, frame). After a thread break the needle goes back over the gap (6 stitches for the top thread, 2 for the bobbin, as Artspira does). Minimize it (–) to keep working while it stitches: the canvas is your design again, and the machine's icon at the right of the status bar shows what it's doing and how far, with a small bar (click it to bring the window back). The window comes back by itself when the machine needs you: a thread change, an error, or the end. The ••• menu also links to Brother's Skitch how-to videos (threading, the bobbin, the frame, a thread break, tension, cleaning). The window's ••• menu can connect to a simulated machine , which does each step on the machine by itself, to try it all without a Skitch. Agents can send_to_skitch and follow along with machine_status . The protocol was reverse-engineered (see NOTICE), so avoid firmware updates. Working out undocumented commands Thread tension isn't a Bluetooth setting on the Skitch: it's the tension dial on the machine. Speed is fixed (about 400 stitches a minute). The machine does report a block of settings, and Artspira has a settings screen, so two tools are here for working out what else it can do: Settings bytes (in the Skitch window, under the machine's details): reads the settings block the machine reports. Read it, disconnect, change one setting in Artspira, close Artspira, reconnect and read again: the bytes that changed are marked. Every read is kept in skitch-settings.log beside the panel layout. On the command line: zigzag skitch settings --label "what changed" --log settings.log . zigzag capture FILE lists the Skitch conversation in a Bluetooth recording of Artspira, by command name, with changed settings bytes in [brackets] ( --all for the upload and polling too, --raw for every ATT operation). It reads both: iPhone: install Apple's Bluetooth logging profile on the phone (developer.apple.com › Bug Reporting › Profiles and Logs), restart it, plug it into the Mac, and in PacketLogger (Apple's Additional Tools for Xcode ) choose File › New iOS Trace; save the trace ( .pklg ). Android: Developer options › Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log, then adb bugreport and take btsnoop_hci.log from it. Writing settings stays out of ZigZag until a layout is known and a write of the machine's own settings, unchanged, reads back the same. Ink/Stitch parity Checked against Ink/Stitch 's features and tool docs: Ink/Stitch ZigZag Running, bean, manual stitch; satin column (two rails with rungs), E-stitch; tatami, contour, circular (spiral) fill ✓ Ripple, meander, cross-stitch and tartan fills; S-stitch, zigzag and multicolor satin ✓ Params per object with fabric-aware defaults; start/end commands; trim and stop commands ✓ (Stitch panel's Sewing row) Auto-route (travel inside fills, underpath along the outline, under what's sewn on top), Jump to Stroke ✓ (document's Connect bar) Simulator, stitch plan preview, density map, stacking-order labels ✓ Lettering (system fonts, arcs, text on a path, multi-line, case, scale), thread palettes, Match All, thread kits ✓ (Brother and Janome charts) Duplicate params, select by type, flip satin direction, test swatches, cleanup, troubleshoot (Issues) ✓ Import stitch files and edit at stitch level; PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC ✓ Gradient fill, guided fill; redwork, cutwork; pre-digitized fonts; 60+ thread brands; PDF print not yet Hatch parity Checked against Wilcom Hatch's core feature set: Hatch ZigZag Tatami, satin, run/triple run, contour fill, blanket, appliqué, manual stitches ✓ Auto underlay, pull compensation, auto spacing, satin auto-split, short stitches ✓ Fabric settings that set densities and compensation ✓ (4 presets) Lettering with TrueType fonts, straight, arc and path baselines, typed on the canvas ✓ (system fonts) Select, move, resize, rotate, mirror, duplicate, copy/paste, align to hoop ✓ Digitize shapes and manual stitches by hand ✓ (pen tool) Remove overlaps, color sequencing, re-order objects ✓ Stitch player, show needle points, grid, measure ✓ Open and save PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3 ✓ (VP3 write only) Production worksheet ✓ (HTML) Auto-digitize bitmaps ✓ (Image Trace: flat logos, posterized photos, centre lines) Built-in embroidery fonts, monogramming, multi-hooping, motif/pattern fills, 3D foam not yet Status Verified: 136 library tests, 153 editor/MCP tests (UI interactions via egui_kittest, a full agent workflow, a real HTTP JSON-RPC session, atomic batches, the Skitch flow against a simulated machine), with and without Bluetooth built in, plus the 222 tests of the vendored Image Trace. Every writer (PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3) reads back through pyembroidery with identical stitch positions; our readers read pyembroidery-written files. PEN output checked against hand-computed sequences. Studio run on Mesa OpenGL and driven by an agent over MCP. Tested on a real Brother Skitch (PP1). Screenshots and videos Start the studio with ZIGZAG_CAPTURE=<folder> and ⌃⌥⌘S saves the window as a full-resolution PNG; ⌃⌥⌘R starts and stops recording it. packaging/media/encode.sh <folder>/take-001 demo turns a recording into demo.mp4 and demo.gif (needs ffmpeg). Credits See NOTICE , and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md for the licenses of the libraries ZigZag is built from (regenerate it with packaging/licenses/generate.sh after changing dependencies). PES/PEC/DST layouts and the Brother palette are from pyembroidery (MIT). Image Trace is vendored from VectorCraft (MIT OR Apache-2.0), whose curve fitting, live corners, snap targets and colour difference were also ported (see vendor/README.md ). Tatami, satin and short-stitch approaches follow Ink/Stitch . About Free, open-source embroidery software for Mac and Windows. Turn SVG artwork into machine embroidery, edit stitches visually, and create designs with AI agents via MCP. zigzag.diy/ Topics brother-skitch embroidery embroidery-digitizing embroidery-software machine-embroidery macos mcp model-context-protocol rust svg vector-editor windows Resources Readme Apache-2.0 license Activity Stars 811 stars Watchers 7 watching Forks 43 forks Report repository Releases Packages Contributors Languages Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc.
