This page is also available as Markdown . GitBook Assistant Ask On this page Models Qwen3.8 - How to Run Locally Guide to running Qwen3.8 quants including Qwen3.8-27B on your local setup. Qwen3.8-27B is a 27B parameter dense model Qwen, featuring vision and reasoning capabilities, a 256K context window, and runs locally on 17GB RAM/VRAM setups. Qwen3.8 excels at agentic coding, vision and chat tasks, and can now run via Unsloth GGUFs, NVFP4 and Unsloth Desktop . Nov 11 Update: Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs now use Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 which improves average accuracy by 5-10% accuracy at comparable sizes including Terminal Bench, DeepSWE and more benchmarks. We're working on an even better version of Dynamic quants which will be applied to Qwen4 and future models. Run Qwen3.8 Guide Download Unsloth Thank you Qwen for day zero access. Unsloth quants also include: Developer Role Support for agentic tools like Codex MTP enabled for fast inference Tool calling: Improved parsing nested objects to make tools succeed more Unsloth quants: Qwen3.8- 27B -GGUF Dynamic 4-bit Qwen3.8-27B in Unsloth Desktop Dynamic V3.1 Update (November 11th 2026) We're excited to release new Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs using our updated Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 (preview) algorithm which improves Unsloth quants by 5-10% accuracy at the same size on most benchmarks and is the best in class for most tasks including coding, agentic workloads and general chat. Most quants from 2bit until 6bit are updated. We found 3bit UD3 quants to do on par with UD3.1, so we do not update them. We are actively working on making all quants better! We ran agentic benchmarks including Terminal Bench 2.1, DeepSWE v1.1 , and general benchmarks like LiveCodeBench v6, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AIME25 and many others. We used 256K context lengths for all agentic benchmarks, and 128K for the rest. We followed the same methodology for Qwen3.8-27B as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next which also utilized our V3.1 preview algorithm. Dynamic V3.1 Full Breakdown Click below to see full details of benchmarking and more: Click to expand Full details and breakdown Exllama-v3 considerations To compare GSQ-RCO and Exllama-v3, we had to exclude the token embedding layer from the x axis, as Exllama-v3 uses BF16 for it. If you consider the full download size and total RAM usage for Exllama-v3, then adding the BF16 embedding table and including all embedding sizes changes the plots. Our main plots's x axis removes the embedding layer sizes from all quant providers. However on pure RAM usage and disk space usage vs accuracy, the below plot is the true reflection of actual usage. We have not investigated why Exllama-v3 keeps token embeddings in BF16, but as the lm_head is still quantized heavily, the embedding layer might have "absorbed" most of the quantization damage from it. We would be glad to benchmark new Exllama-v3 non BF16 token embedding quants like using 8-bit for example, and see if benchmarks change. GSQ-RCO results are misleading For LiveCodeBench, GSQ-RCO showed Unsloth UD3 quants doing consistently worse than ISTA's. However we found the opposite - UD3 quants (our OLD quants) do better than ISTA on LCB on all sizes except the smallest. UD3.1 further improves on LCB as well. We approximate that GSQ-RCO used a context budget of 96K, as that best fits the data for the runs we have. At 96K, GSQ-RCO does somewhat do better than UD3, but at 128K, UD3 does much better. On another benchmark, for ISTA GSQ-RCO's AIME25 benchmarks, their quants reach 100%, 100%, 100% and 96.7% accuracy recovery. And they said our quants do worse. Through out investigations, we estimate ISTA only did 1 trial - we did 14 trials, and we show on average the recovery rate is 93% to 96% - not 100% accuracy recovery. And in fact our UD3 old quants do BETTER on average than their quants on 14 runs vs 1 run of theirs , so we draw the opposite conclusion if you run the trials more. We also checked and graded our answers using Math Verify Dynamic 3.1 GGUFs and also LightEval and we find exactly the same conclusions. We also tried greedy decoding (temperature of 0), and this could not get the 100% accuracy recovery ISTA found across multiple greedy runs, as GPUs themselves are non deterministic. That is why you benchmarks should be run multiple times. Greedy decoding is also not representative of real world use cases. We also checked 96K (which is most likely ISTA's budget) and 128K, and our quants still do on average better. KLD of Unsloth v3.1 vs v3 We did KLD for multiple domains for Unsloth UD3.1 quants and UD3 quants - we reduce KLD throughout most quants and most domains - we did not replace the 3-bit ones, as we found UD3 to do mostly great, and the accuracy recovery on benchmarks was not significant enough with UD3.1 to warrant an update, so we did not update them. Benchmark details and setups We follow the same procedure for all benchmarks as for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as well as discussed in Dynamic 3.1 GGUFs . We used temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0, no presence or repetition penalty, preserve_thinking and xhigh reasoning for Qwen3.8-27B. ⚙️ Usage Guide Qwen3.8-27B Requirements: Qwen3.8- 27B 4-bit quants work on 16-19GB VRAM like RTX 5080, 4090 or a Mac with 24GB RAM. This increases the number of tokens you use, but could increase accuracy in continued conversations. Unsloth has 'Think' and Preserved Thinking toggles for Qwen3.8 (see right): Qwen3.8-27B comes with support for reasoning_effort , which can be used to adjust reasoning depth and control cost. These toggles are automatically enabled in Unsloth: xhigh (default): for complex tasks demanding thorough analysis medium : balancing accuracy and speed low : efficient reasoning optimizing for speed and cost none To change thinking / reasoning effort in unsloth run or llama-server , use --chat-template-kwargs '{"reasoning_effort":"medium"}' If you're on Windows Powershell, use: --chat-template-kwargs "{\"reasoning_effort\":\"medium\"}" Change medium to your desired reasoning level. The reason behind this was to maintain the perception of ongoing high demand and to move an oversupply of semiconductors from TSMC. The WSJ report cites an August meeting between Huang and his senior finance team, including NVIDIA's CFO and acting CEO, Colette Kress, during which Kress pushed for a reduction in circular financing agreements, in response to which Huang allegedly lay into Kress, calling her a "deer in the headlights," after she had pushed to scale back NVIDIA's $250 billion deal with OpenAI . Jensen's push for further investment into small-scale cloud providers was seemingly in response to the changing tide that saw AI hyperscalers move away from off-the-shelf components in favor of custom solutions. The situation described in the report saw NVIDIA on the hook for an "avalanche" of GPUs from TSMC, for which it would have no immediate buyers. Part of the issue highlighted by Kress was also that these small-scale cloud providers NVIDIA was investing in could not afford to buy NVIDIA GPUs, meaning they, too, could be a financial dead end. title: AI unlocks Gödel's notebooks, said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
body_text: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths | Mathematics | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Close dialogue 1 / 3 Next image Previous image Toggle caption Print subscriptions Newsletters Sign in US US edition UK edition Australia edition Europe edition International edition The Guardian - Back to home The Guardian News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Show more Hide expanded menu News View all News US news US politics Midterms 2026 World news Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness Opinion View all Opinion The Guardian view Columnists Letters Opinion videos Cartoons Sport View all Sport Soccer NFL Tennis MLB MLS NBA WNBA NHL F1 Golf Culture View all Culture Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world Lifestyle View all Lifestyle The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money Search input google-search Search Support us Print subscriptions Newsletters Download the app Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us The Guardian app Video Podcasts Pictures Inside the Guardian Guardian Weekly Crosswords Wordiply Corrections Tips Search input google-search Search Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development Gödel’s work inspired Alan Turing and paved the way for the digital age. Photograph: Alfred Eisenstaedt/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Gödel’s work inspired Alan Turing and paved the way for the digital age. Photograph: Alfred Eisenstaedt/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock Mathematics ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems Alex Bellos Fri 13 Nov 2026 11.38 EST Last modified on Fri 13 Nov 2026 13.38 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems , published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age. After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science. Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it. Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about. The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought. View image in fullscreen Albert Einstein presenting Kurt Gödel (second from right) with an award at Princeton University, where the two became friends. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann Archive “I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.” Did you solve it? Gödel’s incompleteness theorem Read more Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation. In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978. Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team. In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature. “In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts. “The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen A microfilm image of an example of Gödel’s shorthand from one of his notebooks. Photograph: Institute for Advanced Study Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice. Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes. The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern. “What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.” Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.” In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].” Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.” Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.” Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.” Explore more on these topics Mathematics AI (artificial intelligence) Finland Europe Austria news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Original reporting and incisive analysis, direct from the Guardian every morning Sign up for our email About us Help Complaints & corrections Contact us Tip us off SecureDrop Privacy policy Cookie policy Tax strategy Terms & conditions All topics All writers Newsletters Digital newspaper archive Bluesky Facebook Instagram LinkedIn Threads TikTok YouTube Advertise with us Guardian Labs Work with us Accessibility settings Back to top © 2026 Guardian News & Media Limited or its affiliated companies. Now What? on December 3 Electronic Frontier Foundation About Contact Press People Opportunities Issues Free Speech Privacy Creativity and Innovation Transparency International Security Artificial Intelligence Our Work Deeplinks Blog Press Releases Events Legal Cases Whitepapers Podcasts Annual Reports Take Action Action Center Volunteer Follow EFF Tools Privacy Badger Surveillance Self-Defense Certbot Atlas of Surveillance Cover Your Tracks Street Level Surveillance apkeep Shop Donate Donate to EFF Shop Giving Societies Sponsorships Other Ways to Give Membership FAQ Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again) DEEPLINKS BLOG By Thorin Klosowski November 13, 2026 Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again) Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did. Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants , rings , and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long. Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps , collaborative software , or your cloud backup solutions , have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are all now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game. Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have. This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense. Let’s break this down by looking at some of the biggest players currently in the game: Apple and Amazon, who have two different takes on transcribing audio throughout the day, as well as Meta and Google, who both have slapped AI and cameras onto eyeglasses. How to Think About the Technical Promises Companies Make Ask Apple about privacy concerns and they’ll point to a white paper that explains all the technical barriers between them as a company and the data generated by the watch. Ask Meta and they’ll talk about all the ways you can customize the privacy controls or how certain details, like faces, may be blurred out when you interact with Meta AI through the glasses (but not during standard recording). Google does this too . Amazon will also talk about how you’re always in control , and no audio is stored (though it’ll also let you enable Amazon store integration, so your conversations can directly result in ads for products). And so on across all the companies making these products. Some of these solutions do a better job than others at cutting out potential law enforcement or company access to this data. There will be a time to dive into these details more deeply, but the technical privacy promises these companies focus on only cover the consumer and user of the device. They ignore every bystander you interact with and their inability to actually opt out. There is no technical protection for you as a non-user of these devices, the person who finds yourself captured by them. Still, we hope to look deeper into the technical differences between this category of devices soon. There Must Be Some Laws to Consider, Right? With something like Apple’s Audio Intelligence and Amazon’s Bee devices, it may be best to treat them similar to an always-recording microphone, even if companies try to claim there’s “technically” no audio recording. These tools still often use a microphone to capture raw audio from conversations and convert it into summaries or transcripts before discarding the audio. Google's blog post notes that it has whole responsible use part of their Terms of Service where users have to agree not to record others without permission or in sensitive places. But it’s not just the question of the legality from the point of view of the user. Law enforcement will eventually try to compel access to the data that these products create (either real-time audio or the summaries and transcripts they create). And while some products, like Apple’s Audio Intelligence, are engineered to make that difficult, not every product will be. We know from history that when data exists, governments will do everything they can to access it. There’s no reason to think something would change today. No Tech and Legal Solutions Will Reduce Social Issues There is a problem humming along in the background that is impossible to address with technical or legal solutions. If secretly documenting conversations becomes the norm, it makes every private conversation less spontaneous and open. It breaks a longstanding social norm that you will not record and document every conversation with friends, family, colleagues, or strangers. The companies that make these sorts of products like to claim they’re no different from tools we already have. You can easily record everything right now with a phone or a camera. Heck, you can do so with a camcorder or cassette recorder if you want. And you can transcribe conversations with pen and paper, too. But those are actionable steps we take that both require effort from the user, and are clear to others around us. This new wave of passive surveillance tech is designed to encourage continuous monitoring and hide its use. Even taken at face value, none of these products can understand the complex social context we all navigate every day. We intrinsically know there are different social agreements we all make when we’re standing on a street corner, at a protest, in a bathroom, at a doctor’s office, at the gym, or in a restaurant. Taking notes in a meeting at work is completely normal. Getting a summary of a conversation with your best friend about their divorce is not. Always-on monitoring of our conversations is an unacceptable burden on our conversational privacy. Google seems to all but admit this problem in a conversation with CNN when it described the company’s experiments with a notification system that would alert people’s phones when someone was recording nearby: “And just alerting bystanders doesn’t do much to help, [Juston Payne, senior director of product management at Google] said. “It can actually be weirdly disempowering to you in that you’re like, ‘What am I meant to do now?’” he said.” What We Can Do About It It’s easy to buy into the tech company line that these products are inevitable, but we’ve seen so many vaporware products over the years that we should take those claims of success with a grain of salt. We’ve seen entire product categories come and go within just a few years, and if the public doesn’t want this stuff, the tech companies will have to throw in the towel. Of course, that doesn’t mean we all just have to sit around and hope that’s what happens. For its part, Apple launched its Audio Intelligence features in beta specifically to get feedback, and we think it’s worth taking the time to fill out their feedback forms (or in the Feedback Assistant app if you’re in the beta) and let them know what you think. Products from the likes of Meta, Google, Amazon, and others might be harder to push back on, but politely and clearly engaging with those who use them in ways that make you uncomfortable is a good place to start. And if you see abusive videos on social networks where these sorts of products are used, report them. If you find these products useful for yourself, make it clear to those around you when you’re using them, and only do so with consent and in social moments where it makes sense to do so. *Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions. title: Show HN: Live map of U.S. flights during tonight's FAA nationwide ground stop
body_text: FAA Nationwide Ground Stop, Nov 13, 2026: Live U.S. Flight Map | Ground Stop Watch grounds.top : FAA nationwide ground stop, Nov 13, 2026 Now — airline flights in the air in the air — of normal departures of normal departures — departures missed since 3:30 pm departures missed Loading — --:--:-- Eastern On Nov 13, 2026 the FAA ordered a ground stop at every U.S. airport at 3:54 PM ET. This page shows tracked flights over the U.S., live and replayable, against the same time a week earlier. Live — ET — Replay the shutdown grounds.top Commercial flights: below 10,000 ft 10,000 to 28,000 ft above 28,000 ft Other aircraft Airport departures, last 30 min vs a week earlier: almost none reduced near normal + − 1× Hold Ctrl and scroll to zoom Loading flight history… Commercial flights: below 10,000 ft 10,000 to 28,000 ft above 28,000 ft Other aircraft Airport departures, last 30 min vs a week earlier: almost none reduced near normal Rotate your phone for a bigger map Commercial flights airborne — — Missing from the sky — flights that were airborne at this time last Friday Airliners climbing out — — Departures missed since 3:30 pm (est.) — — Flight positions: adsb.fi community ADS-B network. Airport delay feed: FAA NAS Status . An independent, unofficial page, not affiliated with the FAA. Hover or tap a dot to identify the aircraft. Jump to or drag the timeline The shutdown so far Read from the tracking data, not from official announcements. Times are Eastern. Recovery by airport Departures in the 30 minutes before the selected time, as a share of the same half-hour a week earlier, at the 16 largest airports. An airport counts as back once it holds three-quarters of its usual departures for two readings in a row. Departure backlog by airport Estimated commercial departures missed since 3:30 pm ET: the count for the same hours a week earlier minus this week's, from tracking data. On the right, how many left, out of the number a week earlier. Dot: departures in the last 30 minutes (red almost none, amber reduced, green near normal). Airborne by carrier Aircraft in the air at the selected time. The bar is the share of the same time a week earlier. Carrier Airborne Share of a week earlier Since 1 pm FAA airport delay feed — . The feed lists only airports with a specific entry; during the nationwide stop every US airport is affected, listed or not. Airport Status FAA reason Delay Trend What was reported From news reports; updated by hand, not live. Past nationwide stops Date Cause Length How to read this. Positions come from adsb.fi volunteer ADS-B receivers. "Commercial" means a callsign with an airline code and flight number, which includes cargo and charter operators. "Climbing out" counts those below 10,000 ft and climbing faster than 400 ft/min, a stand-in for departures. "Over the US" is US land plus about 60 nm of coastal water. The comparison is the same clock time one week earlier: Friday Nov 6, and after midnight Saturday Nov 7. Coverage is not complete, so read these as a consistent sample, not an official count. Freshness. History arrives in half-hour blocks; in between, the map is filled from adsb.fi's live feed every 2 minutes. The FAA airport delay feed ( nasstatus.faa.gov ) is checked every 2 minutes; our record of it starts at 4:56 pm ET. A departure is counted when a commercial aircraft climbs away from one of the 30 largest airports (nationwide: when it climbs through 10,000 ft); the backlog is the count a week earlier minus this week's since 3:30 pm ET, for complete half-hours only, so cancelled flights are included in it. Phil Brink · Monday, November 09, 2026 NVIDIA's headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Authorities are investigating the reported theft of $11.4 million in NVIDIA computer hardware during a shipment from Oakland to Texas. (Photo: NVIDIA) Six pallets of NVIDIA computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million disappeared during a shipment from California to Texas. A truck collected the merchandise in Oakland on Aug. 29 for delivery to Fort Worth. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through several extended stops before losing its trail in Southern California. The Oakland Police Department confirmed an ongoing grand theft investigation following a complaint filed Sept. 13, 2026. The disappearance comes amid reports of nearly $111 million in stolen data center freight involving other high-value technology shipments. According to The Mercury News , the vehicle displayed a food transportation company’s logo during the scheduled pickup. The driver subsequently traveled south, making several stops lasting multiple hours. Investigators eventually lost track of the truck in San Bernardino County. A separate $12 million cargo theft investigation involved suspects who allegedly exploited established trucking identities to obtain freight. Authorities have not linked the two investigations. Oakland police confirm investigation The Oakland Police Department provided FreightWaves with the following statement: “The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026. The investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact the OPD General Crimes Unit at (510) 238-3728.” The Sept. 13 complaint date does not establish when the theft occurred. Police have not confirmed the reported $11.4 million valuation or identified the specific merchandise. Authorities also have not identified the cargo’s owner, shipper, motor carrier or driver. Investigators have not publicly explained the vehicle’s extended stops or established whether criminals impersonated a transportation provider. Police have not announced arrests or confirmed any recovery of the merchandise. FreightWaves contacted NVIDIA for comment and followed up, but the company has not responded. Previous thefts involving NVIDIA products The Oakland investigation follows other significant thefts involving NVIDIA merchandise in Northern California. During 2025, Fremont and Union City police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in NVIDIA products. Those incidents targeted valuable computer hardware at separate locations. Authorities have not established any connection between those investigations and the latest disappearance. In a separate September incident, thieves stole two PlusAI trailers, including one displaying NVIDIA branding , from a Fremont, California, warehouse. The trailers contained approximately 40,000 pounds of sand rather than NVIDIA hardware. Police recovered both trailers in nearby Newark. Investigators have not established any connection between that theft and the Oakland case. Why it matters The reported disappearance of $11.4 million in NVIDIA hardware underscores the financial stakes of transporting high-value freight. Regardless of how this shipment disappeared, carrier verification, shipment visibility and communication remain critical throughout transportation. Click here for more articles on cargo theft and freight fraud by Phil Brink. Compromised communications linked to 40% of stolen loads in Highway fraud report – FreightWaves CBP seizes 1,000-plus pounds of meth in produce truck at Texas border – FreightWaves $500,000 SIG Sauer shipment stolen in fictitious pickup, two arrested in California – FreightWaves Phil Brink Phil Brink is the Head of Fraud Media and Education at FreightWaves, where he investigates cargo theft, freight fraud and transportation security. He owned and operated a freight brokerage for more than a decade before organized fraud targeted his business, forcing him to rethink how freight companies identify and manage risk. The lessons he learned continue to shape his reporting, education and collaboration with brokers, carriers, shippers and law enforcement. He developed FreightWaves' Certified Fraud Compliance Officer (CFCO) program to give transportation professionals practical knowledge and a structured framework for identifying and managing fraud risk. title: A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem
body_text: A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem - Haskell Foundation - Haskell Community = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> Haskell Community A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem Haskell Foundation hasufell November 13, 2026, 5:03am 1 Hi all, the technical leadership committee of the Haskell Foundation has been successfully bootstrapped! We have spent the last few weeks discussing our vision and strategy and are now fully operational. We’re going to actively develop initiatives and proposals that we believe need funding and execution. For that we need companies, contractors and volunteers to help. Everyone can participate, whether it’s by dropping ideas informally, writing a concrete proposal themselves or finding entities that could support or fund initiatives. We tried to keep the community proposal process as light as possible. However, we believe that fairness and participation are vital, especially when funding is involved, so anyone who writes a proposal should be aware that we will open the floor for the community to comment or even deliver counter-proposals. The process may evolve as we make experiences and get feedback. Below is our vision. Feel free to get in touch with us! The TLC’s shared vision We believe that Haskell is awesome and that it can provide unique value to everyone, because it sits at an interesting intersection between human craftsmanship and machine automation: It is good for humans to write by hand: Type safety, powerful abstractions and referential transparency have enabled engineers all over the world in startups and big tech to deliver and maintain complex systems. It is good for responsible AI workflows: review is a significant bottleneck in modern AI-workflows and Haskell’s strengths heavily favor the reviewer. Additionally, the ability to quickly design eDSLs and express constraints where it matters allows to set up strong guardrails for code generation, without losing flexibility. There may be better languages for formal verification or for vibecoding, but there’s no better language for “human in the loop”. Haskell is where we maintain control of our work, build institutional knowledge and ship responsibly. We’re driven to improve Haskell for everyone: Beginners: the onboarding experience must be our benchmark for usability Experts: enabling advanced workflows and improving productivity Industry: focussing on stability and scaling A vision of productivity Imagine Haskell had the iteration speed of golang, the debugging capabilities of C# and the onboarding experience of rust. And all that while providing stronger guarantees and better performance! Iteration speed Modern workflows require fast iteration times: compilation, interactive repl, remote dependency caching, CI and test integration. All of this affects both human and machine workflows. While Haskell scales well in terms of code complexity… it doesn’t scale well in terms of build times. As an example, GHC’s own CI has turnaround times of 6 hours. We want to bring them down to 2. Debugging and profiling Instead of helplessly dumping logs and binaries into LLM chats, we envision deterministic tools that allow precise and ergonomic enquiries: live step-through debugging actually useful stack traces beautiful performance analysis reports And all of that in your editor/IDE as well as through powerful CLI and scripting interfaces, the latter enabling power users as well as LLM-driven debugging (natively, without requiring any custom adapters like MCP). Debugging must be fun again, without littering Debug.Trace.trace all over your codebase. Documentation and interactive exploration will assist newcomers in understanding all caveats of laziness and GHC and should clearly explain how to leverage these tools. Onboarding and DevX In these times of low frustration tolerance, we are going to build the best onboarding experience in the programming language ecosystem, because it is the ultimate benchmark for developer experience as a whole. installation so quick that you’re wondering whether the installer even worked documentation so comprehensive and accessible that you never get stuck tooling so intuitive that you don’t have to constantly ask for support This can only be done if we commit to unix principles, which we summarize as: write programs that do one thing and do it well write programs that work together write programs that are extensible Documentation should be a joy to read, written by humans, for humans. A vision of a secure and trustworthy ecosystem Security and trust don’t get established by accident. Once trust is lost, it’s often irrecoverably lost. To protect our community assets and reputation, we need to: have the fastest incident response time among language ecosystems have penetration testers go through our infrastructure regularly make end users aware of vulnerabilities and mitigations build a robust cryptography library stack harden our supply chain We should further support attempts to utilize or extend the strengths of the Haskell language to boost practical applications of secure design and architecture, such as Information Flow Control or Mandatory Access Control. We’re also monitoring the efforts of dependent types and liquidhaskell . A vision of stability What if we could compile Haskell software that’s 10 years old with the latest GHC, without any source code changes? While this might seem like an impossible goal to achieve… embarking on that journey is going to get us closer to a robust, stable and predictable ecosystem anyway. The questions we need to answer along the way are: how can users opt out of breaking changes? how long can we keep support windows open? how can we make the upgrade experience better? Not only requires this investment in GHC and core tooling, but also potentially support community efforts to maintain stable package sets or coordinate ecosystem upgrades, make cabal more ergonomic for complex use cases, spearhead and support stability policies and gather data about what parts of the ecosystem cause churn. We want Haskell to not only be a choice for fast moving startups, but also for large or conservative companies that do not want their workflows or software stacks disrupted. Stability will benefit both of these types of users, reduce cost and friction and build a reputation for Haskell as a modern language with a predictable ecosystem. A vision of a flourishing open source ecosystem All of the above is an attempt to support the Haskell open source ecosystem that we love. We are committed to open source, its values and the social aspect of it. Collaboration is how we engage with and inspire each other. We want to enable all the maintainers and volunteers who keep this ecosystem alive, many of them unknown, doing their part on a Saturday evening at the other end of the world. We code because we love to ship products. But we also code, because we want to socialize, meet people and have a good time. We’re committed to both of these values. 84 Likes 6d03 November 13, 2026, 12:10pm 2 Thank you @hasufell and the TLC for writing this up; it’s very inspiring to see these goals. I think this ambitious agenda will provide us with a lot of fun and profit. 5 Likes Elland November 13, 2026, 7:26pm 3 That’s really great to see I’ll be doing my part and see if I can submit a proposal for some unglamorous work I’ve been meaning to do. 4 Likes dawkrish November 13, 2026, 10:55pm 4 Woah, this is so inspiring and motivating! I have multiple features I want to add to HLS! Is Haskell Team finally focusing on “Adoption” ? 2 Likes OlaoluwaM November 14, 2026, 12:12am 5 Is there a place to sign up to be a volunteer, or is it just the general “help out where you can”? 1 Like simonmic November 14, 2026, 12:22am 6 Hacker News discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50484235 6 Likes wiz November 14, 2026, 9:29am 7 Don’t start reading without your hypertension pills! Lots of moronic and sloppy takes. 4 Likes tomjaguarpaw November 14, 2026, 2:26pm 8 hasufell: We should further support attempts to utilize or extend the strengths of the Haskell language to boost practical applications of secure design and architecture Can I suggest we do this by promoting the use of effect systems to this end? Effect systems are basically capability systems if you generalise the definition of each of those two terms in a natural way, as I explain in my article Bluefin is a capability system . Capability systems have a long history of development for security purposes. Haskell is the natural setting for capability systems, as it is referentially transparent, which capability systems proponents would describe as “having no ambient authority”. 1 Like prophet November 14, 2026, 3:28pm 9 In what way would Bluefin have any security advantages over plain IO? My understanding is that the security benefits of capability systems usually fall into two camps: OS-level capabilities like FreeBSD’s pledge stop any code (including code from an RCE vulnerability) from performing operations it’s not supposed to. Library level capabilities (like the object capibilities in Pony you mentioned) can mitigate supply chain vulnerabilities by stopping dependencies from calling any code that does more than they need. 1 doesn’t apply to Bluefin and 2 can be trivially circumvented by using unsafePerformIO 1 Like tomjaguarpaw November 14, 2026, 3:52pm 10 To be clear, I’m not suggesting Bluefin specifically as the solution to secure design and architecture, I’m saying that that one benefit Haskell has that will help with secure design and architecture is effect systems in general . In the world of effect systems, Bluefin and effectful have a number of non-security-related benefits that I’ve elaborated in detail elsewhere, but they don’t have an inherent security advantage, per se. I’m not too familiar with pledge , but I don’t think it’s a capability system. I think it just acts to reduce ambient authority. A capability system allows you to run different components of your program with different levels of authority, in a fine grained way, based on what capabilities are in scope in each of those components. Regarding your point 2, yes, effect systems can do that, but of course the dependencies would have to be written with that use case in mind (as they do in Pony, unless I’m much mistaken). Sure, you can circumvent anything with unsafePerformIO , as it allows you to write unsafeCoerce and thereby walk over your entire heap making arbitrary changes. I’m not proposing that Haskell would be a verified system (although I’d be interested to see how close to one it could become with SafeHaskell ). 2 Likes prophet November 14, 2026, 4:08pm 11 I’m not too familiar with pledge , but I don’t think it’s a capability system That’s fair. Fuchsia capabilities are probably a better example. Regarding your point 2, yes, effect systems can do that, but of course the dependencies would have to be written with that use case in mind (as they do in Pony, unless I’m much mistaken). Well, the difference is that (AIUI) pony doesn’t have any escape hatches and so if a function doesn’t receive a capability to, say, access the file system, it literally cannot do so. No matter how fancy your effect system is, a compromised Haskell dependency can always call unsafePerformIO (writeFile ... malware) . I just don’t see any concrete security vulnerabilities that could be avoided by using an effect system. I don’t disagree that effect systems can have benefits for software engineering in general, but I really don’t see how they’re relevant to “secure design and architecture”. tomjaguarpaw November 14, 2026, 4:19pm 12 prophet: That’s fair. Fuchsia capabilities are probably a better example. OK, and what do you see as the fundamental distinction between Fuchsia and Haskell-with-an-effect-system (besides one being an operating system and the other having an additional level of “nesting” within a programming language)? I can only repeat that I’m not proposing that Haskell would be a verified system. Nonetheless, I think a software project written in a capability system, albeit not a formally verified one, would still be easier to implement correctly and audit that one written in the style of “ambient authority”. I would be interested to hear your arguments against that, if you disagree. Regarding Pony, perhaps it always enforces the equivalent of SafeHaskell . I would interested to know where you think “ SafeHaskell plus effect systems” would fall short of providing “secure design and architecture”. Perhaps a mod should split this off into its own topic? 4 Likes Home Categories Guidelines Terms of Service Privacy Policy Powered by Discourse , best viewed with JavaScript enabled

After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
body_text: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models — Haddy Alchaer Haddy Alchaer World models · JEPA · Planning After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models By Haddy Alchaer · November 2026 Solving long-horizon tasks without any extra training 0 / 24 on target · step 0 Vanilla LeWM can be augmented to solve long-horizon physics tasks on out-of-distribution goals. This method uses transformations on a memory graph to generate on-the-fly subgoals without any additional training. Shown here are some of the hardest tasks it solved. There's a big debate in AI right now about what a world model should be. Most of the attention goes to generative world models, which predict the future by generating it, usually in pixels. Many scientists, including Yann LeCun, argue that this is wasted effort. Most of the pixels don't matter for deciding what to do, and many of them can't be predicted at all. [1] The proposed alternative is JEPA, the joint-embedding predictive architecture. It has three parts: an encoder, a predictor and a planner. The encoder turns each frame of observation into a learned embedding, a compact vector that describes the scene. The predictor takes that embedding plus an action and predicts the embedding of the next frame. The planner then tries hundreds of action sequences inside the predictor and picks the one whose predicted end state lands closest to the embedding of the goal. The whole loop runs in embedding space, so the model only has to learn the parts of the scene that are important for deciding actions. The three parts of a JEPA world model. This year a team including LeCun released LeWM [2] , a JEPA world model whose main benchmark is Push-T [3] , a simulation where a robot pushes a gray T-shaped block across a table until the T sits in the green target position shown in a goal image. I've spent the last few months running 600 experiments on it. A goal image from Push-T The planner is given an image like this one and has to make the scene match it. The gray T is the block, the blue disc is the robot's pusher, and the green T is the goal position painted on the table. One detail in this image turned out to affect the success rate more than replacing the predictor with simulated physics. The first thing I wanted to know was how much LeWM is held back by its predictions, so I started by swapping out the predictor for the simulator's perfect physics, while keeping everything else the same. I then gave both versions long-horizon tasks, with the goal 75 steps away, along with the same subgoals: frames from an expert demonstration, one every 25 steps. Vanilla LeWM succeeded 78% of the time. The version with true physics succeeded 77%. Along the kinds of paths it was trained on, LeWM's predictions are already as good as perfect physics for planning. Success on 250 long-horizon tasks 78 % Vanilla LeWM learned predictor ≈ 77 % LeWM real physics the simulator itself That means the next gains for a JEPA world model come from how the trained architecture is used, and that's where most of my 600 experiments went. Without retraining the model once, I found four new planning methods. The first two together took LeWM's success rate on long-horizon tasks from 22% to 85%, about the same as a planner that is handed the ideal subgoals from an expert demonstration. The other two methods extend LeWM to harder goals, and one of them, a single change to how the goal is scored, raised the success rate by 60 points, three times as much as swapping in perfect physics did. 1. Plan through subgoals 25 steps apart Used exactly as published, LeWM succeeds on 22% of long-horizon tasks, where the goal is 75 steps away. [2] When the goal is 25 steps away, it reaches it 89.7% of the time, within a point of the exact-physics version at 90.5%. So the model is accurate over 25 steps and struggles over 75. The usual explanation is that small prediction errors compound over a long plan, which would call for a better model. I tested that against the alternative on the same 250 long-horizon tasks. 250 long-horizon tasks, goal 75 steps away LeWM, all 75 steps at once as published 22% Exact physics, all 75 steps at once the simulator itself 42% +20 LeWM given a new subgoal every 25 steps same model, shorter hops 80% +58 0 25 50 75 100% Exact physics added 20 points. Splitting the task into 25-step segments, each the length LeWM already handles almost perfectly, added nearly 60. LeWM's useful planning horizon is about 25 steps, so it was clear that the way to go further is to chain segments of that length together. LeWM's planning horizon is about 25 steps Plan all 75 steps at once ... one search, far goal 22% A subgoal every 25 steps ... three short searches 80% Chaining 25-step searches through subgoals keeps every search inside the range where LeWM is accurate. This is hierarchical planning: a high level picks subgoals and a low level reaches them. It's widely considered one of the main open problems for world models, and on Push-T it's worth three times as much as swapping in perfect physics. Extra search doesn't substitute for it. Running the planner four times and keeping the lowest-cost plan took four times the compute and added less than one point, because the four runs almost always succeeded or failed together. The subgoals in this experiment came from an expert demonstration, which a deployed robot won't have. The second method removes that dependence. 2. A latent memory graph with a cost on every jump LeWM was trained on expert demonstrations of the task, and its encoder can embed every frame of them, giving about 460,000 embedded states that I connected into a graph. Each state links to the states that follow it in its own demonstration, and to states in other demonstrations that are close in embedding space. To solve a long-horizon task, the planner searches this graph for a path from the current state to the goal and uses the states along that path as subgoals. This only works if distance in embedding space means something physical, and it does. Take one subgoal the robot can reach within 25 steps and one it can't, and LeWM's embedding distance ranks the reachable one as closer 87% of the time. So the embedding space doubles as a map of what the robot can reach. The first version had a flaw. A jump between nearby states in two different demonstrations cost the same as a real step, so the search strung jumps together into paths the block could never follow (318 of 1,015 plans tried to use six or more jumps). The fix was adding a cost on every jump between demonstrations in the graph. Using nothing but LeWM's own embeddings of past demonstrations, success on the same 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) went from 62% to 85%, which is the same score received by the planner using expert subgoals. Can't get much better than that, right? Planning through a memory of demonstrations start goal Jumps are free · 8 jumps · 62% Each jump has a cost · 1 jump · 85% Each thin path is one demonstration. With free jumps, the shortest route hops between demonstrations into a path the block can't physically follow. With a cost per jump, it stays on them. The standard Push-T test is easier than it looks The caveat is that the standard test takes a demonstration, starts the robot partway through it, and sets the goal a fixed number of steps further along the same demonstration. That's a reasonable design, but in Push-T every demonstration ends with the block in the same place. So every test goal sits on a path that demonstrations already travel, heading for the spot they all end at. For 84% of the standard test's goals, the memory graph already held a nearly identical state from another demonstration. demonstrations, all ending in about the same place goals in the standard test goals from other demonstrations The standard test picks its goals along these streams. The harder test asks for goals like the orange ones, which no single demonstration leads to. The usual sample is also small. On the official 50 episodes, LeWM succeeded 68% of the time with the goal 50 steps away. On 250 fresh episodes drawn the same way, it succeeded only 44%. Changing nothing but the planner's random seed flipped 38 of 250 episodes between success and failure. That's where I decided to build a harder test, where each task takes its start from one demonstration and its goal from another, so the robot has to travel between states that no single demonstration connects. It only counts as a success if the block stays on target for the last 10 steps. Under these rules the memory-graph planner succeeds 75% of the time on standard tasks and 45% on the new ones. The third and fourth methods I found work on that gap. 3. Fill gaps in memory with transformed memories A memory graph is only as good as its coverage. When I deleted every stored state near the goal, success fell from 93% to 32%. Push-T has a useful symmetry here. The physics of pushing a block doesn't change if you shift, rotate or mirror the whole table. So when the graph has no states near a goal, it can take demonstration segments from elsewhere, transform them to fit the gap, and plan through those. With these transformed segments, success came back to 85%. They also stretch a small memory a long way (a graph built from 1% of the demonstrations plus transformed copies did about as well as one built from 10%). Filling a gap in memory with transformed demonstrations a demonstration segment from elsewhere the same segment, shifted, rotated or mirrored Block reached its target, 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) 93% full memory 32% states near the goal deleted 85% gap filled with rotated and mirrored copies On the harder test, transformed segments raise success from 45% to 56%, and they help most where demonstrations are thinnest. When the goal lies in the direction the demonstrations flow, the memory-graph planner already succeeds 69% of the time. When it lies the opposite way, plain memory gets 27% and transformed memory gets 46%. Harder test, by where the goal lies about 83 tasks per row Goal lies with the flow of the demonstrations 69% Goal lies across it 39% 54% Goal lies against it 27% 46% 0 25 50 75 100% success rate plain memory with transformed segments 4. The cost was “wrong” I also built an interactive demo where I could place the block anywhere and pick any goal. A goal has to be an image, and an image of the scene has to show the pusher somewhere, so I placed the pusher just behind the goal. In one run, the robot pushed the block to within 14 pixels of the target, close enough to count as solved. Then it pushed the block away from the goal, and kept moving the pusher toward where the pusher was in the goal image. The goals in the harder test are frames from expert demonstrations, so each one also shows where the expert’s pusher happened to be at that moment. A planner that compares its prediction with the whole goal image is trying to put the pusher there too. To measure how much this matters, I took the model out of the question. I ran the exact-physics planner twice on the same 50 tasks from the harder test, and the only difference was whether its cost included the pusher’s position as well as the block’s. Block held on target, same 50 tasks exact-physics planner Block and pusher 9 / 50 Block only 39 / 50 success with either cost 30  succeed only without the pusher 0  succeed only with the pusher included Thirty tasks went from failure to success when the pusher was left out, and none went the other way. A split like that happens by chance about twice in a billion. The physics here is from the actual simulator, not predicted, so the 4x in success comes from how the goal was created . The planner that scored the pusher did exactly what it was asked. On the 30 tasks that flipped, it got the pusher to within half a pixel of where the goal image put it, and lost the block on the way. Placing both the T and the pusher in the exact goal position is a much harder problem to solve. Pusher included vs. not Cost compares the block and the pusher Cost compares the block only target for the block where the goal image put the pusher Replay But LeWM can’t simply be told to ignore the pusher. It scores a plan by the distance between two embeddings, and its embedding of a goal image holds the block and the pusher together, with no part labeled “pusher”. So, as a test, I measured how far a planner gets by searching over the pusher instead. It compares each prediction against 16 versions of the goal image, all with the block in the same place and the pusher moved to positions taken from stored demonstrations, and keeps the closest match. That doubled LeWM’s success on the harder test, from 11% to 23%, without retraining. Sixteen versions of one goal A predicted end state 16 copies of the goal with the pusher moved, and the closest one sets the cost This applies to any robot because a goal should just be a set of end states, not a copy of an image. “Put the cup on the shelf” is solved wherever the robot’s arm ends up, but a goal image picks one arm position and makes the planner match it. A good goal accepts every end state that solves the task, and still includes what the task needs from the robot, like coming to rest at the end. The good news is that large sets of demonstrations already contain many real frames of the same object in the same place, each with the robot somewhere different. Scoring a plan against the closest of those goals allows for a larger set of valid end states to plan for. What comes next None of these four discoveries change the model's weights. They apply to LeWM as published, and they should carry over to larger JEPA world models that plan the same way, at no extra training cost. The biggest open problem remaining is generalizing to tasks that don't have perfect demonstrations. On the harder Push-T test, the best planner holds the block on target 56% of the time, and most of the remaining failures are goals that run against the direction of the data. Closing that gap needs a higher level that can propose its own subgoals beyond the demonstrations, and do it better than today's learned hierarchies like H-JEPA [4] , which so far match or slightly beat flat LeWM on Push-T. Hierarchical subgoal planner on top of LeWM demonstrations in memory subgoals taken from memory a goal beyond the data Going in, I assumed LeWM's predictions would be the bottleneck, but a JEPA small enough to train in a few hours already predicts about as well as the simulator itself, and there are several gains that can be achieved simply by changing the way it plans. What it can't do yet is choose its own subgoals where no demonstration has been. That's what I'm currently working on, and if you want to see more, I'll post about it first on X, @haddyalchaer . References [1] Y. LeCun, A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence . OpenReview, 2022. [2] L. Maes, Q. Le Lidec, D. Scieur, Y. LeCun, and R. Balestriero, LeWorldModel: Stable End-to-End Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture from Pixels . arXiv:2603.19312, 2026. [3] C. Chi et al., Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion . RSS, 2023. [4] W. Zhang, B. Terver, M. Rabbat, Y. LeCun, and R. Balestriero, H-JEPA: End-to-End Learning of Hierarchical World Models for Visual Planning . arXiv:2610.06805, 2026. © 2026 Haddy Alchaer

title: What happened to 3Com?
body_text: What Happened to 3Com: From Networking Giant to Afterthought The Silicon Underground David L. Farquhar on technology old and new, computer security, and more Menu About Archives Home Privacy policy Recent Comments Home » Retro Computing » What happened to 3Com? What happened to 3Com? Dave Farquhar Retro Computing November 12, 2026 November 12, 2026 2 Comments 3Com was a high flying maker of network cards and other network equipment. And then they disappeared with a whimper on November 11, 2009. What happened to 3Com? 3Com at the dotcom boom A 3Com 3c509 combo card like this one was a familiar sight to any IT professional in the mid to late 1990s. But competition from cheaply made cards eroded 3Com’s profitability and the company faded away over time. Around the time of the dotcom boom , 3Com was a 5.8 billion dollar company. They were founded in 1979 by Bob Metcalfe, the co-inventor of Ethernet. And for the next two decades, they were the go-to brand for network cards. While the 3C501 network card is notoriously bad, their other cards from the 1980s and 1990s are very well regarded, and always were. They cost more, but had good driver support, the hardware worked reliably, and they were a known quantity. And 3Com made them in the United States, which was becoming unusual even in the 1990s. I once worked in a shop that didn’t allow network equipment unless it was one of three brands. 3Com was one of them, along with Cisco and Intel. If you plugged a no name NE2000 clone card into the network and had problems, the IT department would replace the card and bill your department. There was a saying in the 1980s that no one got fired for buying IBM. When it came to networking, one could say the same for 3Com, during their prime. And they were huge. In 1995, 3Com bought the naming rights to Candlestick Park, the legendary baseball/football stadium in San Francisco. It held those rights until 2002. How 3Com’s long decline happened Walking away from the profitable network switch business is a key reason why 3Com failed. It ceded market share to Cisco and reversing the mistake cost the company much needed capital. But after the dotcom bust, 3Com faded away. What happened to 3Com, ultimately, was a series of bad decisions that led to a loss of profitability. Some of them may have made sense at the time. But not all of them. The first thing that happened was 3Com walked away from its enterprise networking equipment business. Admittedly Cisco was hard to compete with. But 3Com was the only brand succeeding at doing it. The logic behind the move always puzzled analysts, because it didn’t save any money. Revenue dropped, and 3Com angered its customers and dealers. It’s likely many started buying Intel cards afterward, since they had to change vendors anyway. Many corporations like to buy multiple things from a single supplier. This was one reason IBM stayed in the PC business for several years into the 21st century even though they were losing money on it. The computers weren’t profitable, but they made it easier to sell services, and the services were profitable. There is always the fear that two vendors will point fingers at each other, saying the network problem was caused by the hub and the network card being mismatched brands. Interoperability was the whole idea behind Ethernet, but not everyone understood that. One could commend 3Com for not wanting to exploit that misunderstanding. But it came at a financial cost. It also didn’t help that the company branched into other businesses outside its core. The purchase of US Robotics was a key example. US Robotics made modems and Palm Pilots . For a short time, that was big business. But 3Com paid a premium price for products with a limited shelf life left in them. Nothing good happened to 3Com after that. It took 3 years for Cisco to go from being 90% the size of 3Com to double the size of 3Com. The profitability of selling network adapters dropped. And by the time 3Com realized they needed to get back into network equipment, it was an expensive proposition. From 2000 to 2005, the company didn’t turn a profit. Why 3Com failed 3Com bought naming rights to Candlestick Park in 1995. By 2002 when the naming rights expired, 3Com was past its prime and no longer turning a profit. Ultimately, 3Com failed because it was too dependent on network cards. Network cards accounted for about half their revenue during their bust years. And their cards were expensive. Intel undercut their price to try to gain market share, and they succeeded. And then they did exactly the wrong thing. It was the late ’90s, and they bought their way into the modem business. The dial-up modem business. At that point in time, everyone knew broadband was the future, they just didn’t know exactly when it was going to arrive. Yet 3Com had no plan to get into that business. It was like betting on AOL even though they were in the position to know the future belonged to AT&T . Making matters worse, minimum viable product-style modems undercut US Robotics modems, just like the network card business. Not that Intel cards were a minimum viable product. But pretty much any ’90s network card not made by Intel or 3Com was. 3Com sought partnerships, most notably a partnership with Chinese networking giant Huawei. There were even rumors of Huawei buying 3com, though that deal never went through. And 3Com started making product overseas as a cost reducing measure. But ultimately, nothing could make up for all that lost time and all those bad decisions. Who bought 3com So what happened to 3Com? 3Com didn’t go out of business and they didn’t sell out to Huawei. They got Compaqed . Hewlett-Packard bought them out, which seems to be where every great ’90s technology company went to die. Hewlett-Packard paid 2.7 billion dollars in late 2009 for 3Com’s assets. HP still sells network equipment like switches, routers, and access points. But they’re not as big of a name in networking as 3Com had been. And the 3Com pedigree isn’t the selling point. If they put a brand on it other than HP, it’s the newer Aruba brand, not 3Com. The selling point is the price being lower than Cisco. This makes them attractive to executives or purchasing agents looking to cut costs, consolidate vendors, or both. HP will usually beat Cisco’s price. And if the IT department is under pressure to reduce the number of vendors it buys from, HP sells more things than Cisco. So HP gets in the door for one of those reasons, and when their network equipment turns out to be no worse than Cisco equipment, they stay with it. At least until Dell comes around offering discounts. But the network cards are long gone. When you buy an HP branded network card today, guess what it is? It’s an Intel card with HP’s logo engraved on it. Unless HP is trying to control costs, in which case it just has a sticker. 3Com today Vintage 3Com network cards are very popular with retro computing enthusiasts. It had top-tier name recognition in the 80s and 90s. All but their very earliest cards generally have good driver support, work well, and are easier to configure than most of the cheaper competitors. My favorite retro network card is a very specific Intel card , but if you need a card for anything from the 286 to the Pentium II era, you can do far worse than a 3com 3c509 ISA card or 3c905 PCI card. It’s absolutely period correct and absolutely something a knowledgeable professional would have used at the time. I have better luck with the ISA cards under DOS than the PCI cards, so if I want to run DOS and do any networking, I use a 3c509 ISA card in the system. But for Windows 95 and newer, the 3c905 PCI card works really well and is very cheap and common. If you found this post informative or helpful, please share it! share   share   save     share   share     share     pocket   share   email   RSS feed   Dave Farquhar David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000. Like this: Like Loading… Related stories by Dave Farquhar ← Microsoft Windows first announced Nov 10, 1983 Ira Velinsky, industrial designer for Commodore and Atari → 2 thoughts on “ What happened to 3Com? ” garyohuk November 12, 2025 at 6:41 am Permalink The 3C509 is something I remember, we swapped from WD cards to 3Com when they became a ‘thing’. I also remember visiting their place at Bayfront in the valley a few times, as ultimately Apricot repackaged 3C cards, quite openly as, echoing what you say, people like a one-stop-shop. The other nail in the coffin was the invention by Microsoft of the Network Device Interface Specification (NDIS) which meant that any network stack could talk to any card as long as they had a working NDIS driver. This removed the stickiness of finely tuned stack software, which previously had entirely proprietary interfaces. The final nail was the incorporation of ethernet silicon in the main processor silicon, all you needed then was a physical circuit and job done. Reply David December 8, 2025 at 9:56 pm Permalink The best network card in the 90’s wasn’t 3Com or Intel… It was DEC’s Tulip chipset. Able to have multiple MAC addresses simultaneously, it was the go-to for those who needed to run VRRP and other network HA methods. The chipset licensed to 3rd parties, in particular I remember buying a ton of Linksys LNE100TX cards based on it, which were rock solid. I see plenty on ebay. 0:00 / 0:00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator - Blog blog Blog Blog Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator - Blog All posts / Model Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator The Antigravity Team Â· Nov 12, 2026 Â· 3 min read Share Copy link Share on X Share on Bluesky Share on LinkedIn Share Today, weâre rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency. Selecting Orchestrator (Carbon) from the model selector in Google Antigravity. Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems. For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static âmodel routerâ that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves. Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together.
