You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead. AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. See Security in AWS Emulator . Documentation: AWS Emulator User Guide Quick start With an AI coding agent Install the aws-emulator skill, then ask your agent to set up the emulator. This needs the AWS CLI version 2.35.0 or later. See Getting started with an AI coding agent . aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1 Server mode (CLI and any SDK) Linux: install the RPM or Debian package and run aws-emulator . See Getting started on Linux . Windows / macOS: run the emulator in a container built from a short Dockerfile. See Getting started with Docker . Point your SDK at a running emulator by setting environment variables. See Pointing your AWS SDK at AWS Emulator . Embedded mode (Rust tests) Add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test. There is no endpoint URL, certificate, or environment variable to set. Your test wires the emulator's HTTP client straight into the SDK client. See Getting started with embedded mode , and Building from source below for its build cost. Known issues To see how closely each service matches AWS, check the fidelity scores published with each release on the releases page . To check whether your own project is expected to work, see Checking whether your project works with AWS Emulator . Individual gaps are tracked in the repository's issues/ directory. APIs and behaviors that don't work yet are under issues/things-that-do-not-work/ , and ones that have since been fixed move to issues/things-that-now-work/ . Building from source You need this if you are modifying the emulator, running it from a checkout, or using embedded mode. Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so the prerequisites and build-cost guidance below apply to it too. Most other users install a prebuilt package instead (see Quick start ). Building from source is supported on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64) ; on Windows and macOS, use the Docker path above. Prerequisites A Rust toolchain with Cargo (install via rustup ). A C compiler, such as GCC or clang. Some dependencies build C code. At least 100 GB of free disk for target/ . The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added. A multi-core machine. A cold full build compiles every service crate, so the first build takes a while; fewer cores take proportionally longer. After that, rebuilding after a change to one service is much faster. Build and run cargo build -p aws-emulator-router cargo run -p aws-emulator-router The emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 (self-signed certificate). Embedded mode build cost Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so your project's first cargo test builds the emulator's service crates alongside your own code. Budget a first build and target/ on the same order as building from source above, then fast incremental builds. Recommendation: reuse one CARGO_TARGET_DIR across projects, cache target/ (or use sccache) in CI, and pin the emulator to a release commit so it isn't rebuilt on every change. Repository layout . ├── Cargo.toml # workspace: one member per service, plus the core crates ├── services/ │ └── service-<name>/ # ONE CRATE PER SERVICE │ ├── smithy-model/ # <name>.json — the Smithy model that drives the wire protocol │ ├── build.rs # generates the service declaration from the model │ ├── src/ │ │ ├── service.rs # request routing and refusal overrides │ │ ├── state.rs # this service's in-memory state │ │ └── ops/ # one file per operation │ └── tests/ ├── core/ │ ├── router/ # the emulator binary: mounts every service on one endpoint │ └── embedded/ # the in-process (embedded mode) facade ├── vendor/ # framework crates — do not edit (replaced on update) └── issues/ # tracked fidelity issues Telemetry AWS Emulator is configured to collect and report usage data to AWS, to gain insight into how AWS Emulator is used. Telemetry is on by default. AWS Emulator collects telemetry data with strict data minimization in mind, preventing identification or attribution to specific users, accounts, or organizations. Its records never include what’s in your requests or responses, your code, your credentials, or personal data. We don’t share telemetry with third parties. For details on what is collected and how the data is handled, see Telemetry in AWS Emulator . To turn telemetry off, use one of the following options. Use a command-line option Start the emulator with the --telemetry option (short form -t ) set to off . This setting applies only to that emulator process. aws-emulator --telemetry off In a container, add --telemetry off after the image name in the docker run command. Use an environment variable Set EMULATOR_TELEMETRY to off before you start the emulator. This setting applies to every emulator that you start from that shell. EMULATOR_TELEMETRY accepts on , true , or 1 to turn telemetry on, and off , false , or 0 to turn it off. Values aren’t case sensitive. Any other value turns telemetry off, and the startup notice shows a warning. export EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off aws-emulator Use a configuration file To turn telemetry off for every run on a machine, add these lines to the emulator settings file, config.toml . The file is ~/.aws/emulator/config.toml on Linux and macOS, and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\emulator\config.toml on Windows. To use a different file, set the EMULATOR_CONFIG environment variable to its path. [ telemetry ] enabled = false Use the embedded configuration API In embedded mode, turn off telemetry in the options that you pass when you create the emulator. use aws_emulator_embedded :: { AwsEmulatorEmbedded , EmbeddedOptions , Telemetry } ; fn main ( ) { let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded :: new ( EmbeddedOptions :: default ( ) . telemetry ( Telemetry :: Off ) ) ; let _http_client = emulator . http_client ( ) ; } You might build a tool that includes the emulator, such as a test framework that other people run. If you do, tell your users about telemetry and give them a way to turn it off. You can also ship your tool with telemetry off. Reporting issues and contributing Report bugs and fidelity gaps in GitHub Issues . The most useful report names the service, the operation, your SDK and version, the request you sent, and how the response differed from real AWS. This repository does not take PRs. title: Our software engineering interviews are changing a little
body_text: Jane Street Blog - Our software engineering interviews are changing (a little) Home All Posts Machine Learning Authors Index Jane Street Subscribe to email updates Subscribe to Email Updates Featured Reads Read more Using ASCII waveforms to test hardware designs Read more Finding memory leaks with Memtrace Tags async book c camlp4 code-review comments compiler core hackerschool hg incremental internship interviewing machine-learning ocaml parallel-programming performance ppx real-world-ocaml registers speed ui Get the RSS feed Jane Street Open Source Join Our Team Our software engineering interviews are changing (a little) Nov 02, 2026 | 3 min read Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn By: Matthew Saffer Over the last few years, LLMs have changed how software gets built and that’s no different for us at Jane Street. Most of our engineers now use them every day not only for writing code, but also for reading, debugging, and reviewing code, and plenty of things that aren’t code at all. We’ve talked about this recently in a podcast on how we use AI in our development , and in a post on formal methods that touches on how agentic coding is reshaping the way we work. Our coding interviews haven’t changed, though. The questions we ask software engineers today are the same style of question we’ve been asking for years: sit down with an interviewer or two, program through a problem together, and talk as you go. That style has served us well and the key goals remain the same: we want to see how you solve problems, structure your work, communicate, and collaborate in the pursuit of excellent software development. But the shape of the job has evolved, and we think our interviews should evolve, too. As generating code has become arguably cheaper than ever, other parts of the job have come to matter even more: taste about what to build, choosing abstractions that last, and making sure what got built is actually correct, among other things. So this summer we started trialing some new kinds of interviews in our onsites for campus candidates. Broadly, they involve less code-writing, and lean more higher-level, focusing on software design, on verifying the quality, structure, and intention of code, and on using LLMs to produce code. Most rounds will continue to be traditional coding interviews, conducted without LLM assistance. We know this sounds vague, but that’s intentional: the formats are still evolving, and we’d rather not describe something in detail today that looks different in six months. A few things worth knowing: Not every onsite includes these new rounds yet, and when you come on-site we’ll give you a heads-up about what to expect. The rest of our process is unchanged. If you’ve read our earlier posts about interviewing here , they’re still accurate. While we find LLMs incredibly valuable as part of our daily work, we also recognize that not everyone has deep experience working with them. You shouldn’t feel like you need to have a highly worked out methodology for working with agents in order to do well in our process. In the end, we’re looking for people with great instincts for building software, and we don’t feel like we need an LLM to evaluate that. Different folks have integrated LLMs into their workflows in different ways and to different degrees, and we don’t expect you to have a particular setup or to use them for everything. What we care about is that you think clearly about the tools you use: what they’re good at, where they fall short, and when to reach for something else. As has been the case for some time, our more experienced candidates’ interviews will continue to be more varied, featuring a range of interview styles, from producing software to designing systems and discussing prior work. As always, we’ll keep iterating, and we’ll write more when there’s more to say. If you’re interested in working with us, apply on our website !
